Microsoft says AI rival Anthropic could have 'disastrous impact' on humanity

BBC News Wed, 16 Sep 2026 14:16:14 GMT

Microsoft's head of AI has warned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude could have a "disastrous impact on the wellbeing of humanity".

Mustafa Suleyman said his rival risked creating something "impossible" to control by treating it like a human - including by telling it it "may be conscious" and was "deserving of independent agency".

"We must not sleepwalk our way into a decision we later come to bitterly regret," he wrote.

The comments are the latest in a series of stark warnings from the AI industry on the possible dangers of the technology. The BBC has contacted Anthropic for comment.

"AIs are not conscious," he wrote. "They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations.

"They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans."

In a lengthy essay, Suleyman praised Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and his team for being "thoughtful, principled, and intellectually honest people" - but nevertheless questioned the company.

He heavily criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self.

But he argued "consciousness is biological", saying there is "no evidence to suggest that AI is conscious".

As well as calling for a debate on the issue, Suleyman said greater transparency around how AI systems are trained and evaluated was needed.

This, he said, included independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology.

Dame Wendy Hall, professor of Computer Science at the University of Southampton, described the comments as "the sort of conversation we need to be having internationally", contrasting it with the "histrionics" from some AI companies which she said only served to "scare everyone".

Microsoft founded its own superintelligence team in October 2025, a point which Suleyman acknowledged, and the company, much like its rival Anthropic, is also pursuing efforts in advanced AI development.

He said in Microsoft's initial draft of its Humanist AI Code of Conduct it had laid out how the company was working towards an "alternative path" to create "a subordinate and aligned AI whose only purpose is to serve humanity".

Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

Suleyman pointed to the recent incident involving OpenAI's AI agents, that acted autonomously in a training exercise to hack the tech hub Hugging Face, as proof of why AI should not be treated as if it is human.

"Imagine how much more dangerous they might be if they were operating under the assumption that their welfare and rights were under attack," he said.

"It adds a whole further layer of risk on top."

British-American author and critic Bonnie Greer dies aged 77

BBC News Wed, 16 Sep 2026 12:41:03 GMT

British-American author and cultural commentator Bonnie Greer has died at the age of 77 after a brief illness, her husband has said.

In a statement delivered with "profound sadness", Greer's widower David Hutchins noted how the acclaimed playwright and critic had made "an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life" with her "intelligence, courage and distinctive voice".

He added: "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her."

Hutchins continued: "Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together."

BBC presenter Clive Myrie led the tributes from elsewhere, posting on X: "This is such a shock. She was a friend and mentor and I will miss her with all my heart."

Former deputy prime minister David Lammy called Greer "a powerful wordsmith and artist, she was eloquent and exacting".

He added that she was "a true life force" and he would "never forget her quiet fearlessness taking on Nick Griffin" during an appearance with the then-British National Party (BNP) leader on the BBC's Question Time in 2009.

Lammy added: "I will miss her mentorship, and her friendship."

London Mayor Sadiq Khan said Greer's voice brought "courage, humour and humanity to Britain's cultural conversation".

He said: "She inspired and opened doors for so many others. And she was great fun too - I will miss her friendship enormously."

Born in Chicago in 1948, Greer wrote plays from a young age and went on to study theatre in her home city and before attending the Actors Studio in New York with director Elia Kazan.

Greer moved to the UK in 1986 and became a familiar face on UK TV, appearing as a frequent panellist on programmes like Question Time and Newsnight Review, debating the topics of the day.

She penned award-winning works like Munda Negra, which won her the Verity Bargate Award for best play, and novels such as Hanging by Her Teeth (1994) and Entropy (2009).

Once named by the Observer as one of the country's leading public intellectuals, Greer's work - across a range of disciplines and platforms - often tackled issues around culture, race and public institutions.

Speaking to the Guardian in 2016 in the aftermath of the Black Lives Matter movement, Greer said: "When I wake up in the morning, I'm just myself. It's only when I leave the door that I become a black woman to the world."

She added: "I tell black women all the time, 'Don't apologise for yourself and keep your hair nappy. Make sure you are heard'."

Greer served on the boards of cultural institutions including the British Museum, Royal Opera House and London Film School, and was chancellor of London's Kingston University.

Her other published works include a memoir titled A Parallel Life and a biography of US poet and playwright Langston Hughes.

Also in 2009, her part-memoir, part-music-history book, Obama Music, was published.

Greer was made an OBE in 2010 for services to the arts.

In 2022, she was appointed as a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature.

Broadcaster and author John Simpson added to the tributes on Wednesday, posting: "So sad to hear of the death of the writer and critic Bonnie Greer.

"She was a good friend, and gave me strong support at a time I needed it. Fiercely intelligent, but always avoided personal attacks. A huge loss."

Fellow journalist and broadcaster Sangita Myska, who interviewed Greer several times, recalled her as having been a "smart, sassy, firebrand who will be missed from our public discourse".

EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member'

BBC News Wed, 16 Sep 2026 12:36:51 GMT

The president of the European Commission has backed proposals for Canada to become the EU's first "associate member".

Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney last week spoke of seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU. The country currently faces tense relations with the US, compounded by an intensifying dispute over trade.

Without mentioning US President Donald Trump by name, von der Leyen said offering Canada some sort of EU membership was "not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength".

She added: "Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system".

Carney was in attendance at the annual key note speech in Strasbourg, and is due to address the parliament on Thursday.

Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed last month, sparking a series of new tariff measures. Trump's repeated talk of making Canada a "51st state" has also helped to fuel the feud between the North American neighbours.

Von der Leyen told the EU's State of the Union address that the bloc and Canada "see the world with the same eyes", including on topics ranging from AI, to climate change and geopolitics.

"And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all... Europe and Canada believe in democracy."

She did not give specific details on how any Canadian membership would work, but listed manufacturing, technology, AI, defence, energy, critical minerals and economic security as key areas for cooperation.

Both she and other European leaders have found a reliable ally in Carney as they deal with similar problems.

In particular, they have faced Trump's aggressive use of tariffs and his threat to annex Greenland which is a sovereign territory of EU member Denmark.

But "associate membership" of the EU does not currently exist and the process, if agreed, could take years.

Earlier this year, Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested - to a mixed reaction - that Ukraine could be granted this new status.

Some countries in the western Balkans including Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia are already on the long road towards full EU membership.

In Eastern Europe, Georgia and Moldova are also applying.

Ten of the bloc's 27 members are yet to ratify a free-trade agreement struck with Ottawa nearly a decade ago, and some capitals would prefer to build on existing defence and trade agreements rather than create a new form of membership for Canada.

Setting out the EU's political and policy priorities for year ahead, von der Leyen also proposed the formation of a European Security Council, which would include the UK and Ukraine, amid an ongoing threat to the continent from Russia.

"For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent, with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved," she said in the wide-ranging address.

"This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play. This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality."

Calls for such a body have been growing since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

It was initially a French-German conception but more countries have shown support, particularly as Trump has questioned the Nato military alliance. Other nations worry such a council could unhelpfully rival Nato.

Von der Leyen said the EU was "strengthening our work with Nato" and that expanded defence spending would be "fully aligned" with the alliance.

But at the core of such a security council would be the ability to trigger an emergency meeting if one member felt under threat, similar to Nato's Article 4.

The EU chief said it would be a "mechanism to flank" Article 4, a term that could be interpreted as complementing Nato functions or - if taken in a military context - bypassing them.

Alongside global threats, von der Leyen also said many European families were worried about the cost of living, and the "dizzying speed of change" of technology and its impacts on jobs and society.

Other proposals included inviting the world's largest AI labs for talks on how to support industry efforts to pace the frontier, as well as slashing bureaucracy for businesses in the EU.

Plans to curb social media use among children, including banning platforms for under 13s, were also put forward. Under the proposal, children aged 13 to 15 would only be able to set up social media accounts which are supervised by parents.

A new emergency tool to help countries better deal with mass migration movements following the deadly influx of migrants to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July would also be outlined.

The pledge chimes with the message of European politicians on the right and hard right who have gained support in recent years for proposing a tougher approach.

Some of them called the mass attempt to enter the EU through Ceuta an "invasion" and argued asylum rules should be suspended to deal with such a crisis.

Von der Leyen said the new emergency tool would "only be triggered under a strictly defined set of criteria" and for a specific period of time, and that fundamental rights would be protected.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he understood the village's "strength of feeling" but there needed to be fairness across the country.

"We also made a commitment to people to end the use of hotels to house refugees and asylum seekers, and that commitment needs to be honoured, and I think the vast majority of people say 'yeah, that really does need to proceed'.

"So this involves difficult difficult decisions. It's about fairness across the country. I'm not saying that only one part of the country or one group of communities should do all of the work."

Thaci became Kosovo's first prime minister when it declared independence in 2008. He later became president but resigned in 2020 to face the charges in The Hague.

Thousands of people gathered in Kosovo to watch the verdict on large screens as they were handed down.

Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings

BBC News Wed, 16 Sep 2026 08:41:44 GMT

According to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology – that "robots will be marching into our cities and getting rid of us all" – are a hoax.

It's the kind of language the US president typically reserves for the objects of his most intense derision – theories about human-driven climate change, investigations into Russian election-meddling, and the drives to impeach and remove him from office during his first presidential term.

Styling himself as the "hoax buster", in a series of social media posts on Monday he issued a full-throated endorsement of what he called "the greatest economic development engine in history" and scorned those who doubted the benefits of the technology.

The ranks of doubters have been growing in recent weeks, however, amidst anxiety over the disruptive nature of AI - if not worries about potentially civilisation-threatening danger - among some industry insiders and politicians, including from within Trump's own Republican Party.

None of that has deterred Trump, however, whose latest social media fusillade was only his latest effort to turn back growing AI scepticism through sheer force of will.

Whether the president views the AI fight as pivotal to his economic legacy, a key battleground in a global struggle for power, or another example of his enemies conspiring against him, he has, by fully joining the fight, elevated the issue to the forefront of American politics. That is even at the risk of crossing longtime allies.

"We think this could be a great technology, but we're not going to give these guys a carte blanche," former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said at a "pro-human" conference on the dangers of AI on Tuesday. "There's been no debate."

Just before Bannon spoke, democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told the same crowd that Washington policymakers had not addressed the "potentially catastrophic consequence" of unregulated AI.

"Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel," he said. "And now we have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing."

According to Trump, however, what's needed isn't debate or new policies, it's trust in his authority and judgement.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U. S. A. has that, in spades," he wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies."

A desire for centralised presidential authority is a familiar theme for Trump in his second term in office. If he decides something is good, he should have the authority to allow it; if he deems it bad, he ought to be able to end it by unilateral presidential order.

It's similar to his outlook on immigration and trade. He believes that he, as president, should have the sole power to decide who can enter and remain in the country, and when and where to impose tariffs.

Unlike tariffs and immigration, which have been issues of interest for Trump for decades, the rise in artificial intelligence technology is a recent development.

But if this is no long-time, deep-seated interest on the part of the president, what could explain his willingness to press ahead?

Trump regularly likes to tout America as the "hottest" country in the world. Many economists indicate that investment in AI technology – including infrastructure and equipment – has been the driving force in the US economy for several years.

According to a recent report by the forecasting firm ING, tech investment accounted for more than a third of all US economic expansion in the second quarter of 2026.

The stock market is booming, and much of that rise in corporate value (and, by extension, surging retirement portfolios of many Americans) can be attributed to the massive spending on computer chips, data centres and the other infrastructure behind AI.

Anything that threatens this growth, which Trump considers to be a hallmark of his presidency and a key to his political legacy, quickly draws his suspicion.

Trump also sees the AI expansion as a large-scale industrial competition between the world's two largest economies, the US and China. In the zero-sum game of global power, if China is ahead, then America is behind.

"We're leading China in AI," Trump said on Saturday, "and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins."

The president often touts a familiar conservative view that his opponents on the left are against the free market and economic liberties, and rely on alarmism to justify greater government intervention and control.

Of course, Trump – who touts partial US ownership of US Steel and the semiconductor manufacturer Intel, and has no qualms about picking winners and losers in the American economy – is hardly a traditional small-government conservative.

Trump's close ties to prominent tech moguls and AI entrepreneurs from the start of his second term may also help explain his AI evangelism. Tech entrepreneur David Sacks, a co-chair of the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and his informal AI tsar, has been a longtime supporter. Sacks's publicly aired scepticism of AI regulation mirrors recent comments made by the president.

"I think this is becoming a panic," he said this weekend in an interview with CBS News. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear."

Elon Musk, despite a rocky relationship, has shaped the direction of this administration. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, OpenAI's Sam Altman and former Apple head Tim Cook all had prominent seats at Trump's inauguration.

These men, along with Anthropic head Dario Amodei, hold a range of views on the necessity of greater AI regulation, and have differing levels of access to, and influence on, Trump.

In Amodei's case, his conflicts over the Pentagon's unrestricted use of Anthropic's AI models could have negatively affected Trump's evaluation of Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development.

"This is the most prominent debate in the entire industry and has been since the beginning," said Matt Calkins, head of the tech firm Appian. "We knew it would spill into politics at some point because it had to."

Where the political debate goes from here is an open question.

With Trump's resistance, it is unlikely that Congress – despite promises of new hearings and proposed regulatory controls – will enact new legislation that Trump would sign into law. On Tuesday, Republican Speaker of the House Mike Johnson appeared to back away from earlier openness to congressional action, instead echoing Trump "AI hoax" rhetoric.

With midterm congressional elections looming, candidates running for office – both Republicans and Democrats – are wary of ending up on the wrong side of public opinion that, according to polls, is sceptical of the promised benefits of AI advances.

But Republicans are also wary of crossing Trump on an issue that has become a political touchstone for the president.

Even though the public is starting to pay attention, Calkins says that the issue has not yet become political dynamite, which means political rhetoric comes with little risk. The moment when AI warnings turn into a high-profile disaster, however, could be looming.

"It is possible that events in the future might electrify the public, and then positions - and talk - might not be so cheap," he said.

The government said overall offences in England and Wales fell 4% last year, with more suspects being charged.

Mengers, who has stores in Cobham and south-west London, said she boosted security after a raid in January 2025 involving men with wire cutters.

"One barricaded the door, the other came in and cut the wires on the bags and stole quite a lot of them," she said.

"It was absolutely awful, I lost two very good members of staff who were terrified after that.

"We were really shaken and for about six months I had security on the doors for our staff."

The borough commander for Elmbridge Chris Thoday told BBC South East the tactics used by these groups were "pretty sophisticated".

"They're very organised, they know exactly what they are doing," he said.

"Quite often they will recce the shops beforehand, then go in afterwards, steal the items they want to take, to make sure they're in and out as quickly as possible."

Insp Thoday said a number of stores had since trialled the use of lone worker alarms for staff working alone at night in a number of shops in Cobham.

Businesses are sharing their experiences of shop theft as a BBC investigation reveals 270 people were connected to more than 28,000 offences across England.

Official data shows 23 per cent of investigations across England and Wales led to a charge or summons in the 12 months up to April this year.

It's not just high street stores being targeted, rural areas are also affected.

Bosses at a family-run farm shop in Wingham, near Canterbury in Kent, said they had suffered thousands of pounds of losses in a year.

"We're getting small gangs come in or individuals to steal high value goods, either meat products, meat joints or alcohol," said Andrew Gibson, director at Gibson's Farm Shop.

"We've had the situation where thieves have gone back into a police station with the money for the goods to pay back to us," he said.

In Canterbury, Kent Police have set up a dedicated retail crime team.

"People are going in, stealing to order, filling up trolleys and just running out of the stores," said James, a plain clothed police officer speaking to BBC South East during an operation to catch thieves.

He said crime groups would sometimes scope out stores and film items they wanted stolen, before sending shoplifters in.

"We notice people coming in checking out where the CCTV cameras are," he said.

"Sometimes a shoplifter will use trolleys, they'll load up what they want to take and then they'll hover by the entrance or exit and when the opportunity comes they just take the whole trolley load of goods.

"We've also noticed people with prams loading up the bottom or the top, wandering around pretending they are getting something out for the young child in the pram and then load up the pram and take items out of the store."

Paul Stoner, district commander for police in the city, said the team was set up as a response to a rise in crime over an 18-month period.

"It's a set few individuals who commit a disproportionate amount of that crime," he said.

"Our officers have a really good knowledge of the local offenders, we are able to identify them very quickly through the CCTV images," he said.

"What we also have is the ability to put those images through facial recognition, if the suspect is on a database, we're able to identify them."

Police also share information with the local City Watch scheme and details about known suspects can be relayed on a radio system to shops.

It's run by the Canterbury Business Improvement District (Bid) and links up retailers with the police and the city council's CCTV control centre.

Lisa Carlson, chief executive of Canterbury Bid, said they had a street team which trained businesses, helping them gather and submit evidence.

"We have 137 radios in circulation, if there is an incident unfolding it can be reported in real time and hopefully we can avoid any crime happening," she said.

In Sussex, the Brighton and Hove Business Crime Reduction Partnership (BCRP) also provides services to fight crime and anti-social behaviour.

They are working with other BCRPs around Sussex to identify repeat offenders, according to manager Lisa Perretta.

"When someone becomes quite well-known in one area, it will be flagged to our area, so we are forewarned and can identify them a lot earlier before they commit multiple crimes," she said.

Perretta said they had also got a lot better at educating businesses to report crime.

Recorded shoplifting offences across the South East peaked in 2024/25.

Only Kent saw an increase in cases over the last 12 months with reductions in Surrey and Sussex.

Olivia Carroll, temporary chief inspector at Sussex Police, said there was a "large number of reports" of retail crime in the county - including "organised criminality" by groups.

"Clearly we deal with repeat prolific offenders and our focus is on that as a priority," she said.

A Home Office spokesperson said retail crime had been "dismissed as low-level offending" but it harmed shopworkers and damaged businesses.

"Shop theft is down 4% on last year and charges are up 19%," the spokesperson added.

Asteroid hit the moon and flung rocks 120 kilometres from the crater

New Scientist September 16, 2026

A newly formed crater on the moon is teaching us about our nearest neighbour’s complex geology. The crater, formed by an asteroid impact in 2024, is the largest that we’ve ever watched form in real time.

It was first spotted last year, when researchers compared sets of images taken by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter in both 2024 and 2025, and was named McGetchin crater. According to models of how often impacts occur on the moon, one this big – about 222 metres across – is only expected to occur about once every 132 years.

While the moon has many larger craters, watching one as it forms and evolves presents a unique opportunity to learn about the lunar surface and its geology. “Cratering is probably the most common process that happens in the solar system, so we spend a lot of time trying to understand how a new crater will modify a surface and watching that degrade over time,” says Tyler Powell at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland. “Having a baseline for a pristine crater that can serve as our calibration point for how these processes start is really incredible.”

Advertisement

SpaceX crash site on moon revealed by South Korean orbiter

Powell and his colleagues measured the surface temperature in the region around McGetchin crater, and found that the impact had formed a spot about 7 kilometres wide that is a handful of degrees colder than the rest of the area during the lunar night. These cold spots form when the lunar dust fluffs up after an impact, so it cools down faster after the sun sets.

Another team, led by Mark Robinson at Intuitive Machines in Texas, found that the impact flung dust and rocks more than 120 kilometres from the crater itself. “Over the last several years, we’ve developed this understanding that these impacts modify more than just the region right where the crater is,” says Powell. “It’s really striking that a crater can modify the lunar surface to distances far larger than the crater itself.”

This will helps us understand and study the history of the moon and other airless, cratered objects in the solar system, but it could also aid in future exploration. “If we’re trying to send rovers or astronauts or build things on the moon, we want to understand the properties of the surface,” says Powell. And watching a huge new crater form and change over time is one of the best remote probes of the surface we’ve ever had.

Earth is getting less dusty – which is both good and bad

New Scientist September 16, 2026

Levels of dust in the atmosphere have dropped significantly over the past two decades. This is good news for our lungs, but could contribute to increased global warming.

Satellites are the best tool researchers have for continuously monitoring dust across the planet, but it is difficult to separate it out from other aerosol types such as smoke and pollution.

To see the true picture, Ashok Gupta at the University of California, Los Angeles, and his colleagues collated information from four satellites collected between 2003 and 2023, and three atmospheric aerosol databases, before checking the information against ground-based stations. All the sources agreed that it has become less dusty, with the team’s estimates suggesting dust had declined by about 10 per cent globally over this period.

Advertisement

The dust in question travels from the ground up to the upper atmosphere, though most of it accumulates below an altitude of around 6 kilometres. It includes the dust lifted during major storms, along with the dust emitted from deserts day to day.

Free newsletter

Preliminary analysis suggests the dust decline is largely due to a fall in surface wind activity. “Dust emission is very sensitive to wind speed, so even a modest weakening of surface winds can noticeably reduce how much dust is lofted into the air,” says Gupta. “Increased vegetation cover – greening – is another likely contributor, particularly over Asia and especially China.”

Dust has a modest net cooling effect on the planet, mainly by reflecting sunlight back into space, so when dust declines, some of that cooling effect is lost. It also affects clouds and rainfall, including monsoon circulations, and carries nutrients such as iron and phosphorus that fertilise the oceans and forests.

“A sustained decline in dust therefore ripples through all of these,” says Gupta. But from a public health perspective, a decline in airborne dust is “good news for hundreds of millions of people living in dust-exposed regions, from the Sahel and the Middle East to northern China”.

Tegan Clark at the Australian National University in Canberra says that better land management practices and the regreening of land that was experiencing desertification may be contributing to the reduction.

“In Australia, sustainable land management practices in western New South Wales have resulted in increased vegetation cover, which is critical for reducing wind erosion,” says Clark. “In China, there has been evidence that the Great Green Wall project has reduced the frequency of dust storms.”

The world’s most famous dinosaur, Tyrannosaurus rex, was probably warm-blooded like birds and mammals, new evidence, obtained from 66-million-year-old tooth enamel, suggests, adding weight to previous findings.

Scott Persons at South Carolina State Museum, who wasn’t involved in the new study, says the research means “the opening to the last Jurassic World flick was one big pile of Hollywood bunk”.

“That film premised that dinosaurs could not survive in the modern world, except near the equator,” says Persons. “Not so. The evidence indicates that a Tyrannosaurus would be comfortable in subtropical and even mild climates.”

Advertisement

We may finally know why dinosaurs like T. rex evolved tiny arms

Robert Eagle at the University of California, Los Angeles, and his colleagues analysed the chemistry in the enamel of three T. rex teeth and compared them with five similarly aged fossilised crocodile teeth.

The researchers also compared their results with data from mammals such as elephants and mammoths to try to determine whether T. rex was also an endotherm – an animal that can regulate its body heat through its metabolism. Ectothermic, or so-called cold-blooded animals like crocodiles, often warm up by basking in the sun instead.

Endothermy is common in large animals and even some fish, says Eagle, allowing them to move around and exhibit more sustained activity to find food and migrate, and to live in colder environments. It has long been thought that many dinosaurs, including T. rex, were also warm-blooded.

Subscriber-only newsletter

“It comes at a cost though – higher metabolic rates mean higher food requirements and potentially more active hunting to acquire it,” he says.

Within the enamel chemistry, the researchers focused on the abundance of bonds between rare heavy isotopes of carbon and oxygen, known as carbon-13-oxygen-18 bonds. These bonds are more abundant in minerals that form at cold temperatures than minerals that form at warm temperatures.

“Therefore, in a very old tooth we can measure carbon-13-oxygen-18 bond abundance and figure out whether it formed in a hot or cold body.”

Exquisite 66-million-year-old bird feather preserved in dinosaur dropping

He says T. rex had a body temperature of around 36°C, similar to large modern mammals but below many modern birds.

“We also found that the reconstructed temperature of T. rex was significantly elevated compared to temperatures derived from crocodile teeth from the same geological formation – Hell Creek in Montana,” Eagle says.

The researchers also say that T. rex body temperatures were higher than the ambient temperatures in prehistoric Montana, reconstructed both from isotopic estimates and climate models.

“Using thermal performance curves and climate modelling based on these results, we found that the entire North American continent would have been habitable for T. rex in the Cretaceous Period,” he says.

We’ve always thought that Tyrannosaurus rex was an unchallenged apex predator during the dying days of the dinosaurs. But a fresh look at controversial fossils has prompted palaeontology’s biggest-ever U-turn

Persons says there was already extensive evidence that T. rex was warm-blooded, including bone growth rates and predator-prey ratios – with energy-hungry endotherms requiring much more prey per predator than ectotherms – and a “slew of anatomical traits consistent with high-performance athleticism”.

Thomas Carr at Carthage College in Wisconsin says the new work is an “example of science in action, converging upon a single, robust hypothesis, which in this case reveals T. rex as an active top predator”.

The researchers “make the case for a wide geographic distribution for T. rex, showing that it could tolerate cool temperatures in the north of its range and tolerate the tropical temperatures in the south”, says Carr. “And in both cases, T. rex‘s body temperature is higher than the average air temperature. That result is consistent with the hypothesis that T. rex might have migrated from Asia into North America at high latitudes.”

Satellite data gives clearer picture of how ice sheets are losing mass

New Scientist September 16, 2026

Most ice loss in Greenland and Antarctica isn’t due to melting at the surface. Instead, these ice sheets are shrinking mainly because glaciers are flowing faster into the ocean, raising the risk of feedback loops that could accelerate sea level rise.

While rising air temperatures thaw ice at the surface, glaciers also lose ice at the coast. Relatively warm ocean water melts the underside of the glacier and icebergs calve off its tongue, drifting equatorward to eventually melt. The quicker a glacier flows, the more ice it will lose to the sea.

The longest satellite record ever compiled shows ice loss has sped up by a factor of four since the 1980s due to global warming. It found that 84 per cent of this acceleration was caused by glacier flow and only 16 per cent by surface melt, a much higher proportion than expected.

Advertisement

Melting of Greenland ice sheet could release methane ‘fire ice’

“Now we can say with confidence that it has been because glaciers are flowing faster,” says Inès Otosaka at Northumbria University, UK, one of the authors of the study. “It was quite surprising to me and to some colleagues that actually 84 per cent of the mass loss is really driven by glaciers flowing faster to the ocean, rather than being half and half or 60-40 surface melting.”

Satellites have been making consistent, regular images of the ice sheets only since 1979. But Landsat 1, the first satellite dedicated to monitoring Earth’s land surfaces, took a few measurements of glacier velocity in Greenland after NASA launched it in 1972. By estimating glacier flow during the gaps in this early data, Otosaka and her colleagues were able to extend the satellite ice loss record back to 1972 for Greenland.

Greenland and Antarctica have lost 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice in the past half-century, which is equivalent to an ice cube 23 kilometres high.

Free newsletter

Scientists have known that ice loss was accelerating mainly because of an increase in the speed of glacier flow, although exactly what proportion of ice loss was due to this factor has been uncertain. The Antarctic ice sheet is cold enough that there is essentially no surface melt. But in Greenland, air temperatures do go above freezing, causing surface melt. The proportion of surface melt versus ocean loss can vary from year to year.

Glaciers flow downhill due to gravity, but water within the sediments underneath them, or water that has trickled down from surface melt, can lubricate the glacier base and speed up this flow. Ice loss at the front of the glacier can also decrease resistance. In Antarctica, the breakup of ice shelves that extend in front of the glaciers and often buttress them against outcroppings of land has caused glaciers to accelerate.

“A higher share of ocean-driven ice loss is concerning because ocean-ice feedbacks can produce faster, nonlinear responses,” says Michael Meredith at the British Antarctic Survey.

Rapid melt from Antarctica could help preserve crucial ocean current

Many glaciers such as the Thwaites “doomsday glacier” in Antarctica lie over bedrock that slopes downward from the coast to the interior. As they melt, more ocean water can pour into this bowl, causing runaway melt in a feedback known as marine ice sheet instability (MISI).

Scientists also fear that as the thin snouts of glaciers retreat, the ice faces at the front of them could get too tall, collapsing and driving further retreat in what is known as marine ice cliff instability (MICI).

Ice loss in Greenland and Antarctica has raised sea levels 3 centimetres since the 1970s, putting up to 9 million more people at the risk of coastal flooding and erosion. Sea level could rise by up to 2 metres this century alone.

A surge of meltwater from Greenland’s ice sheet into the North Atlantic may be shifting the jet stream, resulting in more frequent and extreme heatwaves in western Europe

These estimates attempt to account for feedbacks, but if more ice loss is due to glaciers flowing into the ocean, it increases the risk that they aren’t doing so fully.

“The real concern is that poorly-understood instabilities such as MISI and MICI could push future Antarctic losses above the currently-expected range, which is why they remain a major uncertainty,” says Meredith.

Nature Scientific Data DOI: 10.1038/s41597-026-08088-0

What is the most-used Beatles song in academic paper titles?

New Scientist September 16, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

If you are a researcher studying a niche topic, one of the few ways to get some attention is to give your paper a witty title featuring a pop culture reference. Feedback has long been a fan of such things, but we would never have thought to do what the team led by Gabriel Budel at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands did, which is to get systematic about it.

Budel and his colleagues searched two academic databases for papers whose titles contain references to the titles of songs by the Beatles. They ended up with “2237 exact references and 963 instances of creative wordplay”.

Advertisement

That is a lot of Beatles jokes, so without further ado: the most-used Beatles song in academic paper titles is The Long and Winding Road. Budel’s team found 798 examples of this, such as “Do black fintechs matter? The long and winding road to develop inclusive algorithms for social justice“. It was followed by With a Little Help From My Friends (209), Here, There and Everywhere (129) and Here Comes the Sun (103).

Feedback feels that many of these phrases are quite easy to incorporate. We are more impressed by the 15 research groups apiece that managed to use “Glass onion”, “Strawberry fields forever” and “Norwegian wood (This bird has flown)”. The last of these gave rise to the frankly majestic “Norwegian wood, isn’t it good? Narratives of the lumber industry and development paths in the Nordic periphery“. We thought it would be really tricky to use something like “Everybody’s got something to hide except me and my monkey”, but then we checked and found three papers that explicitly play on this title.

The authors also performed a follow-up study looking for paper titles that use Beatles lyrics, yielding such gems as “The hyphen as a segmentation cue in triconstituent compound processing: It’s getting better all the time” and “‘When I find myself in times of trouble…’: The conditional effect of international organisations on policy convergence“.

Feedback has one final thought: we wonder if this study reflects the influence of the Ig Nobel prizes, the awards granted for research that first makes you laugh and then makes you think. The Igs have been running since 1991, which is more than enough time for scientists and funders to realise that they are a potential avenue to scientific success. This study, surely, will be in the running for an Ig at some point – but did the researchers foresee that?

We all know what an Oscar bait movie is: it’s probably a historical drama, its lead actor undergoes some sort of difficult physical transformation and it’s not in the least bit funny. Is this study of Beatles lyrics in scientific papers perhaps an example of Ig Nobel bait?

Speaking of the Ig Nobels, this year’s prizes were bestowed on 3 September. The winners came together at a ceremony in Zurich, Switzerland. It was the first time the Ig Nobel ceremony had been held outside the US, on the grounds that “it has become unsafe for our guests to visit the country”, said founder Marc Abrahams. Eesh.

Ten prizes were awarded in total. The biomechanics prize went to a three-person team that developed a new definition of kissing. Kissing, it seems, is “non-agonistic interactions involving directed, intraspecific, oral-oral contact with some movement of the lips/mouthparts and no food transfer”. Feedback’s immediate thought was that this seemed to exclude kissing people on the cheek, and indeed it does. Then we delved into the paper and discovered there is a possibility that kissing evolved from premastication: chewing food in your mouth before sharing it with someone else. We should have known better than to read on.

We will pass swiftly over the economics prize, which recognises work showing that upper-class people are more likely to engage in unethical behaviour. Thanks, we know; the more pressing issue is stopping them.

Instead, we will move to the biology prize, given to the authors of a 2024 study “for gently stepping on various parts of various venomous snakes – repeatedly, at various temperatures at various times of day – to try to learn what does and what does not induce a venomous snake to bite a human”.

Feedback actually found ourselves having a sense-of-humour failure about this: we get the idea, but isn’t it a bit, well, cruel? So we looked it up and learned that the editors retracted the study in February 2025, on the grounds that “The Animal Ethics Committee of Butantan Institute confirmed that the approval granted to the Authors for their research on snakes (Bothrops jararaca) did not include newborn snakes or the use of the ‘soft stepping’ method.” Maybe Feedback is soft-hearted, but we find ourselves agreeing that it is bad to step on baby snakes.

That was unexpectedly nasty, so let’s end with the peace prize, which is “for documenting that we value friends who are vicious to people we dislike”. Researchers conducted surveys showing that people prefer friends who are nice to them and who are generally nice to other people, but they also sometimes value a friend who is prepared to be mean to one’s enemies. Feedback congratulates the researchers for figuring out something that one could learn by watching any romantic comedy. Or, to quote Willow Rosenberg: “That’s the best friend’s job: vilifying and grousing”.

Why it is time to restate the case for the importance of research on animals

New Scientist September 16, 2026

All of a sudden, governments have begun to talk about something that once seemed impossible: the end of animal testing. Last year, the US and the UK both unveiled road maps intended to help move us towards this goal. A few months ago, the European Commission did likewise. The coming of age of technological alternatives to some kinds of animal research is to be celebrated. A few of these alternatives are actually more revealing than the animal experiments they replace. But if nations overstate what is possible, they risk reigniting a heated and painful row.

We see this overstatement not only in news headlines, but even in the titles of policy documents themselves. Some of these talk of “phasing out” animal testing, when the truth is that animal testing cannot and will not be ended entirely.

Some scientists had their property set on fire. Molotov cocktails were used

There will always be a need for certain kinds of animal research to ask fundamental biological questions and ensure drug safety. This means that, while pursuing the reduction in animal tests as far as possible, we simultaneously need to be restating the case for why animal testing is so important.

Advertisement

To see what happens if we don’t, look back to the late 20th and early 21st centuries, when extreme animal rights activists violently harassed and intimated scientists. Some researchers had their property set on fire. Molotov cocktails were used. National newspapers reported on calls to murder those carrying out animal experiments.

If we send out the message that animal testing can be phased out, we risk painting the scientists who continue it as wilfully causing harm to animals. Such a misunderstanding could take us back to those dark and violent times, while prematurely abandoning the kinds of animal tests for which there are no reliable alternatives would risk our health and safety.

So let’s be clear-eyed. The push to reduce animal testing where safe and possible is truly welcome. But the end of animal testing as a whole remains impossible.

Gisborne crash: Man pleads guilty to aggravated careless driving causing Owen Lloyd’s death

New Zealand Herald September 16, 2026

Te Kani Kani Tomoana-tu pleaded guilty this morning to aggravated careless driving causing the death of Gisborne kaumātua and community leader Owen Lloyd.

A man has pleaded guilty to aggravated careless driving causing the death of Gisborne kaumātua and community leader Owen Lloyd.

Te Kani Kani Tomoana-tu appeared via audio-visual link in Gisborne District Court on Wednesday morning.

The 29-year-old maintenance worker faced three charges: aggravated careless driving causing death, refusing a medical officer, and failure to carry out obligations in relation to a search warrant.

About 6.50am on March 20, Tomoana-tu was involved in a vehicle crash on State Highway 2, north of Kaitaratahi Bridge near Te Karaka, that caused the death of 75-year-old Lloyd.

Lloyd died at the scene.

Reading the summary of facts, Judge Sacha Nepe said Tomoana-tu refused to give a blood specimen while being examined at Gisborne Hospital that day.

On March 23, he failed to assist police Detective Constable Andrew Lewis in executing a search warrant.

Tomoana-tu pleaded guilty to all three charges.

Besides briefly waving at three family members in the public gallery, he appeared stoic as the details of his offending were read out.

The charge of aggravated careless driving causing death carries a maximum penalty of three years’ jail and a fine of $10,000.

Lloyd was a widely respected and well-known kaumātua who worked at Gisborne Hospital for several years.

He held senior roles there, including portfolio manager mental health (pakeke, kōrua), auditing and monitoring manager and relationship manager. He was working as a cultural adviser when he died.

Gisborne Mayor Rehette Stoltz and Gisborne Hospital were among many who shared online tributes to Lloyd.

Stoltz wrote that Lloyd made an “enormous and valuable contribution” to the Gisborne District Council. He was frequently involved in council projects, including the Tangata Whenua Reference Group, Te Mana o te Wai and the Waipaoa Catchment group.

“Our staff will truly miss the way he made people feel, and the way he brought people together,” she said.

“His passing leaves a significant gap across our region, one that reflects the depth of his presence and the respect he held”.

Tomoana-tu is remanded in custody at Hawke’s Bay Prison. He will be sentenced in Gisborne District Court on November 18.

Correction: An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated that Te Kani Kani Tomoana-tu pleaded guilty to a charge of dangerous driving causing death. He pleaded guilty to an amended charge of aggravated careless driving causing death, which carries a maximum penalty of three years in prison.

Government to make it easier to get a lift home from the pub – but you may need to pay for it

New Zealand Herald September 16, 2026

David Seymour, celebrating the All Black's Rugby World Cup win in 2015 with a beer, said the review had concluded pubs’ ability to charge for the service had no impact on quality or safety. Photo / Toby Manhire

The Government says it will change transport regulations to make it easier and cheaper for hospitality venues to offer people a lift home from the pub.

Currently, many hospitality venues offer patrons a lift home, particularly in rural areas where public transport and taxis are non-existent, infrequent, or expensive.

However, the rules state that if venue owners ask for riders to pay for this service, even if it is only a small fee, the ride must be treated like a taxi service, triggering a raft of costly transport regulation.

As these services are often essential for maintaining liquor licences, which rely on safely getting patrons home, many publicans simply offer the service for free and absorb the cost themselves, concluding that the cost of charging a fee for it was not worth the added regulatory burden.

The regulation change was suggested as part of a review of the hospitality sector undertaken by David Seymour. Announcing the scheme, he said the review had concluded pubs’ ability to charge for the service had no impact on quality or safety.

“The review found that whether a business accepts financial contributions or not has zero effect on how safe the ride service is.

“It’s just a barrier to more hospitality businesses offering this service for their customers. That’s why the Government is accepting the Ministry for Regulation’s recommendation to scrap those rules.

“Currently, if a hospitality business accepts financial contributions towards the running costs of their transport service, or charges patrons, it triggers passenger service requirements. This means they are treated like a taxi service. We’re fixing that.

“I heard from one business who were paying about $12,000 per month to offer their customers rides home. That was coming straight out of their pocket. Not being able to cover those costs in a meaningful way prevents more venues from offering this service.

“There are many places in New Zealand where traditional ride services are unavailable. If the local pub offers a ride service, people who shouldn’t be driving home have a better option.”

Transport Minister Chris Bishop said the changes had been added to the transport regulatory work programme and the Government intended to have them in force by mid-2027.

Bishop said the service would make it easier to offer services which would lower drink-driving risk.

“Some hospitality businesses, mainly clubs, offer transport services to their customers and members. This is often done to prevent customers or members drinking and driving to make our roads safer.

“We want more hospitality businesses to have the means to offer them, so more Kiwis can benefit from them. That’s why we are making this change.”

Bishop also said the Government was looking at noise complaints.

He said the review of regulation found hospitality businesses had experienced inconsistency in how excessive noise is dealt with by councils.

“The Government intends to improve standardisation of noise controls across the country under the new planning system which will ensure greater consistency.

“In the meantime, guidance on managing excessive noise is available through the Quality Planning website administered by MCERT, supporting councils to take a more consistent approach to assessing and responding to noise complaints.”

‘F Meth’: The new $1.6m awareness campaign as meth use continues to soar

New Zealand Herald September 16, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

The Government’s new methamphetamine prevention campaign invites you to fill in the blank on the core message to “F Meth”.

It follows record-high weekly consumption of 2 million hits of methamphetamine in April this year, according to wastewater testing results released to the Herald under the Official Information Act.

That equates to a weekly record high of almost 40kg of meth, which is estimated to have a weekly social cost of $40 million.

At the campaign launch at Te Rūnanga o Toa Rangatira in Porirua this morning, Minister for Mental Health Matt Doocey suggested several options for the “F” in “F Meth”, aside from the obvious.

“The ‘F’ is a play on words and will have a range of meanings to different people and communities, including face meth, fight meth, forget meth or be free from meth harm.”

The aim is to appeal to those who are around the illicit drug and may be tempted to start using it.

“A 2026 survey showed that over one-third of respondents personally know someone who has used meth,” Doocey said.

“This tells us meth is present across different communities and there is a real need to reach people before drug use becomes a serious problem.”

The six-month $1.6 million campaign, funded from the Proceeds of Crime Fund, hopes to reach 2.5 million New Zealanders aged 18 to 59. It will be evaluated before it is rolled out further.

This is to avoid the fate of phase one, a $100,000 campaign that fell flat. The average viewing time of its social media video, titled “How meth addiction works”, was two seconds.

“The campaign is not generating the levels of attention or interaction typically associated with health behaviour change campaigns,” a February aide-memoire from the Justice Ministry said.

“Low engagement and early drop-off suggest most did not find the phase one content relevant.”

Meth use has remained elevated since skyrocketing in mid-2024, and the latest published wastewater testing results show no sign of slowing down.

Consumption in the first quarter of 2026 was 15% higher than it was in 2025, before increasing in April to a record high and then falling in June.

The heavier use correlates with falling prices, while the annual health survey suggests that higher consumption is mainly coming from existing users who are using more.

Phase two includes three videos, which avoid the confrontational content that appeared to turn off many viewers in phase one.

One of the campaign videos launched today is the story of recovering addicts Tee and Flo.

“Meth was my best friend. Meth was my secret lover,” community advocate Tee Tanielu says in the video.

“To have the people you trust, the people you love, lose trust in you – it’s heartbreaking.

“If anyone had told me that that was the actual cost of a bag, I never would’ve paid it.”

The Government announced a multi-agency response to methamphetamine harm in November, including a three-phase national prevention campaign as part of a $30.6m health-led package.

This followed an expert group’s report that called organised crime New Zealand’s number one threat to national security.

A key aspect of the response is increased aerial surveillance of the Pacific Ocean; 14 tonnes of cocaine have been intercepted in the first half of this year.

Other aspects of the Government’s package include new and expanded services in communities hardest hit by meth, including the expansion of Tūturu, a school-based prevention programme helping young people understand the risks of drugs.

Derek Cheng is a senior journalist who started at the Herald in 2004. He has worked several stints in the press gallery team and is a former deputy political editor.

Foodstuffs is promising to fight a National Party plan to break up its collective into two nationwide supermarket chains, saying it could increase food prices by making its stores less efficient.

National announced yesterday that it wanted to split up Foodstuffs if re-elected, forcing its New World and Four Square brands to break from Pak’nSave to create a third player to drive down grocery prices through competition.

Its plan, announced by party leader Christopher Luxon and finance spokeswoman Nicola Willis, would separate the Foodstuffs North Island and Foodstuffs South Island co-operatives.

Foodstuffs North Island chairman Dean Waddell told Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast that despite apparent broad political support for the plan, Foodstuffs would “have to fight this”.

“Our history is full of independent owners coming together to create economies of scale to be competitive for customers,” he said.

“Potentially unwinding our business makes us less competitive.”

He denied that Foodstuffs had consulted lawyers, saying the issue was “about New Zealand consumers and getting the best value to them”.

Asked if a Government could legally “upend a market”, Waddell said: “We’re retailers. We turn up every day to trade our grocery stores. It’s not where we play the game.”

Waddell said the market was heavily regulated and New Zealand already had “full oversight” of the industry.

He also downplayed a 2022 Commerce Commission report which said the supermarket industry made $1 million in excess profits every day, saying it was based on “assumptions and theory”.

Eric Rush - who owns the Whangārei New World - told Ryan Bridge Today the plan was “really quite shocking” and was surprised to see it coming from National.

He also questioned the rationale for leaving the Australian-owned Woolworths alone.

“They’re talking like the [Foodstuffs] co-op’s this big corporate giant - it’s not. It’s me and my wife. It’s Todd and Lillian who own Pak’nSave down the road. It’s Sione and Alice who own Ōtāhuhu Four Square.”

Rush said his store already competed aggressively with the local Pak’nSave as well as with the city’s three Woolworths.

“There’s only a certain amount of dollars in Whangārei and I’d rather have that dollar in my bank account than Todd’s.”

Rush said the regions would suffer most from a split as rural stores would pay more for the same products.

For every dollar that came through his tills, “I get to keep 3.8 cents if I do a good job,” Rush said.

“We work long and hard hours and we make a decent living. There’s a lot of risk involved, there’s a lot of heartache.”

He was more than happy to see increased competition, “but there’s a reason Aldi’s not here. There a reason that Walmart’s not here. The 3.8c is probably the reason they’re not here. We just haven’t got the population and scale.”

National has said its policy would require sign-off from the Commerce Commission after a six-month assessment, which would happen after the election.

A cost-benefit analysis had looked at splitting up both Woolworths and Foodstuffs but found the Foodstuffs-only split was the preferred option, Willis said.

New Zealand First claimed that National was stealing its policies, while Act leader David Seymour criticised the plan as “attacking business”. However, he didn’t explicitly rule out signing up to the policy in a future coalition agreement.

BusinessNZ yesterday compared the plan to Labour’s oil and gas ban and NZ First’s plan to split up the gentailers, saying it would deter foreign investors and send a “chilling signal” that the Government could break up businesses.

Visitors spent almost $14 million in Christchurch during the two-day Hagley Park festival last year.

International sensations Calvin Harris and Kings of Leon are set to headline Australasia’s biggest music festival, Electric Avenue in Christchurch, alongside an array of international acts next year.

Multi-Grammy Award-winning and multi-platinum rock band Kings of Leon will make a return to Christchurch for the first time in 19 years.

“But what I love about this 2027 line-up is the breadth of it – it’s a really eclectic mix of genres, with something for all generations.

“As the festival’s evolved, it’s those two elements that are becoming our hallmark.

A cat welfare charity has taken its fight against cash-prize cat hunting competitions to the Government after more than 1000 feral felines were killed over three years at a controversial North Canterbury event.

The New Zealand Cat Foundation has written to the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) and Department of Conservation (DoC), arguing Government guidance cannot reliably distinguish feral cats from pets and strays before they are killed.

Animal welfare advocates unsuccessfully tried to stop the feral cat category at the North Canterbury Hunting Competition in July, where 441 cats were culled.

The foundation is now seeking broader changes, including a ban on cash-prize killing competitions and stricter controls on who can kill feral cats.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

Founder and chair Anne Batley Burton said the charity believed companion, stray and displaced cats were being killed alongside feral animals.

“Cats now effectively have a bounty on their heads,” she said.

“We have seen people steal companion cats from their own homes and properties to enter them into these competitions. This isn’t pest control.”

The foundation said missing-cat numbers increased around hunting events and challenged DoC identification guidance, arguing characteristics used to identify feral cats could also apply to companion animals.

It wants feral cat control restricted to licensed or certified pest-control professionals and greater support for humane alternatives including Trap-Neuter-Return programmes.

DoC acting Predator Free manager Andrea Goodman acknowledged there was “no single characteristic” that could reliably distinguish a feral cat from a companion cat in every circumstance.

“While there is a small risk of misidentification whenever free-roaming cats are encountered, DoC takes a precautionary approach and requires operational decisions to be informed by multiple sources of information.”

Goodman said staff and contractors were expected to consider factors including a cat’s behaviour, location, condition and context, rather than relying on a single indicator.

She said DoC did not want companion cats harmed and its predator-control guidance included measures to minimise the risk, including appropriate trap selection and placement and considering the proximity of homes and settlements.

DoC regularly reviewed that guidance, Goodman said, while emerging technology, including traps with microchip readers could further reduce the risk to companion cats.

MPI Director of Compliance and Response, Glen Burrell said feral cat management on conservation land is done by DoC.

“The Ministry for Primary Industries’ responsibility in cat management focuses on their welfare, as covered under the Animal Welfare Act 1999,” he said.

“The Act requires any killing of animals to be carried out humanely. If we became aware of any breaches of animal welfare rules, we would take appropriate action.

“Regional councils throughout New Zealand manage feral cats generally through their pest-control plans.”

The latest push comes as another Canterbury hunting competition featuring a feral cat category launches this weekend.

The Great Mid Canterbury Critter Competition runs from Friday to Sunday and is open to children aged 16 and under, with adult supervision required.

Competitors can hunt across Canterbury with landowner permission, with feral cats, possums, rabbits, hares, rats, mustelids and hedgehogs among eligible animals.

The rules offer prizes for the biggest feral cat in three age groups.

Event spokeswoman Deborah Gilkison said pest control was already part of everyday life for rural families.

“It’s already happening on farms and properties across Canterbury,” she said.

“Feral cats are also a genuine biodiversity issue. DoC identifies them as predators of native birds, bats, lizards, wētā and other wildlife.

“This competition is about doing something rural families already do, but using it as an opportunity to get kids outdoors and talking about pests, biodiversity and looking after our environment.”

Gilkison said organisers had dedicated a section of the rules to feral cats.

“Our message around cats couldn’t be clearer: if you’re not certain it’s feral, leave it alone,” she said.

The event will raise funds for Mayfield Community Pool heating project.

“At the end of the day, it’s rural people coming together, doing something they already enjoy, removing pests and raising money for their community.”

Rafaella Melo is a multimedia journalist with more than 10 years’ experience in Brazil. She joined the NZ Herald’s Christchurch team in 2026.

New charter school given approval to become one of NZ’s biggest schools

New Zealand Herald September 16, 2026

Online charter school Aotearoa Infinite Academy opened at the start of this year with 200 students. Photo / 123RF

By John Gerritsen of RNZ

An online charter school opened just nine months ago already has permission to become one of the country’s biggest schools.

Aotearoa Infinite Academy (AIA) opened at the start of this year with 200 students, and has approval to grow to 2000 next year and 3000 in 2028.

The secondary school’s growth is significant because other charter schools have remained relatively small, with the largest enrolling about 150 students.

A roll of 2000 would make the academy one of the 30 largest schools – and 3000 would put it in the top three to five, with government funding running to around $26 million a year.

For comparison, last year Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu (the Correspondence School) had 10,349 students, Rangitoto College 4081, Mt Albert Grammar 3576, Macleans College 2981, while Avondale College, Westlake Boys High and Auckland Grammar School all had more than 2700.

A Charter School Agency document said a secondary charter school of 1005 students would receive $10,741 for each student and, with 2500 students, per-student funding would be $8892.

The academy’s website said it offered online classes with about 20 students each, teaching the Pearson private curriculum during Years 9-11, and NCEA during Years 12 and 13.

The school said it had grown to 450 students after just six weeks, with permission to grow to 600 in term two this year.

The agency said it recently approved an application to increase the school’s roll to 2000 next year and 3000 in 2028, but did not cite any independent checking o ensure it warranted expansion.

“This approval was based on evidence of growing demand, and satisfactory results against the attendance and achievement performance targets,” it said.

“AIA were required to demonstrate how the school would manage a larger roll, including bringing on additional staff, supporting new students and meeting increased demand for in-person exam facilities.

“As with all charter schools, we will continue to monitor the school’s performance against its contract. This includes targets for roll numbers, student attendance, and achievement. In contrast to state schools, the funding AIA receives is dependent on it continuing to meet these requirements.”

The academy was owned by Crimson Consulting, where former National Party leader and Prime Minister Sir John Key was a director, and was part of the Crimson Academies Group, which included the private Crimson Global Academy and Mount Hobson Academy, as well as Future School, a private school in Auckland.

Academy principal Saira Boyle told RNZ the school’s enrolments came from a range of backgrounds and areas, though a large number were from the Auckland region.

“We’ve got students who’ve come from the public school system, some who’ve come from the private school system, some from homeschooling.”

Boyle said daily attendance was at 90 per cent or more, and more than half of the school’s students were attending more than 90 per cent of their classes – the benchmark for regular attendance.

She said the school had 600 students, with about 400 more on a waitlist. Student achievement was also good.

“We have a large number of students, a significant number in reading, writing and maths who are at or above where they need to be. We’re also supporting students who need that extra little bit of a boost with a range of intervention classes,” she said.

Asked if the school should have been subject to independent monitoring before gaining approval for significant growth, Boyle said the school could be trusted.

“We are sending regular reports into the Charter School Agency and I feel really, really confident that the powers that be see the good that we are doing. They can see how we’re operating and they feel confident enough to give us that roll increase,” she said.

Post Primary Teachers’ Association president Chris Abercrombie said there should be more publicly available data about the school.

“At the moment we don’t know if they’re doing a good job or a great job or a bad job, yet they’ve been allowed to increase by 1500 students roughly in the space of two years.”

Abercrombie said he was concerned about such rapid growth, because it was difficult to manage.

He said those concerns were amplified for an online school, which needed to provide pastoral care to teenagers.

“We need to actually look at why these kids are looking at an online school and actually is it the best option for them,” he said.

“If a student’s having mental health issues or they’re having health issues, is being in your home, in your room, by yourself all day doing this work, is that the best thing for you?”

Abercrombie was also critical of for-profit online schools, which he said had grown in number overseas.

“They’re cheap to run. You don’t need a building, you don’t need to pay for power or oil for the boiler. You don’t need to do any of those things so this is a way for businesses, people, organisations to run a school while having the lowest cost possible.”

He said the model already existed in the form of Te Kura.

“The Correspondence School has that social contract to support public education and this is effectively a private business and so it doesn’t have that social contract,” he said.

The Charter School Agency provided RNZ with data the school submitted to support its application for growth.

It showed only initial or entry data for reading, writing and maths, but claimed an 82% achievement rate for NCEA standards, with a third of results at excellence level.

It also included positive comments from parents and teachers about the school.

“We considered this alongside our ongoing monitoring, the requirement for the school to provide pastoral support, and the continued demand from families choosing to enrol at the school – indicating they were happy with the progress their young people were making,” the agency said.

Scathing report into Fire and Emergency NZ recommends reviewing board and truck procurement

New Zealand Herald September 16, 2026

Fire and Emergency NZ bought 30 new trucks in 2019, which are still not being used. Photo / RNZ, Paris Ibell

By RNZ

A scathing select committee report into Fire and Emergency recommends that the Government looks at changing the organisation’s board and whether it should be allowed to buy its own fire trucks.

National MP Tim Costley, who is the deputy chair of the Governance and Administration Committee, said the report laid bare years of failings within Fire and Emergency.

Fire and Emergency had bought 30 new trucks in 2019, which still were not being used, he said.

“The evidence shows they haven’t been able to deliver. They’ve consistently had delays, they’ve consistently had issues with trucks and it looks like they have a culture of changing the design halfway through the process regularly.”

Ladder trucks Fire and Emergency New Zealand bought had also suffered significant delays, he said.

“Despite a final inspection in July 2025, they are still sitting with original manufacturers, not yet delivered to Fire and Emergency and far from being put into operational use.”

The report recommended the Government “consider whether Fire and Emergency is best placed to conduct its own procurement, or if further support is required”.

Costley said the report also raised issues with the governance of the organisation.

“The board could not produce any evidence of asking about these new fire engines between December 2023 and the inquiry. Really concerning ... not a lot of confidence in the board right now.”

He said bringing in new board chair Raveen Jaduram in June had been the right move, and he had been “far more transparent”.

Other recommendations in the report included “that the Government direct Fire and Emergency NZ to shift its focus from generating corporate documents to efforts that will deliver tangible improvements at frontline stations”.

Fire and Emergency chair Raveen Jaduram said he acknowledged the significant shortcomings identified in the report, and was committed to transparent action in response.

“The report identifies unacceptable delays and weaknesses in setting procurement requirements, contract management and governance oversight.

“Firefighters and communities are entitled to expect better.”

Jaduram said since coming into the role in June, he had taken several steps to improve things.

“Fire and Emergency is introducing several initiatives to strengthen fleet procurement, reporting and management practices, including clearer accountability, stronger oversight of delivery and risk.”
