The 30 best movies to stream on Paramount+ right now

Sydney Morning Herald September 17, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To help you cut through that, here are 30 great hand-picked titles that span genres and filmmakers. This week: Paramount+. For other movie choices, check out our guides on Netflix, Stan*, Disney+, Binge, ABC iview, SBS On Demand and HBO Max.

Monty Python’s Terry Gilliam subverts the Hollywood blockbuster with this idiosyncratic meditation on love and loss. Bruce Willis stars as the inmate from a post-apocalyptic future sent back in time who meets Madeleine Stowe’s psychiatrist and Brad Pitt’s troublemaker.

Jennifer Garner is a delightful anchor for this fantasy comedy-of-age comedy, playing the grown-up version of a 13-year-old girl whose wish goes awry. Co-starring Mark Ruffalo, it’s a funny, empowering film about being true to yourself.

Broad City’s Ilana Glazer co-wrote and stars – with Better Things creator Pamela Adlon directing – in this complicated, feisty comedy about female friendship. If follows two very different besties, played by Glazer and Michelle Buteau, dealing with their respective pregnancies.

In this misanthropic comedy, Billy Bob Thornton plays an alcoholic thief who works as a department store Santa to set up his Yuletide heist. Hie deadpan failings are memorable, as is Gilmore Girls mama Lauren Graham as an easy-going bartender.

The best instalment of Matt Damon’s action franchise, English filmmaker Paul Greengrass ups the ante with jagged, tactile fight scenes. It’s a propulsive movie, yet the underlying theme is the need to atone for past sins.

Steve Martin is in exemplary form as the writer and star of this giddy Hollywood satire, playing a no-budget producer who decides to make a blockbuster on the cheap by secretly filming an unaware superstar (Eddie Murphy) in chaotic situations.

Straining – and succeeding – at every turn to create an arthouse epic about individual endurance, Brady Corbet’s period epic earned Adrien Brody an Academy Award for his portrayal of an architect and Holocaust survivor who comes to America to build a monument.

Set in a dystopic 2027, where society is slowly collapsing because of worldwide infertility, Alfonso Cuaron’s vivid thriller stars Clive Owen and Julianne Moore as reunited activists in a story that combines humanism and remarkable set-pieces.

It’s a serious flex of star power: Julia Roberts, Jude Law, Natalie Portman and Clive Owen star in Mike Nichols’ scything adaptation of Patrick Marber’s hit play about desire and self-deception. Tone-wise, it’s the opposite of a rom-com.

With Rob Reiner directing, this film based on Aaron Sorkin’s breakthrough stage play updated old Hollywood conventions for a stirring courtroom drama. Tom Cruise plays a military lawyer defending two Guantanamo Bay marines under Jack Nicholson’s intimidating command.

In this absurdist stress test for male friendship, the perpetually wound-too-tight Tim Robinson (I Think You Should Leave) plays a suburban man who becomes obsessed with his new pal and neighbour, a perfectly cast Paul Rudd. This black comedy goes to extremes.

Whether set in snowy Surrey or sunny Los Angeles, this Nancy Meyers romantic-comedy exemplifies cosy reassurance, with Kate Winslet and Cameron Diaz as heartbroken women who swap homes and rebound respectively with Jack Black and Jude Law.

Quentin Tarantino goes full spaghetti western in this alternate reality World War II where the cinema is literally a screen-burning battlefield. Led by Brad Pitt, a special unit rampages through Nazi-occupied France to counter Christoph Waltz’s mercurial sadist.

The film that invented the modern Hollywood blockbuster, opening wide in cinemas and on screen as a shark devours seaside tourists before a mismatched trio hunt it down. The true star? John Williams’ iconic score.

Further proof that Daniel Day-Lewis could do anything. In Michael Mann’s bloody 18th century epic, the English actor plays a hardy frontiersman raised by Native Americans who risks everything for Madeleine Stowe’s British belle. Their chemistry is off the charts.

With a witty Tina Fey script, this high-school satire gave Lindsay Lohan her signature role as Cady Heron, a new student who tries to master high school – and Rachel McAdams’ terrifying top girl Regina George – via anthropological theories. Great, great fun.

Christopher Nolan introduced himself to audiences with this beguiling reverse thriller, where each scene is followed by the one that chronologically precedes it as Guy Pearce’s desperate amnesiac tries to control a world he has no memory of.

Dev Patel’s directorial debut is a heaving mix of crunching combat, Indian corruption commentary and spiritual longing. The actor plays a vengeance-bound survivor of a massacre relentlessly pursuing his corrupt foes.

A Coen brothers masterpiece, where violence is an otherworldly constant as the 1980s drug trade entangles a defiant hunter (Josh Brolin), a nightmarish assassin (Javier Bardem) and an ageing sheriff (Tommy Lee Jones).

Filmmaker Robert Eggers has delivered many takes on classic horror material with pungent detail, menacing period particulars and twisted carnality. His Dracula tale is no different, with Bill Skarsgård as the befouled vampire pursuing Lily-Rose Depp’s tormented wife.

Behind this animated family comedy about a group of forest animals confronted by a new suburban development is a quick-witted critique of reckless consumerism backed by chase sequences that are models of Buster Keaton-like planning.

The Salvadoran surrealist Julio Torres is one of comedy’s truly original voices. His directorial feature debut, in which he stars as an impoverished immigrant working for a blistering widow (Tilda Swinton), is both hilariously absurd and strikingly political.

A paean to American excess, exemplified by Al Pacino’s Cuban refugee turned Miami cocaine dealer, this garish classic directed by Brian De Palma is punctuated by unfettered violence and Michelle Pfeiffer as a mercenary mistress.

With two US Marshals (Leonardo DiCaprio and Mark Ruffalo) arriving at an isolated hospital for the criminally insane, Martin Scorsese gets to riff on vintage horror movies and the history of psychiatry, with Michelle Williams featuring throughout as a haunting memory.

Memorably subverting fairytale cliches at every turn, this fantasy animated adventure about an ogre (Mike Myers) who just wants to chill in his swamp has aged exceptionally well. It remains sprightly, complete with Eddie Murphy voicing a motormouth donkey.

The historic flapping of the butterfly wings that gave us today’s Big Tech storm, David Fincher’s take on the creation of Facebook is an origin story for Mark Zuckerberg (Jesse Eisenberg) that updates previous American studies of wealth and power.

The second – and best – of the Star Trek franchise’s 2010s reboot, featuring Chris Pine as Kirk and Zachary Quinto as Spock, explores the militarisation of space and the perils of buried history via Benedict Cumberbatch’s bravura antagonist.

In her first leading role after a lifetime of supporting work, then 94-year-old American actress June Squibb is an irascible delight as a motorised scooter avenger, pursuing scammers across Los Angeles in a comedy that is both farcical and bittersweet.

Sofia Coppola found her distinctive cinematic voice in this haunting story of five doomed teenage sisters in 1970s American suburbia. With Kirsten Dunst as the rebellious epicentre, this is female adolescence as a dreamy downward spiral.

Led by an eerily menacing Joaquin Phoenix as a hammer-wielding contractor retrieving trafficked children, this crime thriller from masterful Scottish filmmaker Lynne Ramsay attains a hallucinatory power that eschews triumph for torment.

*Stan is owned by Nine, which owns this masthead.

Macklemore pledges his $1m Ed Sheeran tour salary to Palestine

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 21:26:53 GMT

Rapper, who was dropped from tour after his speech in support of Palestine, challenges Robert Kraft to do the same

Macklemore has announced that he will donate the $1m salary he was paid as an opening act for Ed Sheeran’s Loop tour to organizations working with Palestinian people and relief in Gaza, after being dropped from the tour following backlash to his onstage comments in support of Palestine.

The rapper also challenged Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and prominent donor to Israel who refused to let Macklemore play at his Gillette Stadium outside Boston, to match his donation.

“With everything that has happened over the last 48 hours, I want to bring the conversation back to where it belongs: to the Palestinian people who are still being killed, still living under military occupation, and still fighting for their freedom,” the Grammy-winning artist wrote on Instagram Wednesday. “I will be donating the entire $1 million of my net earnings from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour to six organizations working directly to support the Palestinian people. And I invite Robert Kraft to match my donation. Whatever we disagree about, perhaps we can agree on this: Palestinian lives are worth protecting. A Palestinian life is no less valuable than any other life on this earth.”

In a two-minute speech during his set at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on 4 September, Macklemore expressed his desire to see a “free Palestine. I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them.” His remarks prompted a petition from the Israeli American Council demanding his removal from the tour.

Speaking again onstage the following day, he reiterated his support for Palestine and addressed Jewish members of the audience: “Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace, love; for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.”

According to Sheeran, who posted his own explanation on Tuesday morning outlining his desire to remain publicly neutral on political causes, Kraft, along with several other venue owners, informed the English singer that his tour could not play at their stadiums if Macklemore continued as an opener, prompting his removal. A day later, all four of Sheeran’s opening acts for the remainder of the Loop tour – Finneas, Aaron Rowe, Boega and Lukas Graham – withdrew from the tour in solidarity with Macklemore and Palestine.

In his post, Macklemore said he hoped to “center the parents carrying their children into hospitals without the basic resources to treat them, and the physicians, paramedics, journalists and aid workers who keep going back in. I want to center the organizers and activists who have paid real costs for standing with Palestine. Their risk is of a far different order than mine.

“Palestinians have lived for decades without basic rights and should not have to wait another day to be free,” he added. “That is where my focus will remain. I will continue to stand with the Palestinian people and their fight for liberation. When the news cycle moves on, which it will, don’t move with it. Free Palestine.”

Earlier Wednesday, Colin Kaepernick, whose NFL career was effectively ended by the NFL’s resistance to his protests against US police violence, joined the chorus of prominent figures criticizing Macklemore’s removal at the behest of NFL stadium owners. “The part that I hope people appreciate and take away in this moment is what [New England Patriots owner] Robert Kraft and what they’re saying by denying Macklemore the opportunity to go out and perform with Ed Sheeran is they are willing to collude,” the former quarterback said on the MeidasTouch podcast. “The [NFL owners] are openly colluding.”

Kaepernick added that he thought NFL owners tried to hound out Macklemore in a similar way to him. “When we filed the grievance, it was like, well, the owners wouldn’t do that,” Kaepernick said. “Everybody just wants to win within the NFL. And the realization is, no. They want to protect their interests. They want to protect their power. They want to protect their money.”

In his own statement Monday, Kraft has said his decision to ban Macklemore from the Patriots’ stadium was due to his “recent actions” and “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”.

De Cuyper and Brighton pile on pain for Manchester United with comeback

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 21:18:39 GMT

Across four days Manchester United have lost the 199th derby to Manchester City, were told by JJ Gabriel he wants to leave, and have now been knocked out of the Carabao Cup by Brighton.

Capitulating after being 2-0 up may be the pick of these dizzying blows, and when Marcus Rashford skated in with the chance to take the tie to 3-3 late on, there was no surprise he hit Jason Steele rather than the net.

Towards the end, Matheus Cunha was thrown on to join Bruno Fernandes, also a late substitute, illustrating how desperate Michael Carrick was. Yet Charalampos Kostoulas went close to scoring a second for Brighton, as United could not find a route to cancelling out Maxim De Cuyper’s 69th-minute strike that proved the winner.

After taking only four points from twelve in the league, serious questions will now be asked about where Carrick’s team are heading; they have to beat Fulham on Sunday to start correcting a dismal start to the season.

Carrick stated Sunday’s injustice against City would give his side an edge and Shea Lacey provided a cutting one when decorating a full debut with the sweetest of goals.

The 19-year-old shimmied in Brighton’s area, beating Jaouen Hadjam before firing beyond a helpless Jason Steele. As impressive here was Benjamin Sesko’s hold-up work in the buildup as this allowed red shirts to flood forward, Youri Tielemans feeding Lacey.

This was seven minutes in and less than 120 seconds later Mason Mount doubled United’s advantage.

Rashford’s pace and drive took him clear along the left, again inside the area. A trailing Steele boot saved the No 9’s effort but the ball bounced into Mount’s path and he drove home, via the turf, for a first goal since a win at Wolves last December.

Lacey’s strike drew a Carrick grin and delight from Mount, and you wondered how Gabriel – earmarked for this game’s squad, with the chance to become United’s youngest ever player – felt.

Brighton had lost only one of their last five visits here, with a flying start to the league campaign placing Fabian Hürzeler’s team in fifth. Yet Sunday’s 5-0 hammering of Coventry already seemed distant as United continued to dominate.

Olivier Boscagli hit a corner straight out, summing up the visitors’ start, before Matt O’Riley forced Ayden Heaven into an error that led to another. This presaged a Seagulls renaissance that featured a lightning Malick Yalcouyé break but, clear in on the debutant Karl Darlow’s goal, the Ivorian spooned wide. The No 35 lacked the sharpness evident in a Rashford nutmeg of Chema Andrés which embarrassed the Brighton man and when Pascal Gross blasted over this was one more chance spurned by Hürzeler’s men.

But then came a goal – and real hope – for Brighton. Hadjam’s long left-right diagonal cut United’s rearguard clean out, and the slumbering Heaven allowed Kostoulas to scamper free, the striker beating Darlow through his legs.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Carrick, having beaten only Ipswich so far this season, needed a win, and as United (not under him) exited at the earliest time of both cup competitions last year, progressing to at least a second tie in one of them would be welcome.

A wild Tielemans long-range shot that ballooned over failed to restore United’s two-goal lead but at least the home unit were tapping the ball about, operating in Brighton territory, moving the guests around.

A Sesko burst from halfway had the onrushing Steele hacking away just in time so United were in control. But the question was: could they maintain this and register the type of mature, accomplished display that would show an evolution in Carrick’s team? Sesko, in yards of space, dawdling and dispossessed when a simple ball would have fed Lacey, suggested not.

A loose Rashford pass aimed for Sesko – the same. More promising was a pass for Noussair Mazraoui as he drove into the area along the left channel. As was the subsequent corner that created an opening for Tielemans to narrowly miss.

A 57th-minute Rhys Norrington-Davies own goal sent Fleetwood into the last 16 of the Carabao Cup for the first time as the League Two club stunned their Championship opponents, Sheffield United, 1-0 at Highbury, before pulling a home tie against Arsenal out in the draw.

Matt Lawlor’s side, unbeaten now in nine games in all competitions, had another Danny Andrew effort ruled out for offside and twice hit the woodwork in a dominant second-half display. It was a searching left-wing cross from Andrew that Norrington-Davies nodded beyond Michael Cooper to give the fourth-tier club a historic victory.

Tom Cannon did get the ball in the net for Chris Wilder’s visitors who lined up with only four starting survivors from last Friday’s 1-0 league defeat by Wolves. But a flag for offside was raised before the striker slid the ball into the net.

United started positively and Ollie Arblaster had a goalbound effort blocked after only 36 seconds. But Mark Helm forced Cooper into a seventh-minute save before the former United forward Ched Evans put his follow-up header narrowly wide.

Jay Lynch denied Joe Rothwell as the visitors attacked again but Cooper was the busier, saving from Lewis McCann and Crispin McLean.

Helm’s dipping right-foot effort from 18 yards grazed the top netting as Fleetwood finished the first half in the ascendancy and they deserved their break from Norrington-Davies’ own goal.

United finally came to life in the last 10 minutes with Lynch brilliantly denied Sydie Peck and Ben Brereton Díaz, while Cannon saw a goalbound strike superbly blocked.

Everton’s forgotten man Charly Alcaraz stepped up when his side needed some inspiration to score the only goal in the win over Wolves three minutes after coming on. The Argentinian had played just 14 minutes all season but belied his lack of match sharpness with a quick switch of the ball from one foot to the other to guide a left-footed shot past the former Everton goalkeeper João Virgínia in the 80th minute.

It also represented a minor success for Tyler Dibling, whose career has not really taken off since his £35m move from Southampton just over a year ago, as he claimed the assist at the end his most encouraging performance for the club. Everton's reward is a home tie against Newcastle. Press Association

But then disaster. Diogo Dalot’s hoofed clearance failed to find Sesko as Luka Vuskovic headed to Gross; Brighton’s captain made room and netted with ease. Even worse followed. Brighton raided along the right, Kostoulas’s cross pinged off Mazraoui’s backside, and there was De Cuyper to finish.

On 72 minutes Carrick played his ace, introducing Fernandes for Mount, then followed up with Cunha. But United remained toothless.

Enzo Le Fée makes amends from the spot as Sunderland overcome AZ

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 21:06:31 GMT

Sunderland’s captain, Granit Xhaka, believes it is not unrealistic to dream about Régis Le Bris’s side travelling all the way to next spring’s Europa League final.

It is rarely a good idea to dismiss Xhaka but reaching that showpiece in Frankfurt will necessitate considerably more efficient finishing on his team’s part than proved evident on a highly evocative night on Wearside.

Thanks to a second-half penalty from the indefatigable Enzo Le Fée –appropriately the game’s outstanding player – it ended happily as Sunderland launched their big return to Europe with a morale-boosting win. Along the way, though, they missed far too many chances for Le Bris’ liking.

Sunderland’s European comeback was sandwiched between last Saturday’s home Premier League defeat to Arsenal and this weekend’s trip to Manchester City. The latter assignment surely informed Le Bris’ decision to indulge in a little light rotation and leave Brian Brobbey, Dan Ballard and Thomas Meunier resting their legs on the home bench at kick-off.

Occupants of the VIP seats included Jimmy Montgomery, the now 82-year-old hero of Sunderland’s 1973 FA Cup triumph against Leeds and their goalkeeper during that last, albeit fairly short lived, European adventure in the Cup Winners’ Cup 53 years ago.

Down on the pitch, Malick Fofana, the winger signed from Lyon for £30m on transfer deadline day, made his first start following a spine-tingling, ear-splitting, preamble to kick-off featuring a giant tifo of a sailing ship floating above the message: “New shores to conquer”.

Not that AZ were inclined to surrender lightly. Leeroy Echteld’s team arrived having enjoyed an unbeaten start to the season, winning five and drawing one of their opening Eredivisie games. Indeed they would have assumed a very early lead on Wearside had Sunderland’s Dutch goalkeeper Robin Roefs not extended a boot and kept out Ro-Zangelo Daal’s low shot. The moment had arrived for Le Fée to raise the home tone and his half-volley duly tested Jari De Busser before Wilson Isidor failed to make contact with Le Fée’s inviting delivery from the rebound.

Though De Busser was swiftly forced to push Kevin Danso’s fine shot over the bar, Sunderland nearly came undone on the counter-attack and it took on excellent interception on Trai Hume’s part to halt Ayoub Oufkir in his tracks.

Oufkir and the talented visiting No 10, Kees Smit, issued timely reminders that AZ are more than merely deft in possession but Le Bris’ starting XI was hardly shabby either and, after Isidor conjured a glorious chance, Le Fée’s shot hit the post.

Ruben Amorim’s Milan were beaten 2-0 by Marco Silva’s Benfica in the Europa League. Dodi Lukebakio put the Portuguese side ahead at San Siro in the 16th minute and Jakub Kaminski added a second early in the second half.

Bayer Leverkusen, finalists in 2024, began their Europa League campaign with a 2-0 win against the Slovenian champions Celje while Lyon were 2-1 winners at Anderlecht.

The Cypriot champions Omonia Nicosia stunned the La Liga side Celta Vigo 1-0 while Rangers’ conquerors Jagiellonia Bialystok were denied a point at the Greek giants Olympiacos by Roman Yaremchuk’s late winner.

It was not long before another shot, from Hume this time, whizzed fractionally wide of an upright. It is worth remembering that when Hume joined Sunderland, back in January 2022, they were in League One.

Back in the present Le Bris’ team ended the first half thoroughly dominant but unable to convert a litany of chances. Oufkir, meanwhile, was a little fortunate to have collected only a yellow card after sliding in recklessly on Le Fée. Echteld withdrew Oufkir at the interval, replacing him with Weslley Patati.

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 21:02:19 GMT

This was the first competitive meeting between these sides since 5 May 2001, when Coventry’s 34-year stay in the top flight came to an end after defeat at Villa Park. They may be peers now they are back together in the same division but, despite Coventry’s £130m summer spend, in some ways they remain in different leagues. Tom Cannon did get the ball in the net for Chris Wilder’s visitors who lined up with only four starting survivors from last Friday’s 1-0 league defeat by Wolves. But a flag for offside was raised before the striker slid the ball into the net.

Jay Lynch denied Joe Rothwell as the visitors attacked again but Cooper was the busier, saving from Lewis McCann and Crispin McLean.

Helm’s dipping right-foot effort from 18 yards grazed the top netting as Fleetwood finished the first half in the ascendancy and they deserved their break from Norrington-Davies’ own goal.

United finally came to life in the last 10 minutes with Lynch brilliantly denied Sydie Peck and Ben Brereton Díaz, while Cannon saw a goalbound strike superbly blocked.

Everton's reward is a home tie against Newcastle. Press Association

John McGinn, the Villa captain reduced to the role of draught excluder, picked himself up from the turf. Suddenly Coventry were full of confidence, a little giddy even. Thomas moonlighted as a striker, forcing an error from Tyrone Mings but then declined a golden opportunity to shoot at goal and the chance fizzled out. Gustavo Hamer then sent a left-foot shot just past the Villa upright.

Coventry were reborn but Villa responded. McGinn spurned a decent chance for Villa, drilling a first-time shot into the side-netting. McGinn smacked his hands together in frustration. A few minutes later Barkley sent a low drive at goal that Bentley did well to push wide for a corner, from which Villa prospered. Mbaye’s inswinging delivery was on the money and Barkley, totally unmarked in the six-yard box, headed in at the front post to regain Villa’s lead.

Coventry had the meanest defence in the Championship last season but have been porous since promotion. More slack marking enabled Villa to extend their lead from another corner. Netanyahu seeks to strip citizenship from Israelis as threats to NAZA film directors intensify

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 20:54:11 GMT

Israeli prime minister to pursue new laws as directors of Guardian-produced film face threats from far-right officials and activists

‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligence

Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday that he would seek new laws allowing Israel to strip citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers, escalating the campaign against the Oscar-winning film-makers behind the Gaza documentary NAZA, who have faced threats from senior government and military officials and groups of far-right Israelis gathering outside their families’ homes.

NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, concerns the country’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza and is named for an acronym used euphemistically by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike. The film builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian from 2023 to 2025.

The 80-minute documentary won the special jury prize at this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receiving a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record.

Soon afterwards, however, the film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, came under attack from members of Israel’s government, with the culture minister, Miki Zohar, calling for their citizenship to be revoked, and accusing them of “treason against the state”.

Zohar on Wednesday thanked the Israeli prime minister for his announcement to change the law in order to revoke their citizenship, saying it was “time to put an end to this disgrace”.

“We will revoke citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers around the world – he will be deeply hurt in his pocket,’’ said Netanyahu, who intends to promote two government bills concerning defamation of IDF soldiers and the state of Israel.

According to media reports, the first bill, which will be submitted through the justice ministry, will double the amount of a defamation claim to 1 million shekels without proof of damage. The second bill, which will be submitted through the interior ministry, will stipulate the revocation of citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers and the state of Israel around the world.

On Wednesday evening, dozens of rightwing activists gathered outside the home of the parents of Rachel Szor, one of the directors of NAZA. Among the organisers were activists and campaign staff linked to the far-right Otzma Yehudit party of Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister. Messages circulated in activist groups earlier on Wednesday urged supporters to gather outside her house. Some of the messages included explicit calls for violence.

Police and border police officers were deployed at the scene.

One protester called for the “death penalty for traitors” and demanded that the homes of the film-makers’ families be demolished.

The latest attacks followed a series of threats and incidents targeting the directors.

Ben-Gvir had called the directors “a disgrace” while Netanyahu condemned the film as “intolerable”, saying it portrayed the Israel Defense Forces as war criminals.

On Tuesday, the IDF’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, said the military would “not allow IDF soldiers to be made targets through lies and blood libels” and would use “every tool at our disposal” against the film. The Israeli television channel i24 later reported that the military had opened a leak investigation and was seeking assistance from Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security and counterintelligence agency. The agency would respond only after receiving a formal request from the military prosecutor, who would probably first consult the attorney general, the channel reported.

Netanyahu posted a video which included an old clip of Abraham confronting a soldier in the occupied West Bank’s South Hebron Hills, an area where Israeli forces have repeatedly been accused of supporting settlers during attacks on Palestinians. In the video, the Israeli PM says: “The same director who produced that terrible film that slanders IDF soldiers.”

On Wednesday, far-right Israeli journalists, influencers and activists escalated their threats against the two film-makers. Rightwing activists were organising protests outside addresses linked to the directors and their colleagues.

This comes after the Channel 14 journalist Yehuda Schlesinger said the directors should be “pursued” or “hunted” wherever they went, and prevented from returning to Israel. He urged Jews in Israel and abroad to make clear that what he described as “25 minutes of antisemitic applause” in Venice would come at a “heavy price”.

A rightwing activist with tens of thousands of followers separately called for protesters to target Abraham’s family and associates, saying: “We’ll show him ‘collateral damage’.” He shared a photograph of Abraham’s mother and sought information about the director’s return flight so supporters could “welcome” him at the airport.

A mural appeared in Ashdod depicting Abraham and Szor with crosshairs, horns, swastikas and the word “traitors” emblazoned over the top. A video showing its creation was shared by the far-right rapper Yoav Eliasi, who has more than 750,000 followers on Facebook.

In an interview with Israel’s Channel 13, Abraham commented on the campaign of vilification, saying: “Of course it’s hard … [Israel] is my home, it’s the only place I want to live, a place that is important to me. So of course I’m afraid I won’t be able to return.”

As the threats against the directors intensified, film-makers and human rights groups voiced support for the pair.

In a joint statement, 43 local human rights organisations urged Israeli authorities to stop what they described as incitement and threats against the film-makers, and not to prosecute either them or their sources.

“The institutional response to the film and the threats against its creators are characteristic of dictatorial regimes,” said the statement, signed by groups including Peace Now, Adalah, B’Tselem, Physicians for Human Rights Israel and Breaking the Silence.

More than 1,500 Israeli film-makers have also signed a petition defending “freedom of expression and creation” and expressing solidarity with Szor and Abraham.

“In recent days, we have witnessed an unprecedented smear and incitement campaign against the film-makers, with the line between this rhetoric and physical violence or threats to their lives narrowing rapidly,” the petition said.

The signatories said the role of art and journalism was to reflect society and encourage debate, “even when facing a harsh reality”, and called for the film to be released in Israel so audiences could judge it for themselves.

Szor and Abraham won an Oscar for their previous documentary, 2024’s No Other Land (co-directed with Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal), which spotlighted Palestinian resistance in the occupied West Bank.

The NGOs called for a “thorough” investigation into the high number of casualties in Gaza, particularly among civilians, and for journalists to be granted unimpeded access to the territory, from which Israel has largely barred foreign reporters since October 2023.

Prominent figures in international cinema have also expressed solidarity with Abraham and Szor. Laura Poitras, who directed the 2015 Oscar-winning documentary Citizenfour, about the whistleblower Edward Snowden, called the threats by Israeli government officials “a threat to journalists worldwide”.

Diplomatic and foreign ministry sources told Haaretz that threats to punish the directors may have actually have boosted international media attention on the documentary.

“It would have made headlines anyway, but they really helped amplify it,” a source at the Israeli foreign ministry told the newspaper. “The very fact that the government responded drew attention and headlines.”

Late on Wednesday, +972 Magazine posted a video showing a man painting over the mural of the NAZA directors, replacing the word “traitors” with “heroes”.

In a statement, the Guardian said said was “disturbed to see the authoritarian response to NAZA in Israel.

“Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor are brave journalists and filmmakers. The attacks against them come from people who have not yet seen the film.

“NAZA is based on more than three years of investigative journalism. The testimonies it contains are true and we believe they deserve to be heard. The interviews were given by confidential journalistic sources.

“We will robustly defend NAZA – and the team behind it – from any attacks or attempts at censorship.”

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 20:45:19 GMT

Keely Hodgkinson and Gaby Thomas among the stars at London event whose promoter, Alexis Ohanian, has big plans and hopes for women’s sport

The timing could hardly be better. After a week when the discourse around women’s sport has been dominated by the actor Sydney Sweeney posing naked – and the intense backlash and counter-backlash – London will stage a major all-female track‑and‑field event on Friday.

A sell-out crowd at the Athlos meeting at the StoneX Stadium in Hendon will feature Britain’s Keely Hodgkinson, along with the American stars Gabby Thomas and Tara Davis-Woodhall, competing for a prize fund of $1m (£750,000). There will be a red-carpet parade, celebrities galore and a celebration of the best of female sport.

The man behind it all, the US entrepreneur and investor Alexis Ohanian, believes this is just the start. Having made millions after cofounding the social media platform Reddit, and having set up the Angel City FC women’s football team, he is betting that track and field will thrive because of to the running boom and the Los Angeles Olympics.

“You can’t go anywhere without seeing joggers, runners and run clubs,” he says. “London is a hotbed for it; the US, too. It is such an accessible sport. So why can’t it be a hundred times more popular? Or even a thousand times more popular?”

We will talk more about that later, but Ohanian also has thoughts on Sweeney’s controversial advert for the US sports prediction company Novig, and the reaction from hundreds of female athletes from around the globe. He is also aware that Sweeney then retaliated by sharing covers of semi‑nude athletes from ESPN magazine’s Body Issue, including one of Ohanian’s wife, Serena Williams – a post that many took to be implying hypocrisy among her critics.

“I’m not even mad,” Ohanian says. “If she wants to be naked for a commercial, that’s great, fine. It’s the false equivalence that I really support our athletes calling out about. The irony is my feed, at least, has been full of women athletes showing off, doing great women athlete stuff, which is awesome.”

Ohanian also says that when an athlete poses for ESPN or Sports Illustrated it is very different. “You don’t have to look very hard to find reasons to celebrate actual women athletes. There’s a ton of them. They have massive followings. They have incredible stories. And, you know, them deciding to do an ESPN Body Issue is very obviously different from an actress just being naked for a commercial.

“These are professional athletes who have devoted decades of their life towards a physical goal and their body is their résumé. So I have no problem understanding why it is totally OK for an athlete, man or woman, to pose naked tastefully. They are physically fit and showing it off because they grinded in the gym every morning to play football, ski, or whatever the hell they do.” ”

Ohanian makes for engaging company. But he is never more passionate than when making the case that women’s sports will be far bigger in a decade. “Ten years from now, there will be multiple billion-dollar women’s teams in basketball and soccer, and they will be doing at least a hundred million in revenue easily,” he says. “And Chelsea will be the first in England.

“The quality of play is also going to go up, because now there’s a business behind women’s sport,” he says, pointing to how a young girl will get far better coaching and support than 10 or 20 years ago, as money and standards rise. “Women’s tennis is an example of this because you can see the impact Serena and Venus made, where a decade later, the entire nature of women’s tennis looks very different. Consciousness is warped by, or moulded by, excellence.”

Ohanian’s journey into investing in women’s sport began in March 2019 when he started tweeting about how women’s football must be hugely undervalued given the USA women’s soccer team was so successful and had millions of followers. “I laid this all out in a rant and I finished it by saying: ‘I’m going to either start a team, or buy one, and who can help?’”

The USA soccer star Alex Morgan replied. Soon afterwards Ohanian backed words with his wallet by launching Angel City FC. Having invested $7m, the club are now worth £$350m.

“It was one of the first things I did after leaving Reddit. And I feel so blessed that it went on to be so successful so quickly, and had such a ripple effect of investment around women’s sports. For me, the lens after leaving Reddit is everything I build going forward is going to be something I’m really proud to tell my kids.”

So why is he betting big on track and field? “When the Olympics were coming to LA, I said: ‘OK, what’s another sport where you have this massive popularity every four years and then it goes to zero?’ We have 300 million-plus people in America who love sport, who love cheering our athletes during the Olympics, but have no clue outside of that what’s going on. And that’s what I want to break.

“I love the fact it’s the oldest sport. It’s immediately understandable – my eight‑year‑old can understand who wins. You can tell the entire story of an event in a short-form video. Ohanian also promises that Athlos will end up a very different proposition to Grand Slam Track, the Michael Johnson-led venture that filed for bankruptcy after three events last year. “We held our first race five months after our announcement in 2024 and 3.25 million people tuned in,” he says. “We had brands like Tiffany, who are not from this world, to be a part of this. Prince Charles told Earl Spencer days after the death of his sister Diana, Princess of Wales, that “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough”, it is alleged in a memoir to be published this month.

Charles Spencer’s book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, contains the claim that the comments were made by the now king during a heated argument over funeral arrangements.

The Daily Mail, which is serialising the book, said Spencer insisted to the then Prince of Wales that Diana would not have wanted her sons, William, then 15, and Harry, then 12, to walk in their mother’s funeral procession.

Spencer writes that the comments “unleashed” by Charles almost 30 years ago reflected “his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death” the Daily Mail reported.

In his book, Spencer writes that when one of Queen Elizabeth’s most senior aides told him in the days before the funeral that William and Harry would take part in the procession, he responded: “That’s not going to happen,” the paper said.

But minutes later he received a phone call from Charles, who insisted it should. It was during the ensuing argument between the two men that Charles allegedly made the comment, with Spencer reportedly writing: “Rest assured,” he hissed, “we’ll forget her soon enough!’”

Spencer wrote that he was stunned by the alleged remark and took a few seconds to reply, writing: “‘I can’t believe you just said that,’ I said flatly, before hanging up.”

Swan Song is due to be published worldwide next Tuesday – in the UK by Penguin Michael Joseph, a division of Penguin Random House.

Four copies of the Dutch language edition were reportedly taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher’s printers to their warehouse in the Netherlands.

Diana, who died aged 36 after a car crash in Paris in 1997, would have turned 65 on 1 July this year.

Spencer said that he had been inundated with interview requests in advance of the 30th anniversary of her death next year, and wanted to write down his own thoughts and memories rather than “having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others”.

“The aim of this book is to tell the truth about Diana from her brother’s perspective, just as I attempted to do when speaking at her funeral,” he added, referring to the eulogy he gave in Westminster Abbey.

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”

‘Made in Europe’ law threatens UK plans for reset with EU

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 19:39:28 GMT

Government sources say legislation aimed at China poses a risk to British businesses and must be addressed

The UK government’s EU reset summit will be delayed again unless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry, government sources have said.

The “Made in Europe” legislation – formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act – is designed to curb China’s increasing presence in European industry, but was not on the reset plan agreed by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, in London in May 2025.

A follow-up summit was due to be held in July this year, but was cancelled after Starmer’s resignation. The government is now looking to change the roadmap, with one source saying that “Made in Europe should be on the agenda”.

It is understood that Hamish Falconer, the new cabinet minister with responsibility for the reset, told the EU’s trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, this was the UK’s new priority when the pair met last week.

The trade minister, Anas Sarwar, told a gathering of UK business leaders on Tuesday they needed to let their EU partners know the risks posed by Made in Europe, which will prioritise EU suppliers in key industries including car manufacturing and defence.

Ministers have privately expressed fears that the reset has lost significant momentum since Andy Burnham became prime minister, with his focus on the domestic agenda. Agreements have yet to be reached on several key issues, including what tuition fees will be paid by EU students coming to the UK on a mooted “youth experience” programme.

UK sources say that while a food and drink deal and a youth mobility scheme are still on the agenda, the government will not agree to a new summit date until the bigger issues of the Industrial Accelerator Act are included in discussions.

There was talk in London and Brussels that a meeting could be convened on 6 November, but it is understood this could now be pushed backuntil the end of November or beyond.

One government source said: “We are willing to negotiate on the things that matter to them, but they have to be able to negotiate the thing that matters to us. Made in Europe should be on the table, definitely.”

The UK fears the Made in Europe laws could jeopardise billions of pounds worth of trade if British goods are not categorised as European, locking it out of key contracts on the continent.

France, which conceived the Made in Europe laws, is pushing to have the legislation passed by the end of the year, deepening fears that British manufacturing could be left behind.

It is thought that France is sympathetic to the UK’s position, but believes increasing competition from China makes it more important to get the legislation on the books now, and make allowances for third countries later, a process that could take years.

One EU diplomat said that there was substantial backing among key member states for the UK to be included in Made in Europe, though not all agreed. “The problem is the benefits are seen as asymmetrical,” the diplomat said. “The UK gets more out of it than the EU.”

It is understood the Netherlands, Germany, Poland and Italy are all in favour of the UK’s inclusion, but France remains unconvinced.

The government’s newly assertive approach could give the UK some leverage in negotiations over concessions on youth mobility, something that is a political priority for many EU capitals.

Another UK source said a deal on Made in Europe would be “a good faith demonstration that we can find answers and almost everything else”.

A government spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic cooperation.

“We will continue to engage with the EU on Made in Europe and work together, as like-minded partners, to boost growth and open up trade.”

The UK’s desire for a deal on manufacturing rules comes at time when the EU is under pressure from industry across the bloc to loosen China’s growing presence in supply chains.

Last week, manufacturing bosses warned of a potential loss of 300,000 jobs this year unless incentives were put in place to make European products more attractive than cheaper parts from China.

The EU’s deficit with China is now running at €1bn a day, with fears that European companies are being cannibalised from within.

Her surprise offer of an associate membership deal with Canada demonstrated how far Brussels can go to court third-country partners.

Speaking in the presence of the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, the EU chief said: “We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. We must urgently reimagine our partnerships.”

The EU and Canada are to hold a summit in late October to develop their future relationship. The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, though it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, enabling deep economic integration with these countries, which follow many EU rules including free movement – a red line for the UK.

Carney, who is to address the European parliament on Thursday, has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU, as his country seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade.

Burnham met Carney at a football match in Liverpool on Wednesday night, where the two Everton fans watched their team in the EFL Cup. Burnham is also due to meet the US president, Donald Trump, for the first time at the UN general assembly in New York next week.

The potential new alliance between the EU and Canada will worry UK ministers that the bloc’s priorities are shifting. Should Burnham fail to complete a food and drink deal that was already on Starmer’s reset agenda, it could have implications for October’s budget, as the economic effects of easing trade with the EU is priced in as part of growth calculations.

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 18:57:14 GMT

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has been advocating closer alignment with “middle powers” since January in the face of recklessness in Washington.

But what should worry another middle power, the UK, is that it was Brussels that came up with Wednesday’s big reveal in Strasbourg.

To a standing ovation at her State of the Union address, Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted to open the door to Canada becoming the EU’s first “associate member” in a push to forge new ⁠links among allies in “an openly hostile world”.

The European Commission president’s deal could be seen as an “earthquake” offer said Joël Reland, of UK in a Changing Europe, though it remains “deliciously vague”.

But it also sets Canada apart from the UK, which could, once upon a time, have had some sort of associate membership with the EU were it not for the drive for a clean-break Brexit.

The last time associate membership of the EU was mooted was in relation to Ukraine as an off-the-books novel way of bringing Kyiv closer to the bloc without become a fully fledged member state.

New partnerships, von der Leyen said, were needed “in the cold fragility of today’s world” and in the face of an increasingly assertive China.

Just moments earlier she spoke about the need for the EU to diversify urgently its supply of critical raw materials (CRM) and rare earths currently dominated by China, allowing it to follow Japan and stockpile said minerals needed for everything from the car to the defence industries.

It is not a new subject – after all the EU has been grappling with China’s export surplus since 2023 and it introduced the Critical Raw Materials Act as far back as 2024.

The prospect of an enhanced relationship with Ottawa is one that Keir Starmer might have dreamed of.

Canada has something the EU desperately needs – rich supplies of CRM and rare earths – and the EU has something Canada urgently wants: new markets for products it can no longer sell into the EU in the face of a trade war with Donald Trump.

Speaking before von der Leyen’s speech, Tobias Cremer, a German social democrat MEP, said a new deeper relationship between the EU and Canada could be a blueprint for other countries, including the UK.

Bernd Lange, the influential chair of the European parliament’s international trade committee, said associate membership could “become a model for close transcontinental partnerships with democratic countries against the new model of the law of the strongest”.

After Iceland’s rejection of membership of the EU, Fabian Zuleeg, the chief executive and chief economist of the European Policy Centre, suggested it was time that the EU developed new models, beyond the European Economic Area, that might offer “partial, gradual or associated membership options”.

Reland said the vagueness of the offer extended to Canada could be promising for the UK’s hopes for a similar offer.

“Any deep Canadian integration into the EU market would take some very heavy work to negotiate a defined set of treaty-bound rights and obligations, and so it seems more likely that – at least in the short term – cooperation will focus on more vaguely constructed alliances for ‘prosperity’ and ‘security’,” which aligns with the UK government’s desires, Reland wrote on Wednesday.

In the current political climate in the UK, it is difficult to envisage a world in which Andy Burnham would encourage any associate membership of the EU. He has a steely focus on domestic issues and is keen to avoid going down any Brexit wormholes.

The UK is seeking a reset with the EU, but the goals in the first year were modest and have yet to be achieved.

The offer to Canada suggests the bigger ambitions for relations with the EU the better.

Charli xcx Music, Fashion, Film tour review – an electrifying and deafening pop evolution

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 18:55:54 GMT

Barclays Center, Brooklyn

The tireless star brings her latest, somewhat over-explained album to the stage for a dazzling and euphoric show

For more than a year now, I have often returned, when seeking a bar for which to measure true pop transcendence, to the memory of Charli xcx taking the Other Stage at Glastonbury: the unofficial headliner, a year out from her culture-shifting opus Brat, commanded a dizzying 60,000 people with an imperious “don’t fucking play with me” and the stunning brute force of a performer at peak power. It was surreal, as a longtime fan, to witness an artist who was as recently as 2022 playing to cult followings in 2,000-cap venues convert thousands more in real time, to see years of hard-earned pop instincts and artistry collide with the zeitgeist in a career-defining, you-had-to-be-there achievement.

But life goes on, of course, and Charli, like the rest of us who surfed the high of Brat summer 2024, found herself on an inevitable comedown. A lesser artist may have confronted the question of what comes next with blunt commercial logic – more, again – but Charli, a self-professed workaholic and tireless interrogator of one’s own image, proved to be creatively restless, if scattered. A cinephile rebrand, three films at Sundance, an Instagram-dominating celebrity wedding, a defanged satire of her own sudden ubiquity, a windswept soundtrack that more or less saved the otherwise dreadful Wuthering Heights – all suggested a self-aware ambivalence with mainstream success that threatened to corrode all that came after. With the release this July of Music, Fashion, Film, her eighth studio album, I worried that she had succumbed to a seemingly manic drive to stay visible. The album, a deceptively vulnerable and winking pivot to rock that was either self-aggrandizing pastiche or genius, depending on what angle/substance/context you beheld it, did not seem to stand up the scrutiny and over-explanation of relentless celebrity promotion.

But on Tuesday night at the Barclays Center, for the third night of the album’s tour, Charli proved doubters wrong with the most satisfying answer yet to what comes next: a full-volume tribute to pop’s euphoric potential for obliteration that substantiated the album’s most potent themes (the fragility of self, egoism, mortality), a thesis statement of artistic evolution that seamlessly integrated her past and present. After essentially conquering the art of abrasive minimalism with her solo stunting for Brat, Charli has embraced just enough maximalism to freshen up an arena tour – pyrotechnics, backup dancers (in club-ready bras, of course) and most evocatively, a pyramid set composed almost entirely of layered speakers, befitting a pop artist refreshingly in touch with her death drive. Forget toothless escapism – more than any other main pop girl, Charli has embraced the notion that, as David Cronenberg advises in a spoken-word outro blared from the screen, oblivion is freedom. Fitting, then, to strut and writhe and scream at the altar of a giant, smoking amplifier.

Loudness can, in fact, count for a lot. After several festival headline slots this summer proving the new material’s live mettle, the blown-up Music, Fashion, Film tour confirms the album’s caustic yet restorative vision, or at least that the contested MFF opening salvo Rock Music has its time and place. The new songs suddenly make sense when delivered on high by Charli and her band of underfed musicians that would be seen on stages in 2007 (not coincidentally, also the name of the album’s catchiest track), amped up to the max and crackling with live guitars – deliriously searching, itchy and jagged, even if the crowd’s head-banging in response was at best polite.

The bristling arrangements cast the album in a flattering grayscale light, less a pop departure and more an extension of Charli’s longstanding search of catharsis and embrace of contradictions, brash fiendishness by a different name. The transitions from Wuthering Heights track House – a show highlight dripping in strobe-lit distortion – to “surprise” fan-favorite throwback Next Level Charli to new track Dying for You to a relentless five-song Brat mini-show were near seamless, if appropriately deafening from all sides. You can’t really accuse her of riding the contrails of Brat when the tracks – Von Dutch, 365 remix, 360, Sympathy is a Knife among them – still have the propulsion of a jet engine; I may forever hear the echo of gay men, women and apparently children screaming “bumpin’ that” off the Barclays ceiling.

But Charli is far, far savvier than to resort to sandblasting fans into ear-ringing submission; the show keeps just enough of her minimalist bent to suggest a morphing of her club-rat persona, embodying the mesmerizing highs and crushing lows of ego. No CGI visuals, no guests, no stage banter, just a singular vision of persona: one minute she’s strutting down the runway under fashion lights flanked by an army of imitators to the dead-eyed shopaholic requiem Card Declined, the next she’s alone on the floor, then merely a solo silhouette disappearing into fog.

Nothing lasts forever, Cronenberg reminds us in the Music, Fashion, Film song of a similar name – No One Lasts Forever – that serves as both the album and show’s sticky finale. Flanked by dancers, Charli struck and held a pose meant to be captured for posterity, backed by the looping certainty of impermanence – “they are dead, they are gone, nothing lasts forever,” no more explanation needed. There are now, conservatively, 10,000 photos of that final tableau, and 10,000 more from the night before that will live in the iClouds of hardcore and bandwagon fans alike probably forever. But the moment is inevitably, sadly, thrillingly gone.

‘Newsnight’s kindest critic’: Bonnie Greer was always effortlessly in command

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 18:54:48 GMT

Playwright was an unusual mix of originality and authority and in high demand as a cultural critic

Bonnie Greer, who has died at the age of 77, moved to the UK from New York in 1986. She grew up in Chicago with six younger siblings. Her father worked in a factory and her mother “kept house”, she said once – in a tone so elegantly ominous, she conjured an image of a woman holding up a full dwelling with seven children in it, with her bare hands. Greer was ambitious and, academically, a high flyer, but abandoned her law degree, facing baked-in sexism from professors. Yet, given she started writing plays aged nine, arguably she was only hastening a creative career that was inevitable.

The Actors Studio was what drew her to the West Village in Manhattan in the late 70s, and she was there at the height of the Aids crisis, a brutal time of mass bereavements and poisonous prejudice. She lost about 35 of her friends, and later told the Sunday Times: “I owe those people my life. If I hadn’t met my gay friends I would be a suburban SUV-driving granny. They taught me the value of insurrection and fun. Nearly 30 years on, I’m still that 25-year-old, on top of some bar, in one of those vintage dresses, dancing with those guys.” But when she arrived, touring, at the Edinburgh festival, it felt like a release, from the “shadow of death”, and a New York theatre scene bereft of its heart. She stayed in the UK permanently.

Greer was a remarkable talent as a playwright: witty, dry, serious, unflinching. She was playwright in residence at the Soho theatre in the late 80s and was writing plays for Radio 3 and 4 by the early 90s. Marilyn and Ella Backstage at the Mocambo, in 2005, is perhaps the most famous, and was later adapted as a stage musical. It dramatises the solidarity between the actor and the singer – Monroe persuaded the club to book Fitzgerald, with the promise that she (mid-1950s, the height of her fame) would sit in the front row every night. Fitzgerald later said she never had to play a small jazz club again thanks to this intervention, and it redrew the boundaries of what was acceptable, in racism, in jazz, in Hollywood. In Greer’s telling, there is no white saviour narrative, only a dynamic creative symbiosis between two geniuses.

Bonnie Greer was a joiner. She was on the board of everything, from the Women’s prize for fiction to the British Museum, she was president of the Brontë society – she got stuck in. An unusual mix of originality and authority, she was in high demand as a cultural critic, particularly in broadcasting. She was a regular contributor to Newsnight Review on BBC Two, as well as a critic for Time Out and a political commentator for newspapers, including this one.

Out of all that came her appearance in 2009 on Question Time with Nick Griffin, then leader of the BNP. It was a frankly bizarre, though not uncharacteristic, bit of political curation from the BBC, since Griffin was a holocaust denier and racist, tried three times and once convicted (in the late 90s) for inciting racial, Islamophobic or antisemitic hatred. Many wondered why the BBC felt such a duty to platform so toxic a figure, and Sayeeda Warsi, also on the panel, asked Greer before whether she was OK to sit next to him (Greer replied: “I’m from Chicago, I’m not scared of this guy”). She said later to the Evening Standard that it was “probably the weirdest and most creepy experience of my life”, but onscreen she was unruffled and effortlessly in command, and she later turned that weird creepiness into an opera for the Royal Opera House, on whose board she also served, along with the London Film School’s.

She was very generous on a panel, receptive and softly spoken while absolutely trenchant, and vividly engaged; she was never without a view. She wrote two novels, Hanging by Her Teeth in 1994 and Entropy in 2009, but her more natural metier was in the discursive, collaborative arts and broader culture. She was once called “Newsnight’s kindest critic”, and said of her stage writing: “I was taught that theatre is supposed to slow the world down so it can be looked at, and the person who looks is not supposed to be the same when they walk out. Otherwise, there’s no fucking point. Art is not a leisure activity. It’s about engagement.”

Nato needs “more UK and more Europe” to deal with the most dangerous security environment faced by the west in a generation, the secretary general of the 32-country military alliance said this afternoon on a visit to the UK.

Mark Rutte praised Britain for promising to increase defence spending in line with US demands after a meeting prime minister Andy Burnham – but argued that the military and financial effort must continue into the future.

“It is essential that your armed forces continue to provide the hard power Nato needs,” Rutte said in a speech to a specialist audience at Ditchley Park, a wartime retreat used by Winston Churchill in Oxfordshire.

It was a plea for the UK to make progress towards an alliance-wide target demanded by Donald Trump of spending 3.5% of GDP by 2035, about £30bn in real terms, money that has to be found from extra taxation, borrowing or reducing other spending.

Britain has so far only budgeted to increase defence spending to 2.7% of GDP by the end of the next decade. Short-term financial pressures have meant that the army has been told to stop non-essential training by the end of the year.

Chancellor John Healey resigned as defence secretary from Keir Starmer’s government in June because the former prime minister would not commit to 3% by 2030, arguing that it would require too great a step up in the next decade.

But Healey refused to recommit to the interim target when he was appointed to the Treasury by Burnham a month later, raising questions that the new government was backloading spending increases until after the next election.

Rutte said that he had discussed Britain’s “Nato commitments” when he had met Burnham at a science business park in Oxford earlier on Wednesday, without offering any details, in the first one-on-one meeting between the two.

Prior to that meeting, Burnham acknowledged that he had replaced Starmer, but insisted that there was “never any change in the UK’s unwavering commitment to Nato and our Nato obligations”.

The Nato chief, a former Dutch prime minister, said many in Europe had made the “casual assumption” that the US would “always provide most of the muscle and pick up the bill, no matter what” until Trump returned to the White House.

Instead, he noted that during a summit in The Hague in 2025, the UK and other alliance members had agreed to increase their own defence spending to match US levels, in response to Trump’s demand that Europe take the lead in defending the continent.

“We need more UK and more Europe in the alliance,” Rutte said, because Nato “faces the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with a return to wars in Europe and the Middle East, and wider geopolitical uncertainty.

Citing “Russia and its war against Ukraine, terrorism, Iran and the tectonic shifts of global geopolitical competition”, Rutte argued that the UK and Europe needed to invest more, because otherwise “our collective defence will not be credible”.

Britain, he said, had “a central role in building this stronger Europe in a stronger Nato” and noted that the UK was spending billions to upgrade the Trident nuclear deterrent, which is pledged to the defence of Nato members.

The UK is also gradually upgrading its conventional forces, though the UK’s overall defence spending, long the second largest in the alliance, is now behind Germany. By 2029, Berlin’s military budgets are on track to be twice that of the UK.

The UK was “leading the pushback” against a Russian campaign of provocation and sabotage across Europe, Rutte said, and that the UK had been “a good friend to Ukraine”. Britain spends £3bn a year supporting Ukraine with weapons.

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 18:41:00 GMT

The Prison Service has drawn up plans to “double up” hundreds of prisoners in temporary prefabricated cells built for one person, at the request of the Ministry of Justice, leaked documents show.

Amid an ongoing overcrowding crisis in England and Wales, governors of 10 category C prisons have been asked to sign off the installation of second beds in “rapid deployment cells [RDCs]”.

The units, some of which measure 2.9 metres by 3.4 metres and include a bed, toilet and shower, were placed in the grounds of more than 15 prisons as a temporary solution to past overcrowding problems.

Estimated to have a 15-year lifespan, the steel-framed “pods” can be stacked to be two storeys and are usually occupied by low-risk prisoners, some of whom have been allowed to move into them as a reward for good behaviour.

According to leaked emails, the planned doubling-up suggested by Ministry of Justice officials would increase the overall capacity of the prison estate by 476.

Responding to the leaked documents, governors and prison officers said the numbers being proposed by Whitehall could breach health and safety laws and make jails unsafe for prisoners, staff and the public.

The plans were disclosed in an email sent on 27 August by a senior Prison Service executive to governors.

“As you are aware, maximising available prison capacity is of high ministerial interest, and HMPPS [His Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service] have been asked to explore the viability of crowding Rapid Deployment Cell accommodation,” the executive wrote.

“The physical viability of installing a second bed in these units has been worked through at pace, and the assessment … is that ground floor units only are suitable to install a second bed.

“Given continued high population growth, and less supply coming online than anticipated, it is important that all potential capacity is identified quickly, and as such the panels need to take place over the next few days.”

The email was sent three days before Andy Burnham announced a substantial narrowing of prisoners’ eligibility for the government’s early release scheme, blocking hundreds of violent criminals from being freed.

According to a second leaked document, the doubling up plans would include beds being added to temporary cells in the following prisons: Wayland, in Norfolk (43 beds); Littlehey, in Cambridgeshire (60); Erlestoke, in Wiltshire (66); and Rochester, in Kent (60).

Other prisons asked to find extra capacity in temporary cells include The Verne, in Dorset; Wymott, in Lancashire; Channings Wood, in Devon; Whatton, in Nottingham, which is a prison for people convicted of sexual offences; The Mount, in Hertfordshire; and Huntercombe, in Oxfordshire.

The second document also shows that the doubling up proposals would breach “operational capacity”, putting the number of prisoners above safe occupancy levels.

Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the Prison Officers Association, said capacity breaches could prompt industrial action by his members. “By law our members cannot strike, but I know they would walk out on health and safety grounds if asked to oversee prisons which cannot cope with the numbers being proposed,” he said.

“Creating more space increases the pressure on an already overcrowded prison estate and risks the stability of prisons. If the government are convinced that early release schemes are sufficient, you have to ask why they are now insisting prisons source every available bit of spare capacity.”

Tom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors Association, said a full risk assessment would have to be carried out on each prison to ensure the public and staff remained safe if doubling up occurred.

“RDCs are amongst the least secure accommodation in the prison estate and prisoners located in them will have to be risk assessed. If you don’t do this, the prison won’t be sufficiently safe or secure,” he said.

“Increasing the operational capacity of a prison isn’t as simple as putting bunk beds in cells. There needs to be staff available to supervise the additional prisoners and there needs to be additional regime activities.”

Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League for Penal Reform, said the proposal was an act of desperation.

“Rapid deployment cells were themselves meant to be a short-term response but, ironically, they have come to be seen as being among the more positive parts of the prison estate, with fewer issues related to violence, debt and drug misuse. The risk now is that all this will be undermined as more and more people get crammed in,” she said.

There are 87,111 people in prison in England and Wales. Under the Ministry of Justice’s own definition of safety and decency, the prison estate should not hold more than 81,616 people.

Reacting to the leaked documents, a ministry spokesperson said the department was investing up to £4.7bn creating 14,000 new prison places.

“As the public would expect, we’re pulling every lever available to ensure there is always space to lock up dangerous offenders,” the spokesperson said.

“Cells are only doubled up where it is safe to do so, and no final decision has been taken on these units.”

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 18:06:29 GMT

Men with heart, kidney or liver conditions more likely to be offered intervention compared with women, global analysis finds

Women with the same medical condition as men are less likely to be offered treatment such as surgery, a stent or a strong painkiller, research has found.

A review of global research found that for several health problems, including cardiovascular conditions, kidney disease and Parkinson’s, women were less likely to receive the same treatment as men, revealing the extent to which women have significantly unequal care.

Researchers at the University of St Andrews analysed 38 studies and found that in 33 of them women were less likely to be offered active treatment. Women with myocardial infarction, heart failure or an irregular heart beat were more likely to be given medication, whereas men were more likely to receive a coronary bypass, stent or other surgical treatment. Women were also less likely to be prescribed statins, according to the analysis, which was published in the journal Plos One.

Men with Parkinson’s were more likely to be referred for deep brain stimulation, while those with liver failure were more likely to receive a transplant than women. Female kidney patients requiring dialysis were less likely to be given permanent access and had to spend longer using a catheter. And women were also less likely to be given opioids for pain management.

For stroke and diabetes, however, there was no significant difference between the sexes in treatment. And women were more likely to be treated for dementia.

The findings come amid growing concern about the gender health gap. In March, the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, said women were being let down by “medical misogyny”. The previous Conservative government appointed Lesley Regan as England’s first women’s health ambassador, to help tackle the gender gap.

The analysis concluded the discrepancy was not a result of the need for different clinical approaches to women’s health. It found that none of the studies identified any guideline recommending different treatment by sex, raising the question of whether unequal care was a factor.

Dr Andrew O’Malley, who co-led the study, said: “For clinicians, the findings are a prompt to check whether treatment is being offered on clinical grounds rather than assumption.”

He said studies showed doctors more often attributed women’s symptoms to anxiety and made more diagnostic errors with female patients, even when test results were positive.

Dr Miriam Veenhuizen, an honorary lecturer in the School of Medicine at St Andrews, said: “While the direction of the findings was not a surprise, the consistency was. The same pattern appeared in cardiology, surgery, transplant medicine and emergency care, and it survived statistical adjustment in most studies.”

The research highlights the challenge Labour faces in holding on to the Holborn and St Pancras seat in the face of a challenge from Zack Polanski, the party leader in England and Wales, at next month’s byelection.

The study’s authors warn that evidence from previous electoral battles between the two parties suggests Labour politicians should dial down direct attacks on the Greens for fear of looking as if they are “kicking a puppy”.

Christabel Cooper, one of the report’s authors, said: “The previous administration [under Keir Starmer] had always banked on the fact that Labour would be able to say to people who vote Green that they would get Nigel Farage as prime minister.

“But in the 40 seats that we have identified, that is no longer the case – the Greens can claim to be the progressives’ party of choice.”

She added that evidence from other elections where the party has gone head to head with Labour suggests that progressives dislike aggressive attacks on the Greens.

“The sorts of people who would consider voting Labour consider attacking the Greens like kicking a puppy. They think, we are all supposed to be nice and liberal, why are we having a go at the Greens?”

The findings, which have been discussed with strategists in No 10 as they look to solidify separate polling gains made in Burnham’s early weeks as prime minister, show Labour faces a difficult task winning back urban progressives who helped the party win the last election.

ThinkLabour’s former chief executive Alison Phillips is now Burnham’s chief of staff, while other alumni of the organisation have senior roles across government.

The research was carried out as Burnham was about to take office in Downing Street, meaning it will not have captured the full effect of the “Burnham bounce”, which has seen Labour gain ground with progressive voters and pull level with Reform UK.

The poll shows that support for the Greens has increased by 12 points in major cities since the general election, while Labour’s vote share has fallen by 20 points, leaving Labour only 4 points ahead in some of its most reliable strongholds.

It found that the move from Labour to the Greens has been more pronounced among voters who are financially struggling, undermining the stereotype of Green voters as affluent liberals.

The report warned that urban voters felt they did not know what Labour’s values were, in part because of some of the counterintuitive measures taken by Starmer in his early days as prime minister, such as cutting winter fuel payments.

It also warns that winning these voters back will mean focusing immigration reforms on tackling small boat crossings rather than wider measures to tackle legal migration.

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is bringing in measures to make it harder for legal migrants to achieve settled status, which have proved controversial with Labour MPs and activists.

The report said: “On divisive areas such as immigration, where liberals and social conservatives can agree on some outcomes – reducing small boat crossings, for example – it should primarily focus on these.

“Where its policies appear tough or restrictive, Labour must be able to make a convincing progressive case for them, showing how they solve practical problems rather than simply signalling to the right.”

The researchers also found that attacks on the Greens over foreign policy had the most effect with the voters Labour is trying to win back, in part because they found these more credible than other criticisms.

While urban voters did not like Green policies on legalising drugs – which Labour focused on during the failed campaign to win the Gorton and Denton byelection – they did not view them as a particularly credible threat.

Personal attacks on Polanski, meanwhile, went down badly among those considering voting Green, who viewed criticisms of his CV and his past as a hypnotherapist as especially non-credible.

The Green leader has previously come under fire for telling a journalist in 2013 he could enlarge women’s breasts with hypnotherapy – comments he has since said he regrets.
