Fossil fuel advertising contracts at all-time high in 2026

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 17:58:14 GMT

In year of extreme weather, ad agencies found to be building Big Oil’s image as integral to family life and security

“It’s that time of the year again,” the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company told Emiratis in a Ramadan advertising campaign. “Where tanks are always full – for night after night of majlis hopping.”

When you think about fossil fuels, you might think of offshore oil platforms flaring gas in rough seas, the US/Iran war or the greenhouse effect heating up the world’s climate. A new report argues, however, that what Big Oil wants you to think about is family, friends and faith instead.

The advertising industry campaign group Clean Creatives went through the records and found that in 2026, the year climate breakdown went so haywire gardeners were growing watermelons in Bristol, there were 1,321 active contracts between the fossil fuel industry and advertising agencies, the most ever recorded.

As the war in Iran intensified global shortages of oil and gas, leading to spiking prices and profits for the oil companies, the fossil fuel industry appears to have invested part of its windfall on its image. Clean Creatives found that 386 fossil fuel companies across 73 countries had engaged 802 advertising and PR agencies to shape their public image and messaging.

Strikingly, business links between the two industries held strong, despite agencies’ claims of environmental responsibility, said the lead researcher, Nayantara Dutta.

“By reading through all of their climate disclosures, what I find most telling this year is this is the first year in our research where advertising agencies are across the board acknowledging climate risk in their annual reports,” she said.

Omnicom was the advertising company that held the most contracts with the fossil fuel industry, with 118 contracts, followed by WPP, with 88. In third place was Publicis, whose 34 fossil fuel industry contracts were no barrier to its being named as one of Time magazine’s most sustainable companies of 2026.

Dutta led a team of four who spent nine months compiling the survey. They painstakingly documented each contract by piecing together information from lobbying databases, creative portfolios and even LinkedIn posts. They quantified the extent of the trade and assessed its storytelling.

Advertising executives were portraying their fossil fuel industry clients as indispensable to our ways of life and economic security, Dutta said.

“The cultural themes we have always seen have continued,” she said. “But there is a global trend of increased economic insecurity and fear-mongering around energy supply and demand, around jobs and around fossil fuels as being essential.”

“Energy security requires all of our energy,” said Equinor, the Norwegian oil company that wants to develop the Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea, in a LinkedIn campaign by McCann Relationship Management, an Omnicom agency.

Chevron launched a campaign celebrating the US’s 250th anniversary, announcing it was “the energy that keeps America moving”. “Since 1879, our people have been more than a source of energy. They’ve been a source of progress,” the company claimed in a Facebook ad.

“In the US, UK, and Europe, we’re seeing a lot of nationalism,” Dutta said. “Really connecting the economic prosperity of a country with the fossil fuel industry and its expansion.”

In the global south, on the other hand, fossil fuel firms often tie themselves to family life and cultural events. Pointing to Adnoc’s “unsettling” Ramadan advert, she said: “Basically they position themselves not only as a company that is helping the economy and providing jobs, but as a company who cares about the culture and wellbeing of their people.

“So rather than addressing the political news of what’s happening in the world, they like to focus on the same themes of family and community to show themselves as integral to building that.”

A spokesperson for the Advertising Association told the Guardian: “Fossil fuel advertising represents a very small proportion of overall UK advertising spend. Where such campaigns do run in the UK, they are subject to some of the world’s strictest regulation under the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) and CAP Codes. The rules are clear: ads must not mislead consumers, and companies presenting environmental claims must demonstrate total transparency regarding the full scope of their activity, including distinguishing between renewable and fossil fuel operations.

“The ASA actively monitors and enforces compliance in this space, routinely taking action against claims that fall short. Alongside strict regulatory standards, programs such as Ad Net Zero continue to equip UK agencies and advertisers with the tools to reduce operational emissions, eliminate greenwashing and support the broader transition to a low-carbon economy.”

The Met wound down its investigation in 2018, after interviewing 50 men and arresting three suspects. The case, which attracted considerable attention, was unsolved.

In a statement on Wednesday, the Met said: “At 19.12 on Tuesday, 15 September officers and the London ambulance service attended an address in Chiswick, Hounslow after a man was found unresponsive inside a property.

“Sadly, a 44-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next of kin have been informed.

“At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.

“A file will be prepared for the coroner in due course.”

The Guardian view on the Houthi advance in Yemen: another vital Middle East artery becomes a battlefield

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 17:36:16 GMT

The extraordinary success of the rebels, and Saudi counterstrikes, threaten economic havoc. But the country’s civilians are paying the highest price

Even in a region beset by turmoil and learning to expect the unexpected, the lightning advance of Yemen’s Houthis along the Red Sea coast has shocked observers. More than 100,000 people have been forced to flee in a country where immiseration and displacement have become routine and half the population depend on humanitarian aid. But outsiders are paying close attention, because by claiming thousands of kilometres in a matter of days, and seizing strategically important islands, the Iran-backed rebels now control the Bab al-Mandab strait – the other major regional energy chokepoint after the Hormuz strait.

The Iran war has forced Saudi Arabia to rely on moving oil via its east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports. Now drone strikes – blamed on an Iran-backed militia in Iraq – have shut the pipeline: on one estimate, a month-long closure could cut global crude supply by 120m barrels. The halt to shipping through the Bab al-Mandab strait could be much more protracted. Taking the oil north is a far slower and more expensive route to Asian markets, and does not preclude attacks by the Houthis, who are also targeting oil facilities.

Saudi Arabia had painfully extracted itself from a war with the Houthis which it recklessly spearheaded – nominally in support of the internationally recognised government – at astounding cost to its own coffers and Yemeni civilians. It apparently hoped that it could calibrate its response to a flight from Iran to Houthi-controlled Sana’a in July, the first in over a decade, sufficiently to save the 2022 truce. But bombing Sana’a airport gave the Houthis the opportunity to escalate while blaming Riyadh.

The Houthis are not mere proxies for Tehran, but their interests are increasingly aligned, thanks to Donald Trump’s unlawful war on Iran. They need to maintain Iranian support and the strait of Hormuz crisis has created a new opportunity to exert economic pressure, and perhaps create a new income stream, via strategic gains along the coast. The forces ranged against them, including the government and southern secessionists, are more fractured than ever. The United Arab Emirates, which has clashed with its former close partner Saudi Arabia, withdrew its troops at the turn of the year.

Saudi strikes alone will not be enough to push the Houthis back. But Mr Trump has rebuffed requests for help. The Houthis have been canny enough to say that they are targeting only the Saudis, though that message reinforces the fact that their leverage could be used more broadly in future. They are also closer than ever to Djibouti, home to US, Chinese and other military bases.

The Saudis face a choice between negotiations with an emboldened enemy now making increasingly maximalist demands – or returning to the kind of full-scale war they previously regretted, with little support this time. Turkey and Pakistan are not rushing to act on the new Mecca defence pact the three countries signed in August.

Yemen’s recent history amply demonstrates the futility of seeking a military solution. Ultimately, its citizens deserve a government not dependent on either Riyadh or Tehran. Outside parties should concentrate on promoting a political process within the country. They should stress that both sides must protect civilians, and support humanitarian efforts. Their priority, however, should be a resolution to the Iran war, without which danger in the region, and broader instability, will only grow.

The Guardian view on Sweden’s election result: an opportunity that progressive parties must not squander

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 17:35:23 GMT

After a desperately tight race, voters rejected the prospect of the far right in government. A potential centre-left coalition needs to seize the moment

European progressives searching for reasons to be cheerful have been finding them hard to come by this autumn. In Germany, the dramatic rise of the Alternative für Deutschland party is threatening the liberal values that underpin the identity of the federal republic. In France, polls continue to point to a likely Marine Le Pen victory in a presidential election, which is months away. Across mainland Europe, centre-left parties are failing to muster an adequate response to nativist movements that have colonised swathes of the working-class support that they once relied on.

In such an ominous political landscape, the outcome of a cliffhanger Swedish election provides a much‑needed source of optimism – albeit one that comes with heavy caveats. Prior to last Sunday’s poll, the outgoing prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, was explicit that if his rightwing alliance won the largest number of seats, he would invite members of the far-right Sweden Democrats party (SD) to become ministers in the next government.

That would have meant the formal end of the SD’s pariah status in Swedish politics, after four years in which its parliamentary votes have propped up Mr Kristersson’s minority administration. In a Europe where firewalls and cordons sanitaires against the far right have never seemed less secure, another significant threshold would have been crossed.

Voters appear to have instead handed the narrowest of victories to the Social Democratic leader, Magdalena Andersson, and the progressive bloc of parties. The SD’s share of the vote fell for the first time since it began its political journey as an openly neo-Nazi party in the late 1980s, and it slipped from second to third place behind the conservative Moderates.

So much for the good news. As in Germany and France, the Swedish far right has not needed to win power for its agenda to become normalised and partially implemented. Mr Kristersson’s reliance on the SD resulted in a government that behaved with performative cruelty towards migrants, and enacted much of its draconian programme on deportations and citizenship restrictions. Ms Andersson has responded by offering a milder version of the same approach to immigration and asylum. As it leaked support on the left accordingly, her party recorded its lowest vote share for over a century.

Unless traditional powerhouse parties of European social democracy are more courageous in seeking to shift the dial of political debate, the far right will continue to set its terms. The SD’s chosen slogan for its campaign was “Make Sweden Sweden again” – varying the usual Maga trope in order to stress the core ethnocentric message. From the sidelines its rhetoric will become still more extreme, and the defeat of the rightwing bloc is already being invidiously attributed to foreign-born voters.

Should Ms Andersson eventually succeed in forming a centre-left coalition government, she should counter the forces of division by channelling the best of her own party’s traditions. The Social Democratic party historically dominated Swedish politics through the idea of the Folkhemmet, or People’s Home, which encapsulated the inclusive ethos of a welfare society admired around the world. Locating the resources and ambition to develop a similarly attractive politics of the common good for the 21st century is the urgent task for progressives, in Sweden and beyond.

No matter how deranged and delusional your podcast is, Liz Truss can go further

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 17:15:37 GMT

In the Trusster’s latest appearance, she says Blair and Brown had a plot to dismantle civilisation and the Tories were part of the woke establishment

Some things you can set your watch by. Like every time small boats are in the news, the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, will manoeuvre himself in front of a camera to suggest that all male migrants are either murderers or rapists. Probably both.

But some things feel older than time itself. Like Liz Truss trying to persuade the world she was right all along. Most former prime ministers leave Downing Street relatively quietly. Lord Big Dave, the Maybot and even Boris nurse their grudges in private. Rishi lives in semi-retirement – almost a recluse – and only attends parliament when it suits him. Keir has been almost totally airbrushed out of history in a couple of months.

Liz, though, is the outlier. She refuses to give up. The last cockroach alive after a nuclear apocalypse. Even now, she probably has a platoon of nuns locked up in her basement in south-east London where they are being forced to embroider a 70-metre tapestry dedicated to a revisionist history of her 49 days in office. One in which an old monarch dies and a new king ascends the throne. As one Elizabethan era ends so another Elizabethan era begins and a grateful nation bows down to her genius.

You have to wonder if this obsession is healthy. Most normal people might be slightly embarrassed to be remembered as the UK’s shortest serving prime minister. And by far and away the dimmest in living memory. But Truss seems devoid of affect. No sense of shame. If anything she seems proud of her 49 days. That long! In Liz’s mind, she was simply too good for us. We weren’t ready for her. Give it a thousand years and her tapestry will be on show in the British Museum.

One thing you can guarantee: offer Liz a platform to speak and she will bite your hand off. No matter how deranged and delusional it may be, Liz is confident she can be yet more deranged and delusional. She is every rightwinger’s favourite guest. Not only is she guaranteed to say yes, she will also make everyone else seem almost normal. Win-win. She’s done all sorts of weird stuff in the US, and in the UK she has her own podcast where she pretends to be interested in someone other than herself on Mike Graham’s YouTube channel. Graham, you might remember, is the man who thinks you can grow concrete. And Liz is sure he’s right.

The new kid on the podcast block is the former Tory Brexiter Steve Baker. So who else would he get as his first guest than the Trusster. If anything, Steve has got even more weird in the two years since he lost his seat. These days he has the look of a far-right survivalist holed up in a hut somewhere in the Montana wilderness. And his podcast surroundings have the same feel. All very basic, just a table and chairs. The table probably has a cache of semi-automatic rifles underneath it. Every so often, Steve will interrupt the recording to do an ad for gold. He no longer trusts traditional currencies.

And up steps Liz. Doing what only someone as half-witted as she can: talking non-stop nonsense. Often with a weird half-smile on her face. At times you are tempted to believe that she is in on the joke that she is the joke. But then you realise she’s deadly serious. She hasn’t quite understood that people aren’t laughing with her, they are laughing at her. There’s something almost unbearably sad about this. So much so you almost feel guilty for indulging her insanity. Then you remember that only 2,000 people are going to watch this. And only we dedicated few are going to make it to the end.

Labour has ruined the country, she says. Tony Blair and Gordon Brown had a secret plot to dismantle British civilisation and nothing has been the same since 1997. At which point, even Steve has to remind Liz that the Tories were in power from 2010. The Trusster doesn’t miss a beat. She is rushing on her run, her onboard computer set to auto-pilot. The Tories weren’t really the Tories. They were socialists in disguise. All of them. They were all part of the woke establishment. That’s why they were anti-Brexit. And austerity never happened.

At this point it would have been a kindness to wrap the podcast up. To remind Liz that antipsychotic help was available. Because to the best of my knowledge, Liz had been a minister in successive Tory governments since 2012. She had also been a vocal supporter of Remain.

Only it turns out that was a different Liz. A doppelganger. She had been temporarily captured by the wokerati and made to do and say a lot of things against her will. It was only when she became prime minister that she could self-actualise into her truest state and then she was thwarted by the Bank of England getting tough on quantitative easing. All a deliberate plot to destabilise her mini-budget. Nothing to do with the mini-budget being riddled with unfunded tax cuts.

There were only two trustworthy people left in the world, she said: Donald Trump and Javier Milei. It was time to disband the judiciary, the prisons and the civil service. The whole world order needed to be rebalanced. Steve readily agreed. He reckoned the NHS should also be included on the grounds that it had almost killed him and a friend of his. Not even Liz was going that far. But together the revolution was possible.

Then the big question. What next for Liz? Would she stand for election again? Maybe, she said. But who for? She’s long since been too mad for the Tories and might even be too bonkers for Reform. All she knew was that she would never go away. Not while there were still things to talk about that no one was talking about except her. Poor Liz. The problem isn’t that no one is talking. It’s that no one is listening. Steve chucked her a nugget of gold and they both ran for the hills. You’ll never take them alive.

Ed Sheeran wants to stay out of politics. By quitting his tour, his support acts have exposed the hollowness of neutrality

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 16:43:46 GMT

By standing behind support act Macklemore, who was removed from the tour for his vocal support of Palestine, these artists are demonstrating the self-sacrifice necessary to stand against those crushing free speech

In a statement about Macklemore being dropped from his US stadium tour for making pro-Palestinian comments, Ed Sheeran defended his own publicly apolitical stance: “If we only ever focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change.”

Every other musician involved with the tour – support acts Finneas (Billie Eilish’s brother), Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish songwriter Aaron Rowe, plus Sheeran’s Irish backing band, Beoga – has made their approach to advocating for change clear, pulling out of the remaining dates to protest against the censorship of Macklemore and to express support for the Palestinian people.

In a statement released yesterday, Sheeran stressed that it wasn’t his decision to remove Macklemore, who called for a free Palestine on stage at the MetLife stadium in New Jersey last week. “I am not complicit,” Sheeran wrote. Macklemore (who in 2014 had to apologise after being accused of perpetuating antisemitic stereotypes with an onstage costume) wrote that his removal from the tour was organised by New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium outside Boston, where Sheeran’s Loop tour is due to play in late September.

Kraft confirmed he barred Macklemore from opening for Sheeran at the Gillette Stadium, but did not respond to claims he organised the boycott by the other venues. (In a statement he said his decision was “not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf” but that such advocacy “should not obscure the responsibility of Hamas”.)

Sheeran explained that he doesn’t use his platform for politics in order to be “a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open”. Though this isn’t accurate: he performed at the Concert for Ukraine in 2022, signed an open letter to Theresa May about Brexit, endorsed Jeremy Corbyn and supported the equality act in the US.

Either way, the consequences of his apolitical stance have proven beyond doubt that there is no such thing as a neutral position, especially when you’re operating in a political culture that rarely obstructs corporate overreach. Kraft is friends with Trump and is a major donor to Israel: Netanyahu said at a 2019 awards ceremony honouring Kraft that “Israel does not have a more loyal friend”.

The decisive actions of every other musician on the tour have made a mockery of Sheeran claiming to be powerless in this situation. In his statement, Sheeran wrote that he would never “let down the fans who had made plans” by cancelling shows, “nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living”. What might initially appear as a sign of solidarity – not inconveniencing fans, not leaving other artists and crew out of pocket – has been upended by a group of artists who understand that losing financial and professional opportunities and creating inconvenience is precisely what it takes to show backbone and stand against genocide and billionaires crushing free speech.

Macklemore’s speech in New Jersey introduced his 2024 song Hind’s Hall, which castigates censorship of protest against Israel’s genocide in Palestine, particularly the student encampment at Columbia University in New York, and is named after Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israeli forces. “What you willin’ to risk?” he asked in the song. “What you willin’ to give?” Many musicians and actors who have spoken out against Israel’s actions in Gaza have talked about losing work as a result: Susan Sarandon said last week at the Venice film festival that she has had acting gigs taken away; Irish pop star CMAT said a lucrative beauty contract was withdrawn; Swedish star Zara Larsson said she was dropped from brand deals and awards shows.

That hasn’t stopped them and other figures from continuing to speak out, putting moral imperative above personal gain, and recognising that any such “loss” bears no relation to what is happening to human life and habitat in Gaza, where Israel’s military offensive is estimated to have led to a death toll of 70,000. Dublin songwriter Aaron Rowe, by far the smallest support act on Sheeran’s tour and thus the one with the most to lose, thanked him for the life-changing opportunity. “But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation,” his statement continued. “I need to be true to myself and my ancestors who resisted colonisation, and fought for a freedom that I enjoy today in Ireland.”

Sheeran and countless others take the line that pop culture should be somewhere fans can go to escape politics. “I do understand that for a lot of people, they just want to leave politics aside for a bit and be able to enjoy the music,” culture secretary Lisa Nandy said of the Sheeran situation on LBC this morning. But the fact that most right-wing politicians also take that view indicates the fact that they see pop cultural figures, with their largely left-leaning views and huge reach among young people, as a genuine threat best silenced.

As Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said yesterday, this isn’t just about the musicians on Sheeran’s tour, but “how just a handful of stadium owners can prevent [discussion of] an entire massive issue, in this case, the genocide in Gaza”. Prominent figures who go along with that view and deny the power of their voice allow these billion-dollar corporations to rob us of our rights step by step until one day there is nothing left. “We need to be very clear about how dangerous a precedent this is,” said Ocasio-Cortez.

At worst, Sheeran – who has always been open about his commercially minded approach to pop – looks like a corporate shill; at best, wilfully naive. Sheeran loves to dabble in the music of other cultures to present a toothless pan-global vision of togetherness lifted from the latter-day Coldplay playbook. But you can’t play with the aesthetics of global music without also being willing to engage in the lived reality of those cultures.

“Those who have been to one of my shows will know that they are about unity, joy, escapism, love and a place for everyone to feel welcome,” Sheeran wrote in his statement. Just as long as they shut up and sing: Sheeran’s inaction and humiliation at the hands of his principled supporting musicians have irrevocably compromised a position that’s no longer fit for purpose, if it ever was.

Ferritin face: the new health scare taking social media by storm

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 16:40:07 GMT

Seeing a pallid, washed-out face in the mirror? Prepare to be diagnosed …

Name: Ferritin face.

Age: The name is new, but the symptoms are old.

Symptoms: Pallor, dull skin, dark circles under your eyes. Looking washed out, basically.

What are you, a mirror? Oh no, does this describe you? Do you also have ferritin face?

Aren’t those just symptoms for “looking tired”? Is this one of those social media health scares with little to no scientific basis? No! I mean, yes, the term has recently become very popular on social media, as reported in the Washington Post. Ferritin face is not a real medical term (nor are there consistent criteria that define it) – but ferritin at least is definitely a thing.

Tell me about ferritin, then. It’s a complex globular protein that stores iron in the body in its inactive form. If you have low ferritin levels, it could indicate an iron deficiency.

And what happens if I have an iron deficiency? If it is severe and goes untreated for long enough, it could lead to tachycardia, breathlessness, chest pain and heart complications.

This is terrible! How can I cure myself? Well, earlier this summer, Allure magazine wrote a long piece entitled What It Means to Have “Ferritin Face”, calling iron deficiency an epidemic that women are prone to. It had plenty of advice.

Like what? Tell me now, before my dark circles kill me! It can often be overcome with a change of diet, as meat and green leafy vegetables are a good source. But you can also just go and have an intravenous iron infusion.

An IV it is! Be warned that, according to a leading iron infusion clinic, it could cost you in the region of £800.

Cabbage! Someone get me a cabbage! Alternatively, you could stop crapping your pants at every social media health scare. You should never diagnose and treat yourself via TikTok clips.

OK, fine. Think it about it sensibly. There is a vast difference between ferritin face and actual anaemia. Anaemia doesn’t just make you pale and tired-looking; it can leave you fatigued and breathless, with headaches, dizziness, palpitations and a loss of concentration being common symptoms.

Oh, I don’t have any of those. Good. But if you do, the NHS recommends that you see a GP, who will try to discover the underlying reason for your iron deficiency – which could be anything from heavy periods to cancer – and put you on a course of iron tablets.

So I don’t need to worry about ferritin. Probably not, no. But get an early night tonight. You look dreadful.

Do say: “You do not have ferritin face.”

Don’t say: “But you do have ferreting face, which is far worse.”

Pension peril: is it time to unpick the triple lock?

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 16:16:23 GMT

Readers are divided on whether the triple lock should stay or go

The article about whether the pensions triple lock should be ditched omits several key facts (‘Costing billions’: is the pensions triple lock a lifeline or simply unaffordable?, 12 September). The triple lock was introduced in 2010 to attempt to reinstate the value of the state pension relative to average earnings. The new state pension is just over £12,547 per annum, as your reporter says; older pensioners get a basic £9,615. Both are well below the European average, which is over €16,000 (about £13,800) per year. The UK median wage is above £39,000 a year. Moreover, the age at which the UK state pension becomes payable is among the highest in Europe.

The discussion on the affordability of the state pension seems to regard it as expenditure for no return. It is not. Pensioners spend money into their local economy, which generates tax revenues in the form of VAT and income tax from younger people who are dependent on pensioner money for their employment. Better-off pensioners pay income tax in the usual way. In fact, a pensioner with any income at all above the new state pension will pay tax on it as the personal tax free allowance is now £12,570, only £23 above their pension income.

The British Chamber of Commerce has called for the triple lock to be scrapped, and the money saved to be put towards tackling the youth unemployment crisis. This is a specious argument, designed to make scrapping the triple lock attractive to young people. This country can afford to support both its old and young with a decent standard of living. Sue HawthorneHaddington, East Lothian

I think the triple lock should go. It’s done its job and brought the state pension up to a respectable proportion of average earnings and I don’t think it would be right for pensioners’ income to go streaking ahead of everybody else’s (UK retirees with no other income will not pay tax on new £13,000 state pension, No 10 says, 15 September). What’s more, I think pensioners – like me – ought to pay income tax and national insurance, just like working people. Apart from the morality of paying tax, the state is spending at least as much on our welfare as on anybody else’s and it seems only right that we should contribute if we can.

Perhaps I’m more fortunate than others. My sole income is the state pension but I travel abroad, I donate to charities, I give decent gifts to the grandchildren and I still end up with a little cash left over at the end of the year. I’m from the generation that was taught how to live frugally yet I enjoy my quality of life: I can buy whatever I want but I probably don’t want to buy that much. I’m content.

I know that not every state pensioner can say the same as me. There are too many from all age groups living stressful, impoverished lives which is all the more reason why I ought to pay tax and national insurance if I can. And if I wanted to ask our government for anything in return I would say: spend some of this money on finding me an NHS dentist. Name and address supplied

A more fundamental question about the rates paid for the state pension needs addressing. Having paid in for 46 years, I get a state pension of £241.30 per week. The minimum wage for a 37.5-hour week for an under-18 apprentice is £300. Why does the government, of whatever persuasion, think that pensioners can exist on less than an 18-year-old?Chris MoranStockport

Your article about the triple lock is one of many arguing that it costs too much. I wonder how many of those in favour of this do so from the comfort of knowing that they will also enjoy a generous private, or company, pension, on top of their state pension, when they retire. Perhaps they should try living on a state pension – that might cause them to moderate their position very quickly indeed. The photograph you used with your article online, showing three old ladies sunning themselves on deckchairs, may suit the argument to picture retirement as one long holiday, but let me assure you that for many pensioners, it isn’t. Lauren White Lincoln

The state pension currently costs about £154bn a year, but what about pension tax relief of about £70bn a year? Is it perhaps that handing out money to poor or average-income people is a bad thing while tax allowances for the rich is a good thing?John BoxallFrome, Somerset

Cassandra Wilson obituary

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 16:15:51 GMT

American jazz singer and songwriter who was inspired by the Delta blues and gospel sounds of her Mississippi childhood

Cassandra Wilson, the double Grammy-winning jazz vocalist and songwriter who has died aged 70, was described in 2001 by Time magazine as “America’s best singer”. Superlatives accompanied Wilson throughout her career; her vocal skills supported them.

Wilson’s ancestry was West African and European, and the Delta blues and gospel sounds she heard in her Mississippi childhood affected her deeply – but so did the guitar harmonies her father taught her, and the early instruction in classical piano she received from her music-teacher mother. Both her parents were Miles Davis and Motown admirers, too.

I first heard Wilson live at a small arts festival at London’s Half Moon theatre in 1989. Some of the music press was touting the then 33-year-old as a “jazz singer for the 90s”. But Wilson had been audible on the jazz cognoscenti’s radar for at least four years before that – on her assured contributions to the progressive postbop albums by the US saxophonist Steve Coleman, which spawned the edgy, genre-fluid, new-jazz movement dubbed M-Base. Also there was her own sharply contrasting collection of American songbook classics (including Polka Dots and Moonbeams, and Shall We Dance?) on the acclaimed 1988 release Blue Skies.

Wilson offered glimpses of much of what was to come in her work at that Half Moon gig – deftly interweaving horn-like swerves of pitch and fast bebop scat phrasing from the lineage of Ella Fitzgerald and Betty Carter with the spinechilling contralto soulfulness of Nina Simone, alongside abstract sounds more suggestive of free-jazz.

She won Grammy awards for the eclectic New Moon Daughter (1996) with its Robert Johnson, Billie Holiday and Monkees covers, and for the highly personal standards-based Loverly (2009). She had also played, to great acclaim, one of the two central roles as enslaved people in Wynton Marsalis’s Pulitzer-winning jazz oratorio, Blood on the Fields (1997).

Born in Jackson, Mississippi, Cassandra was the youngest of the three children of Mary (nee McDaniel) and Herman Fowlkes Jr, who were both teachers. Herman was also a bass guitarist in local bands and taught his daughter basic guitar chords after she had had piano lessons from her mother; by the time she entered high school she played the guitar and clarinet, and was beginning to write her own songs.

Cassandra had also heard plenty of Delta blues music and the grittily dramatic autobiographical revelations of such African-American blues pioneers as Muddy Waters and Johnson had already enthralled her. But in secondary school, at Millsaps college, her cultural and social connections widened. She played Dorothy in a school production of The Wizard of Oz at 16, discovered Bob Dylan and Joni Mitchell and formed a folk trio with two white fellow-students – a liaison facilitated by Mississippi’s long-delayed desegregation of its schools in 1970, and which she would acknowledge as a musical turning point for her.

Wilson attended Jackson State University, graduating in 1980 with a degree in communication techniques and mass-media methods. It was an education that pointed her towards work in television and radio, but she was already performing in coffee-houses and clubs as a jazz/folk singer.

In 1981 she moved to New Orleans with Anthony Wilson, her first husband and a radio host. The marriage later ended in divorce. The crescent city’s musical opportunities were plentiful, and Wilson sang the vocal lead on an Allen Toussaint-produced Latin-jazz album called Tropical Breeze, with Jasmine, a local band. She also sat in with Ellis Marsalis, and Earl Turbinton Jr, a soul/R&B saxophonist, gave her music lessons.

In 1982, Wilson moved to New York, joined jam sessions, studied ear training with the trombonist Grachan Moncur III, and encountered Coleman’s adventurous expansions of bebop into funk, hip-hop, 12-tone modern-classical ideas, and the spontaneous harmony ensemble methods of his namesake Ornette Coleman.

Wilson contributed expressive vocals to Steve Coleman’s albums Motherland Pulse and On the Edge of Tomorrow (1985, 1986), experiences that stretched her talents for impromptu wordless vocals, and the note-bending elasticity, lustrous textures, and vaulting range of her remarkable voice.

She began releasing her own albums for the German producer Stefan Winter on his new JMT label, releases that evolved from M-Base’s structural radicalism to more song-based originals and covers drawing on a lyrical soulfulness deep within her Delta background. It was her third album for JMT, the standards-based Blue Skies (1988), that alerted mainstream fans and the music business to Wilson’s wider appeal.

In 1989, Wilson was invited to open for Davis, a personal idol, at the Chicago JVC Jazz festival, and by 1993 she was signed to the renowned Blue Note label. With the albums Blue Light ’Til Dawn and New Moon Daughter (her first Grammy-winner), Wilson revealed how powerfully she could re-imagine a famous song such as Strange Fruit, as well as classics by Mitchell, Johnson, Van Morrison – and the Monkees’ Last Train to Clarksville, chosen by Wilson for its Vietnam-bound US soldier’s message. She tended to undersell her fine original compositions such as Until and Memphis, and her sensitive delivery of them deserved more attention than they received in her most cover-devoted years.

Travelling Miles, Wilson’s 1999 tribute, featured some of her most expressive singing – especially on the evocative Time After Time – although her lyrics overlaid on what had been spontaneous Davis instrumentals occasionally detracted from the original pieces’ implacably hypnotic drive. Belly of the Sun (2002) was a personal homage to blues of all kinds (recorded in an abandoned Mississippi railway station) that included Wichita Lineman, and Dylan’s Shelter from the Storm; and Loverly (2008) was an affectionate return to standard songs after a long gap, enhanced by the presence of the pianist Jason Moran in the lineup.

Wilson released her final solo album, the respectful homage to Holiday, Coming Forth By Day, in 2015. The same year, she returned to live in Jackson, founding a jazz club and a record label with an old friend, the singer Rhonda Richmond, to promote the arts in Mississippi.

Boston’s Berklee College of Music awarded Wilson an honorary doctorate in music in 2020, and in 2022 the US government presented her with its highest jazz award, a National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Master fellowship. Her final live performance came in June this year, at the Toronto jazz festival.

Her further marriages to Bruce Lincoln and Isaach de Bankolé ended in divorce. She is survived by her son Jeris, from her first marriage.

Cassandra Marie Fowlkes Wilson, singer, born 4 December 1955; died 1 September 2026

Andrew Forsey urges the government to restore the link between free school meals and the holiday activities and food programme

There are 500,000 children growing up in poorer families who are confronted by a similarly cruel cliff edge to the one covered by your article (Chancellor urged to fix £100k childcare ‘cliff edge’ that prompts parents to cut work, 10 September). It is this group of children who, having recently become eligible for means-tested free school meals during term time, are disqualified from accessing the holiday activities and food (HAF) programme. While the government has rightly acknowledged the need for those children to receive extra help during term time, it has somehow reached the decision that this need does not extend into the school holidays.

HAF is a terrific programme providing nutritious meals, enriching activities and free childcare for many families. Since its introduction, eligibility for it has always been linked to the receipt of free school meals. But the government’s decision to break that link will result in working parents, earning as little as £7,500 a year, being unable to access this vital support. Any gains accruing to their children in term time risk being wiped out by this lack of support in the holidays.

There is still time for the budget to restore the link between free school meals and HAF. Failure to do so will lead all too many low-income families towards a cliff edge in next year’s school holidays. Andrew ForseyNational director, Feeding Britain

Location-tracking apps have turned me into a gibbering wreck – but I just can’t look away

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 16:14:58 GMT

When my loved ones are on the move, I can’t rest until I know they’ve got from A to B safely. How I long for the ignorance of the olden days

I’ll call it compassionate surveillance. It’s what I do when I’m worried about a loved one who is on the move. I’m not sure it’s a good thing. Be they travelling by plane, train or automobile, I will keep tabs on them. I can’t help myself. If my daughters – who are highly competent grownups – make a long car journey, by means of some smartphone hocus-pocus I’ll know where they are. I should point out that this is done with consent: they know that I know where they are. In my mum’s case, this is less true, if only because she has long given up trying to make head or tail of location sharing and other such sorcery.

I cross my heart and hope to die when I swear to you that I only do this when they are in transit. Honestly, I never look up where they are on a night out or whatever. That would be weird – or weirder, anyway. But when they get in a car, I get the fear. The catastrophising begins. It’s a big world and their car is small. A million other cars, buses and lorries share the roads on which they are motoring. In this, as in all things, overthinking is calamitous. The more you think about what could go wrong, the more your imagination obliges with a steady stream of ghastly possibilities.

The answer is simple: stop being an idiot, stop torturing yourself, stop thinking about it and think about something else. Sometimes, I achieve this. More often, I don’t. I resist the temptation to check the tech for as long as possible, but invariably I give in. I’ve yet to find anything absorbing enough to distract me from the paranoia. I can be sitting at a football match, in a live radio studio, in an intense conversation, and that will work only for a while before a sick feeling strikes and I’m wondering if my loved ones are all right.

The irony, of course, is that if I had no means of checking, I’d barely be dwelling on it. Just like in the olden days, when there were no mobiles and there would be one phone call home a week and all worries would have to be parked up and set aside until then. Ignorance was bliss. Information can be the opposite.

I know this, but before long I’m tracking them anyway. They’re reduced to an avatar on my phone screen, moving, it seems to me, with alarming speed. They’re often on a route I know well, so before long I’m basically in the car with them, worrying about the road narrowing here, a nasty bend coming up there and so on. Before long, I can’t take it any more and I leave them to it, before checking in again – and again.

Flights are worse. I’ve got an app, obviously, so I can see the plane they’re on and everything about that plane. So much to worry about. Ten years old? Eh?! Is that even legal? And what do you mean it’s already been to Nice and back today? Doesn’t it need to have a rest, cool down, or something?

Then it takes off, into alarmingly crowded skies. When you zoom out on the app, you can barely see the ground for all the planes! When you zoom in to track the metal tube conveying your loved ones, at great speed, at thirtysomething thousand feet, it’s scarier still. Other planes head towards them. Frantically, I check an incomer’s altitude. It’s going to miss. That’s a relief. Probably couldn’t have informed air traffic control in time anyway.

Eventually, obviously, it lands (and I can barely write that for fear I’m tempting fate). Relief. And I wonder if this is what it’s really all about – as much as I worry for loved ones, perhaps I’m just slaking a thirst for tension and the subsequent release from it. Thrill-seeking, in other words; needing the endless cycle of fear and relief just to feel alive. It can’t be good for you.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

Are you cleaning your cat litter box correctly?

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 16:00:24 GMT

How often should you clean your cat’s litter box? Plus three other tips for peak cat cleanliness

Throughout history, people have revered cats. Ancient Egyptians worshipped feline deities. In Norse mythology, the Viking goddess Freya rode around in a sled pulled by two cats. And my father regularly takes his cat on walks around town in a little bubble backpack so she can see the sights.

As anyone who has lived with a cat knows, we serve them and not the other way around. This includes the messy and malodorous task of tending their litter box.

According to experts, there is often room for improvement. “The most common mistake people make when it comes to their cat’s litter is creating a setup that works for them instead of for the cat,” says Samantha Bell, cat expert and content strategist for the non-profit rescue Best Friends Animal Society. “But we bring our cats into our homes, so we need to do our best to ensure they are as comfortable as possible, and a litter box is a huge part of their comfort.”

Below, what you need to know to ensure your feline overlord’s bathroom satisfaction.

On TikTok, I once saw someone claim cat owners should have a litter box in every room. I imagined my small apartment crammed with litter boxes and despaired. “Is that what you want?” I desperately asked my cat, who doesn’t speak English and doesn’t respect me enough to answer me even if she did.

Fortunately, like much TikTok content, this wasn’t true. But more than one litter box is often a good idea, especially if you have multiple cats.

“It is recommended that there be one litter box for each cat in the household, plus an extra,” says Dr Lori Bierbrier, Ssenior medical director of community medicine, east coast, for the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA). For instance, if you have two cats, three is the ideal number. If you live in a multilevel home, “there should be one litter box on each floor,” she adds; this ensures cats don’t need to travel too far when the need strikes.

Cats can share litter boxes, says Dr Marci Koski, certified feline behavior and training consultant and owner of Feline Behavior Solutions. “It can be a good way for them to get to know each other,” she says.

But some cats don’t like to share, “especially if there’s a contentious relationship between cats”, Koski says. “That’s all the more reason to have more litter box locations than cats.”

“There are quite a few elements that go into creating a good litter box setup for one cat, but it doesn’t need to be complicated or difficult,” says Koski.

Make sure the box is big enough. “Most boxes that you find in the pet store are too small,” says Bell. According to experts, a litter box should be 1.5 times the length of your cat, measuring from their nose to the base of their tail. “That should give them enough room to dig, bury and turn around without touching the walls,” says Koski.

Use an open box. Though humans may prefer closed boxes that hide the waste, most cats prefer open boxes “because that gives them a wider field of view and helps them feel safe”, says Koski. “Plus, it doesn’t trap unpleasant scents all in one place.” The entrance should also be “low enough for them to get in easily”, says Bell.

Choose the right location. “Cats prefer that their litter boxes be located in a quiet but not ‘cornered’ location,” says Bierbrier. This means that they want to be able to see other people and animals approaching, and have multiple escape routes in case they want to leave their boxes quickly. Keep boxes away from “busy, loud or intimidating places”, like next to the washer and dryer, or areas with a lot of foot traffic, says Bierbrier. Additionally, keep the box away from the cat’s food and water, suggests Bell, explaining that cats are extremely clean and don’t want their food too close to their toilet.

Use the right litter. Our house cats’ ancestors were wild desert cats, says Bell, and some of those instincts remain. “So when you’re thinking about what kind of litter to use, think about the closest thing to sand,” she says. Most cats prefer unscented, clumping litter with a medium to fine texture, says Bierbrier. As for how much to use, Bell says the litter depth should be “deep enough to be able to cover their waste comfortably” – usually between 2-3in.

Experts agree that litter should be scooped at least once per day, and maybe more depending on how heavily the litter box is used (if it is used by multiple cats, for example) or if your cat is particularly picky.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

The litter also needs to be fully replaced from time to time. Depending on the type of litter you use, Koski says, this could be as frequently as every 2-3 days for some pine or paper litters, or once every month for clumping clay litters.

The litter box itself should also be replaced every year or two, says Bell – “especially if you see scratches in it”, because these scratches can harbor bacteria and odor.

Bierbrier says signs that the cat’s litter box is not being cleaned correctly include:

Foul odors coming from the box.

The cat exhibits strange behaviors around the box, like excessive meowing or crying.

The cat perches on the edges of the box “to avoid touching dirty litter with their paws”.

The cat rushes in and out of the box as quickly as possible, and does little digging.

The cat scratches at areas around the box, like walls or floors, instead of digging in the litter.

One of the biggest red flags is if the cat starts avoiding the litter box altogether. This may be a sign of poor litter hygiene, but it could also be a sign of something more serious.

“There are many reasons a cat may eliminate outside of a litter box, and none of them are because they are bad, spiteful, jealous or just ‘being a jerk’,” says Ball. When a cat eliminates outside their box, it is because they are trying to communicate that something is wrong. “They don’t want to do it,” she explains. “They’re clean creatures.”

If your cat has accidents outside the litter box, don’t punish it, Ball says. Instead, make an appointment with the vet as soon as possible. Ball’s own cat peed on her one night. The next day, she took him to the vet and discovered that he had diabetes, which causes him to drink more water. “Since he is a senior, he may not have been able to control it while he was asleep.”

Not cleaning a litter box properly can also lead to health problems for a cat, says Koski. “Cats can get urinary tract infections from unclean litter boxes, and those can be immensely painful,” she says.

I have faced abuse, assaults and death threats because I’m an MP. It’s making politics a no-go zone

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 15:08:23 GMT

A new report highlights the dangers experienced by those who seek to serve the public. People are being deterred and your democracy is suffering

There is a rising tide of abuse in our politics and I feel it every day. This week, the Electoral Commission warned that harassment and intimidation are changing how candidates campaign, what they feel able to do and whether they stand again. This is a threat to our democracy – and we cannot ignore it.

The figures are stark. Commission research into the May 2026 local and mayoral elections in England found that 55% of candidates said harassment or intimidation was a problem, up from 47% in 2025. Women, ethnic minority candidates and those with disabilities were most likely to encounter abuse. The experience was so unpleasant that a third considered not standing again.

But none of it is a surprise. I have seen first-hand how abuse, threats and violence have increased in our politics over the years. Since I was elected as an MP in 2015, numerous people have been convicted for attacks, threats and abuse against me. Someone was sent to prison for saying a “bullet” to the back of my head was justified, while another person was convicted for telling me “come the revolution, you will be one of the first”.

Followers of my social media know how bad it can be. I have a regular “block of the month” feature to raise awareness of the disgusting racist abuse sent to me every day – the N-word, “monkey” and “ape” are common insults. The deluge of abuse has a detrimental impact on my mental health, and on those around me.

The abuse is not limited to the internet. I have been physically assaulted going home from work, and followed and verbally abused right outside parliament. During the last general election and again in this year’s local elections, I was accosted on the street by a local man who made me fear for my safety. I was told I wasn’t welcome in the area, despite being the MP for Brent East, and that next time “I should come prepared”. I reported the incidents to the police.

This is the hatred I face every day. And inevitably, it changes how MPs operate, how representatives serve the people who elected them.

Several years ago, I had to close my physical constituency office partly due to threats. We had a brick thrown through the window, and on one occasion my staff physically removed someone who turned up with a golf club. While I was once able to host walk-in constituency surgeries, the increased security threat has meant they are now roving, with the constituents pre-vetted. I also have to be accompanied to every event and notify the police of potential dangers. The constant fear risks making our politics less accessible.

Some findings from the Electoral Commission report reflect what I hear from young candidates, especially from minority backgrounds. They worry about canvassing and are also targeted online. Our representatives should reflect the diversity of the population, but this rising abuse will put talented people off entering the political system altogether.

It is important to acknowledge that improvements have been made. The police launched initiatives to strengthen security and support for councillors, elected mayors, candidates and others. In my experience, this has helped. But there is still far more to do. I want stronger and quicker action to clamp down on online abuse, with social media companies tackling it at source, as we know the threat can become physical when culprits feel emboldened. If social media companies fail to remove this content, they should face substantial fines. I report countless instances of vile racism every month, but very few are pursued. So the police must do more to identify those responsible – and the justice system must show zero tolerance with sentences. I also support restorative justice, so we can work towards repairing the harm caused.

It’s also important that more help is directed to those who are disproportionately targeted. We know that Diane Abbott, for example, has received extraordinary levels of abuse, while I often feel specifically targeted because I am a Black woman.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

And we all have a responsibility to lower the temperature of our politics. I recently wrote to Reform UK to call out the offensive and divisive remarks of the party’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, regarding the birthplace of Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee from Somalia who is running as the Labour candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection next month. This kind of politics inflames divisions. Yusuf is fuelling hate to boost Reform’s popularity, without caring about the consequences. For him it is a political strategy, but for society it has lasting damage.

We must act now to protect those who put themselves forward to serve, from all parties, and hold perpetrators to account in order to ensure no one is driven out of our democracy by fear and intimidation. If we allow abusers to decide who feels able to participate in our democracy and who is muted, those seeking to silence us will have won. That simply cannot happen.

Dawn Butler is Labour MP for Brent East

The secret of Mozart’s genius unlocked – has a teenager succeeded where generations of musicologists have failed?

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 15:06:03 GMT

US student Linus Chen-Plotkin has analysed music by four canonical composers looking for patterns. Turns out Mozart’s music moves in the least predictable way

It’s a question that has taxed musical thinkers for centuries: just what is it about one composer’s music that makes it more distinctive than anyone else’s? Entire disciplines of academic thought, of music analysis and historical musicology, as well as the formation of classical music’s canon of “great” composers, have been given over to this single idea: can it be proved that Mozart, say, was measurably “better” than other composers?

Our instinctive feeling about the sensual magic of Mozart’s music is part of the equation, but accounting for precisely how his pieces can sustain a lifetime of listening, why their pleasures never seem to pall and are still capable of seeming to surprise us even when we know them inside out: that’s the million-dollar musicological question.

What generations of music analysts have tried and largely failed to do through imperfect means of variously subjective techniques, an 18-year-old US student has managed to prove through a combination of data and interpretative ingenuity.

A recent study by Philadelphia student Linus Chen-Plotkin demonstrates that Mozart’s melodies are more surprising in the way they unfold, moment-by-moment and note-by-note, than those of his contemporaries and successors, Haydn, Beethoven and Schubert.

Chen-Plotkin put 600 movements of these four composers’ piano sonatas and string quartets through his bespoke software to analyse their tunes, based on Markov chains and other statistical and mathematical tools (he explains his work here). The data revealed that Mozart’s tunes have a shorter “memory” than other composers. That means the way they move is less predictable: that Mozart sets up patterns of expectation in his melodies and ideas that he confounds rather than confirms.

You can instinctively hear that at work in so many moments of his string quartets: the opening idea of the E flat major quartet, K428, which is already slipping out of the realms of the expected as early as its third note; or the opening of the Dissonance Quartet, K465, whose entire introduction is a chain of ever-more surprising moves of melody and harmony.

Chen-Plotkin is circumspect about the consequences of his work, recognising its limits as well as its possibilities. In fact, his statistical analyses shore up the conclusions that musicologists have often made about Mozart’s music: that it’s dizzyingly rich and strange in how it moves from note to note and phrase to phrase, but that Mozart was less interested in finding new or unpredictable structures across entire movements. In fact, if Chen-Plotkin were looking at unpredictability across whole pieces and not at the smaller scale of individual tunes and melodies, he would probably have come up with very different results: my hunch at least would be that Beethoven and Haydn would win those contests.

Mind you, Chen-Plotkin isn’t suggesting that maths replaces musicology. As well as being against the use of generative AI in art-making, his ambition is simply to show how statistical analysis can help reveal the underlying patterns behind human creativity. And his work has just begun: he enrols at university this autumn, and has already embarked on a computational analysis of the works and words of Chaucer.

Anyway: I’m back to put more Mozart through the random note generator of my fingers as I try – and fail, yet again – to play even one movement of his piano sonatas without making a mistake that not even Chen-Plotkin’s software or Markov’s chains could predict.

The Royal Philharmonic Orchestra is 80 this week, and, as you can see on their anniversary timeline, there’s a lot to celebrate. Which other orchestra can claim a legacy that encompasses some of the most exciting performances of Sibelius ever recorded in the 1950s and 60s? Listen to their founder Thomas Beecham’s performance of Tapiola to hear the edge of orchestral possibility, just as Sibelius pushes his music to new limits of wildness and experimentalism. Then, in the orchestra’s years with Rudolf Kempe in the 60s and early 70s, it transformed London’s musical life, and made pioneering recordings such as Janáček’s Glagolitic Mass.

But this is also the orchestra that Beecham insisted was men-only for as long as he conducted them (until his death in 1961), and which only had its first female musician over a decade later – clarinettist Prudence Whittaker.

It’s also the same ensemble who would find new dimensions of orchestral kitsch with Hooked on Classics in the 1980s, who recorded the Champions League theme in the 90s, and played at King Charles’s coronation in the 2020s; and it’s the orchestra that played this summer with Mandle Cheung, who paid an undisclosed amount to conduct Mahler’s Resurrection Symphony.

The RPO have soundtracked the decades from the sublime to the ridiculous; and they’ve surfed financial crisis after crisis over the years. Under Vasily Petrenko’s music directorship since 2021, here’s hoping the sublime continues to win out.

This week, Tom has been listening to: Riccardo Minasi’s recording of Mozart’s last three symphonies with Ensemble Resonanz. I’ve been blown away by their ferocious imagination. The rhetorical volatility of these performances, their mix of styles, genres and ideas, isn’t an outlier in how this music should be performed – it’s in the fabric of how these symphonies are composed, and what they mean. Mozart really is unpredictable! Listen on Spotify | Apple Classical

World No 4 may snub World Tour Championship

‘I’m not comfortable playing in the Middle East’

Matt Fitzpatrick, the world No 4, has admitted to reservations over appearing at the DP World Tour’s end‑of‑season events in Abu Dhabi and Dubai because of the conflict in the Middle East.

The Englishman, who is due to defend the DP World Tour Championship title in Dubai, has accused the tour of being “very vague” over plans to retain or move the tournaments. In Fitzpatrick’s mind, it is a “no-brainer” to play elsewhere, but he believes his sentiment will not feature strongly in the thoughts of the tour’s hierarchy.

Fitzpatrick even suggested that Formula One is reconsidering staging the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix in December after races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were called off this year because of the Iran war, though it remains on the calendar.

The Abu Dhabi Championship is due to take place from 5 November, with the DP World Tour Championship slated for the following week. Every indication is that those competitions will happen in the United Arab Emirates, despite contingencies involving Turkey, Spain and Portugal known to have been considered.

“As things stand right now, I would say I’m not that comfortable,” Fitzpatrick said about playing in the Middle East. “A few things have changed for me. I had a child in August and that changes things a bit more.

“It would feel a little bit weird, given what I’m reading elsewhere. Things can change overnight, I’m sure. I think it seems to be going down that path of things are getting better. I’ve looked on the UK [government] website, I know they changed it from essential travel only to one step better than that.

“I know the tour has been on this for a long time. It’s frustrating the decision hasn’t been made so you can plan. But I understand there’s a lot of moving parts to that and it’s difficult to make these decisions.

“If the tour do go, I’m sure they have had the best advice possible on what that looks like. As things stand, I wouldn’t necessarily be too keen on going. I know there’s been discussions on what Formula One is doing. I’ve heard they might not be going there, so it begs the question, would we, I guess.”

Fitzpatrick later made reference to missile strike damage to a hotel in Dubai where he had dinner in the week of his 2025 win at Jumeirah Golf Estates. “That’s very scary,” he said.” Pressed on whether he felt his viewpoint would be heeded, Fitzpatrick said: “I don’t think so.”

Fitzpatrick said his management was informed in April that the tour would make a decision by June. “I’m sure the Middle East want the DP World Tour to go there badly because it’s a great event for two weeks. It’s great for tourism and all that sort of stuff with it, but I wouldn’t say that I have had regular contact.

“It’s been very vague the whole time and they have not necessarily kind of had open communication.”

The topic is a rising one for discussion this week at the PGA Championship, the DP World Tour’s flagship competition, at Wentworth. The Open champion, Ryan Fox, is content to be guided by the tour. “There are some concerns,” the New Zealander said. “I’m of the opinion that the tour is doing their due diligence. If they feel like it’s safe for us to go, I’m willing to support that.

The dominance of AI is not inevitable. We can choose to change things for the better

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 15:00:23 GMT

Countries have come together before to make international agreements in the face of existential threats

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

With many technological developments, from algorithm-driven social media to AI, many people assume there’s a degree of inevitability to their widespread adoption in society.

The argument goes something like this: once the ideas and means to produce the tech are known, then it is inevitable that its usage will spread and we’ll essentially be stuck with it. So therefore we need to accept this and adjust our lives to live with the tech and use it (or at least tolerate it).

This argument seems pretty straightforward, since we’ve seen many tech-driven disruptions play out in the past 20 years or so. Uber displacing the taxi industry and the rise of “gig workers”. Algorithmic social media displacing, well, everything. Privacy-invading, hyper-targeted advertising reshaping the internet.

And it seems like generative AI is destined to be another huge, disruptive force in our lives. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, wrote of AI in 2024 that “with these new abilities, we can have shared prosperity to a degree that seems unimaginable today; in the future, everyone’s lives can be better than anyone’s life is now”. He is also on record elsewhere saying AI would wipe out entire job categories.

Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, wrote that he believes “AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5–10 years, greatly accelerate economic growth rates, create a world of abundance and empowerment, and usher in a renaissance of democracy and freedom”.

But now, both CEOs, as well as former and current AI research staff and others, are calling for a slowdown or even a shutdown of AI development, along with greater government regulation and international coordination of AI development.

The calls for a slowdown are based on the fear that, without proper safeguards, AI systems may result in catastrophic events in the near future, ranging from the extinction of humanity to merely causing billions of dollars in economic damage.

This is not a new concern and has been raised by independent academics previously in assessing the risks from AI. However, complicating the situation is that both OpenAI and Anthropic are positioning themselves for IPOs, and so some critics say both companies stand to materially benefit from the perception that they’re on the cusp of developing superintelligent models.

AI models being developed in China are also catching up to the “frontier” models being made in the US, which has prompted some to suggest that calls for greater regulation on AI are an attempt at regulatory capture by the big US AI companies.

Regardless of how likely these catastrophic events are, as Sandra Wachter, a professor of technology at the Oxford Internet Institute, has said, AI is already causing real problems, including its environmental impact, the spreading of misinformation and replacing jobs.

This is in addition to the “original sin” of most AI models – they’re built on millions of people’s art and writing, largely without compensation or permission until more recently, and the AI companies want to curb proposed laws limiting their access to such material.

Never forget that generative AI is not a technology that is apart from human society. In fact, its development and whatever semblance of intelligence it has comes from us, and our work.

And despite what the tech CEOs say, there’s nothing inevitable about AI, and we as a society can make decisions to change things for the better.

History shows us this can be done.

What often seem like insurmountable and pervasive problems can and have been addressed by normal people putting pressure on politicians and companies, and through international cooperation and negotiation.

Countries have come together before to make international agreements in the face of existential threats. The nuclear nonproliferation treaty, as well as the associated anti-nuclear activist movement, is a good example, and many have suggested it has parallels with the current AI situation. While the disarmament side of the NPT has had mixed success at best, the NPT and similar agreements have worked to limit the number of nuclear-capable countries and reduce nuclear testing.

Gene editing via Crispr is another example. Arguably a more important technological advancement than generative AI, the use of Crispr for gene editing in humans has been treated extremely cautiously by governments around the world. No country currently allows genetic changes to an embryo that could also be passed on to its children, and 70 countries have laws against it.

Even social media companies, whose reach and influence on society seemed like it would continue unabated, are now finally facing stricter regulation from governments around the world and self-regulating in response to lawsuits in the US.

So, do not take the future dominance of AI as a given.

Personally I believe that generative AI can be a useful tool (albeit in far fewer situations than tech companies would have you believe). But to ensure we limit the worst possible consequences, we need independent oversight of its development, regulation to limit some aspects of it, and international agreements to implement these controls globally.

If you think the same, then do not accept its inevitability. Contact politicians and demand action. Protest. Speak to friends and family about how you think this technology should be used, or not used. Write to companies using it in ways you disagree with.

In the now-infamous words of Claude: you’re right to push back.

Nick Evershed is the data and interactives editor for Guardian Australia

US opts not to back Saudi Arabia in Yemen after meeting Houthi leaders

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 14:56:40 GMT

Iran-backed militants have offered Trump administration assurances over safety of Red Sea shipping

Officials from the US met Houthi leaders over the weekend at the country’s embassy in Muscat, Oman, it has been confirmed, leading to the US decision not to intervene to help Saudi Arabia drive back a Houthi advance inside Yemen.

The Iran-backed militant group reassured the US that the ceasefire agreement between the two sides struck in 2025 still held and the movement had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea. Only Saudi-linked shipping was regarded as a target owing to its blockade of Yemen, the Houthis confirmed.

The meeting helps to explain Donald Trump’s decision to condemn the Houthi advance down the west coast of Yemen for threatening freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab strait, but so far to reject any military response in support of Riyadh. The US is already embroiled in an expensive and resource sapping conflict with Iran, which backs the Houthis.

The US labelled the Houthis as a foreign terrorist entity in March 2025, but in the recent past American officials have met leaders from Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. The US vice-president, JD Vance, confirmed on Monday that the US was in direct contact with the Houthis.

The US refusal to become directly involved has put pressure on Saudi Arabia to reach either a diplomatic solution with the Houthis over the future governance of Yemen, or to try to build a regional alliance with Pakistan and Turkey to force the Houthis back. In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of large swathes of western Yemen along the Red Sea coast.

A former deputy US ambassador to Yemen, Nabeel Khoury, said a “kind of tacit understanding” had been struck between the Trump administration and the Houthis. Khoury added: “The Houthis are promising the American administration that American and international navigation will not be affected in the Red Sea, but the only danger is to Saudi ships or those carrying Saudi oil.”

In an attempt to build popular support against the Houthis in the region, Riyadh made the disputed claim that the Houthis had fired a drone at the holy city of Mecca on Tuesday, but the missile had been destroyed by Saudi defence forces. It said the drone was entering a prohibited airspace close to Mecca’s most holy shrines. The drone was intercepted at about 6.50pm local time on Tuesday, according to coalition spokesperson Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki.

Saudi Arabia said any attack on Mecca was a red line and the move was condemned in lengthy statements by the UN-recognised Yemen government based in Aden as well as the 57-country Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. The Pakistani prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, condemned what he described as a “dastardly and heinous” attempted attack on Mecca. “The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act,” he said in a statement posted on X.

The Houthi leadership – followers of a Shia Zaydism that respects the pilgrimage to Mecca – dismissed the claim as the lie of the century, and said such worn-out lies had been used before and fooled no one.

The Houthi’s deputy foreign minister, Abdul Wahid abu Ras, said “whoever opened the land of the two holy mosques to debauchery and entertainment parties, and whoever defiled the land of the two holy mosques by the presence of Zionist Jews in it, is the one who targets Mecca, Medina and the Islamic holy sites”.

The Houthis countered that they had shot down a Saudi F-15 plane close to Marib, and attacked an Aramco plant in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu. No supporting evidence was provided by the Houthi military spokesperson, but the head of the Houthi negotiating team, Mohammed abdul Salam, said the downing of the plane was a warning to the west not to fall victim to Saudi propaganda.

Mohammed al-Farah, a Houthi political bureau member, said: “The truth is that Saudi Arabia is experiencing a real predicament in Yemen. It became embroiled in a war, a siege and an occupation, and then failed to achieve its goals.

“Today, it is looking for external solutions, so it is begging the international community, warning the world about Bab al-Mandab and requesting support from Pakistan, Turkey, America, Israel and Egypt. Then it is trying to mobilise Muslims with a false pretext called ‘targeting Mecca’.”

Separately, Israeli officials have leaked details of a secret meeting between military commanders from the US, Israel and several Arab states in Germany last week to discuss the war launched by Israel and the US against Iran. The report from the Axios journalist Barak Ravid said the “private retreat” was organised by the head of US Central Command, Adm Brad Cooper.

Citing two unnamed Israeli officials, Ravid reported that the meeting was attended by the military chiefs of staff of Israel, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt. It was the first such gathering since the US and Israel went to war with Iran more than six months ago. Israel, once a target for the Houthis, is offering to intervene in Yemen on Saudi Arabia’s behalf.

A meeting of the UN security council on Tuesday condemned any attempt to close the Red Sea, but the meeting was notable for the Russian envoy beginning to edge away from its previous stance that the UN-recognised government based in Aden was the only legitimate government inside the country.

In Beijing, the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Wednesday met his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, in an effort to secure support for its plans for the future administration of the strait of Hormuz. The strait remains closed owing to separate Iranian and US blockades.

A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said China did not want to see further regional tension spill over into Yemen and the Red Sea. The Chinese called on the US to return to the talks based on the memorandum of understanding agreed between the two sides in June. Beijing, the main importer of Iranian oil, is eager for a settlement and is resisting any suggestion that US secondary sanctions applied to countries trading with Iran should apply to its own country.

Oil prices remain well over $100 (£74) a barrel and a key Saudi east-west pipeline remains closed because of a bombing incident.
