‘Very authoritarian, very brutal’: three decades after the UK’s anti-rave crackdown, why is France doing the same?

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 14:29:46 GMT

With tear gas, grenades and a new law, French authorities are targeting unlicensed music gatherings. Those in the rave scene explore the parallels with the UK in the 90s

When Spiral Tribe fled England in 1992, they left behind an indelible mark on rave history. The itinerant sound system collective are best known for their involvement with Castlemorton Common festival, an unlicensed free party drawing more than 30,000 people and lasting nearly a week. After a drawn-out and notoriously expensive trial for public order offences, Spiral Tribe were acquitted of all charges. They decided to drive their repurposed military caravans out of the UK and never look back.

Their documented history often stops there. But little known is the fact that they then kicked off “the biggest illegal underground movement that Europe had ever seen”, says Spiral Tribe associate Sebastian Vaughan, AKA electronic musician 69db.

Many Spiral members, including Vaughan, settled throughout France after a warm response to the Spiral sound – a 160bpm sped-up version of hip-house with delayed kick drums, known as hardtek or tribe – and to the collective’s punk-rave aesthetic. Over the last three decades, their underground Teknival parties in France grew from about 1,000 attendees in 1993 to tens of thousands in 1995 and up to 100,000 people by the early 2000s, far exceeding the turnout at Castlemorton. French ravers, Vaughan says, “completely understood what the concept was, and they weren’t just following it, they were creating it themselves”. He attributes Spiral’s underground appeal to the country’s likeminded appetite for resistance.

But equally, “the French have always been very authoritarian and very brutal in their response to free parties”, says Mark Harrison, another Spiral Tribe founding member. He says he has witnessed the French riot police, known as Compagnies Républicaines de Sécurité (CRS), descend on dancefloors armed with stun grenades and rubber bullets in events from the mid-90s onwards.

In 2019, a police raid caused revellers at a Fête de la Musique concert in Nantes to fall into the Loire river, and 24-year-old Steve Maia Caniço was found drowned. Two years later, the CRS raided a Teknival rave in Rendon held in Caniço’s memory armed with tear gas and sting ball GM2L grenades. There were no attempts beforehand at dialogue or de-escalation. The violence resulted in a 22-year-old partygoer losing his hand. Another woman had her cheek pierced and teeth broken by a grenade fragment. Amnesty International France reported on the unnecessary use of force at the Rendon event as a human rights violation.

Now, the French parliament has formally enacted the Ripost public disorder law, targeting unlicensed music gatherings of more than 250 people. Free party organisers could face two years’ imprisonment, confiscation of their vehicles and sound equipment, and a fine of up to €30,000. Even attendees could face up to six months in jail and a €7,500 fine.

It feels similar to the crackdown Spiral Tribe faced in the wake of Castlemorton: two years later, the UK’s Criminal Justice and Public Order Act criminalised gatherings of more than 20 people where “the emission of a succession of repetitive beats” was deemed to “cause serious distress to the inhabitants of the locality”.

The newly enacted French law aims to protect rural communities whose land has been misused by ravers, such as a May 2024 party thrown in heritage vineyards in the Loire Regional National Park or one in September 2025 in Aude shortly after the region was devastated by wildfires. In May, interior minister Laurent Nuñez, who publicly championed the bill, visited a protest against the policy in his home town of Bourges. The demonstration, he told the press, only served to “strengthen the government’s determination to crack down more harshly on this kind of wild event, which our fellow citizens do not understand”.

But critics argue that the law disproportionately affects young, working-class citizens, and free party proponents claim that the gatherings that have gone awry are only a few out of the thousands held every year.

Mouillette, a volunteer with the Fonds de Soutien Juridique des Sons, a group of French lawyers supporting free party sound systems, distributes literature on how to properly prepare a party, choose a location and secure and manage the event within legal grounds while also making sure that the rave is a good experience for everyone involved. “Many organisers are very young and need to learn,” she says, “but with the government against us, we cannot educate them.”

She says that the prison sentence for partygoers is an illogical move for legislators. The French prison system is already facing a dangerous overcrowding crisis – considered the second worst in Europe in a 2025 annual penal statistics report – with records earlier this year revealing 86,229 inmates in spaces only suited for 62,000. “We will be locked up alongside murderers,” Mouillette claims.

When Spiral Tribe and other free party sound systems were created more than 30 years ago, they were a reaction against capitalism and state powers enforcing “a path of normativity that [was] very obedient and subservient”, says Harrison. He thinks that the underground rave movement remains an important laboratory for alternative forms of society. However, “the narrowing of imagination, the narrowing of opportunities created by this authoritarian direction that we’re all being pushed [into] is very disturbing”, he says, calling it “anti-culture”.

“For us, Ripost is part of the ongoing trend towards the gradual erosion of individual freedoms and the right’s state surveillance of the population that we are facing since the Covid pandemic,” says Kamille, a pseudonymous spokesperson of Tekno Anti-repression. This collective of French free party advocates assembled in 2022 to change the mainstream narrative around the underground movement after 30 years of virtually no organising power. “There is more and more repression of social movements and protests,” Kamille says. “We consider [this] a global shift towards the right and their desire for mass control of people who are against the system.”

How strictly the French government will enforce the Ripost law remains to be seen. But Spiral Tribe members believe that more and more young people are waking up to the hypocrisy and corruption around them.

“You would have to be living under a rock to not see the double standards imposed on the population by the establishment,” says Vaughan, citing the abuses exposed in the Epstein files. “The world we live in is a nightmare.” He urges ravers to vote for the far-left La France Insoumise, the only party supportive of the free movement.

“We have to remain optimistic,” Harrison adds. “I think this is one of the reasons why power attacks free parties. They want to kill that spirit because they know that one of the most powerful things about a good party is that you feel connected. You feel that unity.”

Unmasked presents: Spiral Tribe Exhibition is at Reinstate, London, 16-19 September. An accompanying rave, SP23, is at Distillery, London, on 19 September

Chewing Gum Dreams review – Michaela Coel’s horny teenage heroine is still a force to reckon with

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 14:28:35 GMT

Theatre503, LondonLauryn Ajufo makes Tracey her own in a vibrant revival of Coel’s monologue, capturing the cruelty, confusion and comedy of adolescence

The self-flagellations of adolescence and its suddenly streaking hormones can make great fodder for comedy. Harry Enfield’s 13-year-old defined its comic pains for one generation. His Kevin is every bit matched by Michaela Coel’s exuberant and offensive Tracey. This revival of Coel’s 2012 debut proves her eternal relevance as a character: Black British and downtrodden, she is upstart, bully, trusty friend and a bewildered girl defined by class and race by her own schoolteacher. She is also horny and desperately infatuated with a white boy, Connor.

Beginning as a monologue performed by Coel herself, it is about friendship, sexual discovery and abuse, with Tracey telling us about everything from the girl in class who can lick her own vagina to her beautiful best friend with a controlling boyfriend 10 years her senior. The show went on to be adapted for the Channel 4 TV series Chewing Gum, which turned Coel’s one-woman polyphony into an ensemble of immensely colourful characters and fabulous comedy, but also lost some of its intensity and darkness.

Here it is again in its original, distilled form, vibrantly directed by Anthony Simpson-Pike. But like Tracey’s travels through time, this tiata fahodzi co-production is also a fascinating exercise in retrospection. You can trace Coel’s talent to this starting point – it spurts out of the script, like the characters’ sexual eruptions.

Lauryn Ajufo takes the character out of the shadow of the TV series to make Tracey her own – more pugnacious, earnestly schoolgirlish yet also streetwise, her youthful fears mixed with a child’s dead-eyed cruelty. This is a convincing showcase of Ajufo’s talent as an emerging actor.

Tracey’s offensive language often grates. The use of a disability slur and numerous references to fat girls in her class might be dated aspects of the script but more likely reveal the unlikable part of Tracey, a teenage girl learning to use language as a weapon, a cudgel with which to beat a threat.

Bits from the first series of the TV show can be sourced back, word for word, such as the brilliant scene in which Tracey tries to extract the morning-after pill from an intransigent pharmacist. As knowing as the show was on screen (like in Fleabag, also based on a one-woman stage show, Tracey confided directly to camera), there is a different kind of theatricality here. Yimei Zhao’s non-realist set has a distorted, dream-like quality and a tube suggesting the temporal portals through which Tracey rolls.

It is intelligent, inventive and still arresting. A blast from Coel’s teen past which feels nostalgic and fresh.

At Theatre503, London, until 17 October

Why are two college football teams playing at Wembley on Saturday?

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 13:20:59 GMT

Kansas are taking on Arizona State in the Union Jack Classic, with 60,000 and noisy fans expected at Wembley

By No Helmets Required

There have been as many college football games played in Tanzania and Italy (one) as there have in England, and twice as many in China and Australia. It’s nearly 40 years since 6,000 or so intrigued spectators watched Richmond Spiders beat Boston University in Crystal Palace. “The gray, misty ways of Richmond proved far more compatible in the Land of the Overcast Sky,” reported the Boston Globe at the time.

The 1980s was a time of international expansionism for American college sports, with games in Japan, Milan and Dublin. They have returned to Ireland time and time again over the years. The College Football Classic has become an annual event at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin, where it has drawn in crowds of around 50,000 for the last five years, prompting the NFL to visit the city for the first time last September. It’s the other way round in London, where 20 years of NFL matches have paved the way for the college game.

The match between Arizona State and Kansas at 5pm on Saturday – dubbed the Union Jack Classic – is an inevitable reaction to the NFL’s work in the city over the last two decades. “We move a little bit behind the NFL,” says Brett Yormark, the commissioner of the Big 12 Conference – a league of 16 of the most successful teams in college sports.

“It’s important for the NFL to open up these markets before we do and develop a fanbase. The NFL have played 42 games in the UK so it seemed to be a mature enough market to bring college football here, versus breaking into a new market that might not have the appetite for the sport or the game. The timing just felt right.”

Money and exposure. College sport is becoming increasingly professional and universities want to keep the cash flooding in. The top coaches are paid more than $13m a year and the players are paid substantial sums for their image rights. Arizona and Kansas pay their squads around $20m a year.

Most of that money comes from TV revenue. Teams in the Big 12 bank nearly $32m annually from broadcasters, with games shown on ESPN, Fox, TNT, CBS, and NBC. Having an international presence is a very handy carrot to dangle to broadcasters.

“Our media partners really like it when we go global, because it creates a big-event feel that they can capture – and they are in the big-event business,” says Yormark. “Fox will host their whole college football show – Big Noon Kickoff – here in London. It will be the first time they have ever taken that show international. They’re going to be here all week, making this game into something really big, not only here, but back in the US.”

“I’ve always had global ambitions for the conference - it’s good for business,” adds Yormark. “When I was the CEO of the Brooklyn Nets, we took the team to Mexico City, London and China. Football is a global sport. We were presented with an opportunity to come to the UK and took full advantage of it.”

There is another reason the universities want to play abroad: to market themselves to international students and advertise their global campuses (six of the universities in the Big 12 have campuses abroad). Having a successful college football team is a way of attracting students. “There’s real rationale behind it,” says Yormark. “About 14% of our student athletes are international, so how do you drive enrollment? How do you drive global appeal and fan engagement? All of that helps you to rationalise that going global does matter.”

“Our goal isn’t just to play here once,” says Yormark. “In sports, you’ve got to have continuity, you gotta build something. If there’s two Big 12 teams playing every year, British fans start gravitating to the Big 12 conference. They get to know our schools, our athletes, our coaches. Our ambition is to take many of our sports globally and take the conference global.”

Young and loud. With ticket prices half what NFL International Games cost, the organisers are hoping for a crowd of 60,000. “That would be a tremendous number for us,” says Yormark. “We can build on it”. With family offers and cheap tickets for NHS and education workers, the event should beat the Big 12’s average attendance last year of 50,000.

Wembley is attractive to promoters as they can still make a handsome profit even if only two-thirds of the seats are filled. It’s why the RFL have kept the Challenge Cup final at the stadium despite not selling it out. Several thousand fans from Arizona and Kansas are travelling over for the away game of a lifetime. The match should feel different to the NFL, too, with both teams flying over their huge marching bands and half a dozen performers booked in for the pre-match and half-time shows.

“This isn’t just a game,” say the organisers. “It’s a full-scale celebration of sport, energy and culture: from pre-game tailgate parties and marching band pep rallies, to a half-time show that lights up the stadium.”

They volunteered. “Our schools were very excited about it, specifically Kansas, who said they wanted to move a home game to London. They were playing Arizona at home and Arizona were more than happy to come here,” says Yormark. The timing is perfect for Arizona, who have just opened a London branch, running a dozen or so degrees out of a University of London building in Clerkenwell.

As for the players, they are very excited. “About 90% of the student athletes coming over didn’t have a passport,” says Yormark. “For them to enjoy a wonderful international experience, while playing the game they love, doesn’t get much better. The students’ experiences are the most important thing to us.”

Africa is bigger than we’ve been led to believe – what next?

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 12:00:19 GMT

A new map of the world rescales the size of Africa and calls into question our perception of land, power and influence

This month, the UN passed a resolution, brought to the assembly by Togo, to phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe and replace it with another that shows the real scale of territories. That’s right – when it comes to size, the map of the world we have all grown up with is not accurate. The main loser of land on the Mercator map is Africa, and the new “Equal Earth” map reflects its true proportions. I spoke to our west Africa correspondent Eromo Egbejule about his extensive reporting on the map changes, and why people feel so strongly about it.

Seeing the new map transposed over the old might make you feel oddly disoriented. Logically, there is absolutely no immediate tangible impact on one’s life that comes out of knowing that the entire top part of the northern hemisphere is so much smaller than you were led to believe. And yet, there is still something agitating about it, like you’ve been the subject of a lifelong trick, or at least a breach of trust.

The vast geographical inaccuracies of the old map include the shortening of Africa, and the relative expansion of North America and Eurasia. The new projection shows Africa as taking up almost double the ratio of total land area shown on the map. It all feeds into a sense that there is something domineering about it, portraying some countries as not just political and economic powers, but geographical ones as well, and therefore natural hegemons. It is an emotional response more than anything, but a testament to how much our perceptions of the physical world are linked to our estimations of stature.

No, the world map has not gone ‘woke’

The Guardian’s west Africa correspondent Eromo Egbejule is struck by how, despite its disproportionality, there was still opposition to retiring the 16th-century map. The US was the only country that vetoed the UN resolution, and six other nations abstained. The US dismissed the effort as “superfluous”, but Eromo sees this as a euphemism for “ideological” or “woke”. “I don’t see why it feels so strongly,” he told me. “This is a scientific discussion. It’s not an imposition.”

There is nothing binding about the resolution, and yet, there is something revealing about the world’s superpower opposing it. It suggests that the US would like to preserve that connection between size and status, even when appearances are deceiving. US president Donald Trump’s interest in Greenland was reportedly influenced by its inflated size on the old map, an acquisition that would swell US territory in the political imagination. Greenland is “massive” said Trump – but in actuality, it’s a fraction of its size as shown in the Mercator projection. The old map depicts it as roughly the same size as Africa, despite it being 14 times smaller. Could huge geopolitical tensions, and confrontation with Europe, could have possibly been avoided by simply showing Trump an accurate map?

Do maps really matter?

“It does matter. Make no mistake,” said Eromo. In his view, the significance is in the momentum such a resolution triggers. “There’s two proverbs we have in pidgin,” Eromo said: “every dance begins with a clap” and “it’s grains of rice that fill up a pot”. In other words, this might feel like a small change, but the boost of one successful campaign could pave the way to what Eromo describes as a “multipolar world order”. He points out that this resolution comes on the heels of a separate landmark one – the UN vote to recognise the transatlantic slave trade as a crime and call for reparations, an effort also led by an African country.

There is a growing traction around a particular kind of advocacy: one that uses the procedures of high-profile international institutions to challenge dominant western understandings of history and reality. These interventions in how we make sense of the world may be symbolic – but they are meaningful, and they are gaining ground.

Moving towards a shared reality?

Sign up to The Long Wave

Nesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the world

after newsletter promotion

It is staggering that the Mercator map has pretty much remained the unchanged standard for over four centuries. In questioning what was once assumed to be fact, the resolution has not only addressed issues of accuracy. It has also, somehow, punctured the vast and abstract unrealities established throughout history by the west. The theft of resources and people is only one part of what was stolen from many regions of the world during colonisation. Countries were then stolen from, again, in terms of landmass on maps, and also the subordinating cultural and political associations that followed. There is something intangible and deeply political about the map’s significance – which is symbolic and threatening.

Eromo said that this sort of change makes people nervous because it ties in to all the ways in which legacies of literally carving out the continent and enslaving its populations still resonate. Hanging over the resolution are questions of precedent, of the floodgates being opened – the sort of building pressure that has resulted in calls to decolonise curriculums, for example. If the map that hangs in classrooms all around the world is changed, people may ask: “What else are my children going to be taught now?” Eromo said that there is something diminishing about learning that behemoths such as the US, China and Russia “can all fit into Africa with some space to spare.”

There are broader anxieties at stake – about what constitutes our shared reality, one that is increasingly fractured by social media and AI. These make tussles about maps a matter of holding on to the little that we can establish as concrete and true, in the face of vast political and digital forces that are warping our perceptions of the world. Eromo cites a statement that stood out for him, issued by Africa No Filter, an advocacy group that has been a part of the map justice campaign: “If we got something as basic as Africa’s size wrong for this long, what else about Africa have we simply accepted without questioning?”

If you could bring a resolution to the UN related to the Black diaspora, what would it be? Send us your thoughts by emailing us at thelongwave@theguardian. com or replying to this email and we may include your response in a future issue.

The best life hack I’ve ever heard? Monetise what you’re bad at

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 11:00:17 GMT

Phil Heckels has turned his awful pet portraits into a full-time job. As a blueprint for success, embracing your lack of talent has obvious appeal

What do you get if you cross a complete lack of artistic talent with making lemonade out of life’s lemons? Phil Heckels, that’s what – or, rather, who. The former estate agent from West Sussex has turned being bad at drawing animals into a full-time job after posting a hilariously terrible portrait of his dog on social media. Friends started asking him to do awful pictures of their pets, word spread, and he’s now received more than 100,000 requests. His rules are that he only sees the photos immediately before he picks up his pen, he never restarts a drawing, and he doesn’t spend longer than 10 minutes on a creation. He also refuses to charge for his artworks – suggesting charity donations instead – but makes money through merchandise and books.

“I do get criticism sometimes that the portraits are getting too good,” Heckels said recently. “But people have been saying that since about my 12th portrait. You never have to wait too long for a real stinker to appear, though.”

Perhaps statues will be erected to this man, because let’s be honest: monetising what you’re bad at is an amazing life hack. Not to mention an inclusive one that everybody can try, because we all suck at something. There’s also surely a much faster return in taking advantage of weakness than doggedly – not intended – working hard to improve. And imagine the creative freedom! Heckels loves to draw, and that’s now how he spends his days. Maybe you’re a tone-deaf singer, a dancer with two left feet, a ceramicist who can only make mugs with holes. So what? Envision a world where rather than holding you back, a complete lack of talent and skill is a guarantee of success. Where if you aim for the moon, it’s better than fine if you can’t even get one toe off the ground. Nobody’s going to heckle that idea.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

It’s my self-care tip of the year: I quit our local veg box scheme, and set my mind free

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 05:00:12 GMT

Being a member felt like the right thing to do – and it was a boon during the pandemic. But oh, the emotional labour. I can never look at a turnip again

Last week, as summer gave way to pumpkin season, I found myself contemplating the final squash. Like the horror movie trope of the final girl staggering out of the woods after the massacre, this squash is the sole survivor. All her sister squashes had either been cooked and eaten or left to rot. Now, my killing days were almost over. There would be no sequel.

Or, to put it less dramatically: after six years, we have quit the local organic veg bag collective, which delivered to a nearby pickup point a bag of organic, local seasonal veg once a week. And as a result the mental load and emotional labour of having to contemplate and devise a use for various esoteric kinds of veg is finally, mercifully, over.

I approached the final squash the way I had many, many of her contemporaries. First, I tried to identify her so I could work out how to cook it and whether the skin was edible or not. “Medium-sized frilly orange pumpkin type” I wrote into Google. No match was forthcoming. Then I took a picture of it and did an image search. Still no match. For all its supposed miraculous capabilities, during my own experiments AI has never successfully identified a single pumpkin.

Usually, this is the point where my cortisol soars, but this time it stayed stable: this was the last time that I would expend precious time and energy trying to correctly identify a vegetable, before giving up and doing what I always do, which is chopping it up and roasting it.

Now that it’s done, I cannot tell you how liberated I feel. No more kohlrabi. No more Jerusalem fartichokes. Only my husband will miss the turnips.

Historically, I have always been a great quitter. To use hideous modern parlance, anything that no longer “served” me, whether a job, a relationship, a university course, a country, would always be efficiently dispatched. No looking back.

Leaving the local organic veg collective didn’t feel like this, though. Being a member felt like the right, ethical thing to do (“Don’t be mean about them,” my husband says. “They are a great service”). Raised by a veg box mum – and being a Guardian writer to boot – surely this was my destiny, my birthright? It gave me a warm, self-satisfied glow, albeit an ephemeral one lasting only until I was once again scrubbing layers of caked mud from all of the potatoes just so I could make my kid some sodding chips. “What is this? Wartime?” I muttered to myself.

I’d say my heart hasn’t been in it for at least two years, probably longer, but despite the fact that the relationship had become toxic I felt guilty for wanting to leave. Ever since I had my son, the veg bag has been an albatross. During the long winters, I cursed the endless beetroot. By March we were all about 65% parsnip. “More bloody parsnips,” we would sigh, as we unpacked on a Wednesday. “I’m not sure I can do this any more.” Yet another season was always around the corner. The green promise of spring. “Soon! There will be asparagus!” And we would stick it out for another year.

Well, it’s done now, even though I keep picturing Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall shaking his head in disapproval, along with you, dear reader. The veg is more ethical, better for you, and tastier than anything from a supermarket. All of this I acknowledge. Maybe I’m just lazy. And yet, I am a confident – some might say even good – cook. I make meals from scratch, I understand about vitamins and nutritional value. I sometimes open, and look at the pictures in, recipe books by Nigel Slater. It was just that something finally had to give.

It may sound hyperbolic, but getting rid of the veg bag has saved me from a breakdown, possibly. My mental load feels far lighter. “I feel so fucking free, you guys!” I posted, on Instagram, and was inundated with people who had been on the same journey. In some cases, arguing about the rotting veg in the bottom of their fridges was affecting their marriages. We all wanted to do the right thing, it’s just that modern life simply didn’t feel compatible.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

I have some fond memories of the veg bag. I’m grateful to the collective for feeding my family. I will miss being a member, especially at Christmas. We joined during the pandemic, when not every item was always available in the shops. My son was weaned on pureed celeriac. We got to try things I never would have otherwise – winter purslane! Land cress! – and I adored the rainbow chard. The kohlrabi actually made a very nice rosti. Even the final squash was completely and utterly delicious, as if to try to tempt me back. But no. It’s over. And I am finally free.

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist

Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 05:00:12 GMT

Dozens of Bank of England directors and founding subscribers invested in trafficking of enslaved Africans

The Bank of England and the British financial system were for centuries deeply involved in the enslavement and transatlantic trafficking of millions of African people, according to new research on Britain’s slavery history.

Research by historians compiling the Register of British Slave Traders has found that the scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged. The Bank of England, the central bank owned by the government since nationalisation by Clement Attlee’s Labour administration in 1946, had dozens of financiers involved in its foundation who were also significant investors in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.

Dr Michael Bennett of the University of Sheffield, who has conducted extensive research on the Bank’s historical involvement in enslavement, has found that 24 directors were investors in the trafficking of enslaved African people. Four were among the London elites who were founding directors of the Bank in 1694. The other 20 were in office at Threadneedle Street over the next century.

The last, Christopher Puller, was a shipper of weapons for the slave trade and co-owner of a 1786 voyage that trafficked enslaved people from the Gambia to Jamaica, according to the register. Puller was a director for 11 years before he died in 1789. Nine of the 24 were also governors of the Bank.

Bennett also researched the founding subscribers to the Bank of England, finding that at least 30 invested in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. At their head were the king and queen of the day, William III and Mary II, who held shares in the Royal African Company. It is clear, Bennett said, that wealth generated from the slave trade formed part of the Bank’s initial capital.

“Slave traders and their wealth were firmly embedded within Britain’s, especially London’s, private banks and financial corporations during the 17th and 18th centuries. They shaped the development of the financial system,” he said. “Banks and other institutions, like insurers, provided the financial services that supported, and made great wealth from, the transatlantic slave economy.

“The Bank of England supported this system throughout, and directly provided financial services to the slave trade. Its clients included the Royal African Company and the South Sea Company.”

An archetypal example of a Bank of England director in the register is John Rudge, the MP for Evesham. He was a director of the Bank between 1699 and 1740, and governor in 1713-15. Rudge was also a shareholder and assistant (director) in the RAC and deputy governor of the South Sea Company.

The findings of the register add to the research carried out by historians behind the Legacies of British Slavery (LBS) archive at University College London, which documents owners of enslaved people on plantations. That research found that 16 past governors of the Bank of England and 26 directors had a financial interest in the ownership of enslaved people and plantations in the period before abolition in 1833. The Bank itself, and the Treasury, were centrally involved in paying out £20m, the equivalent of £23bn today according to one method of calculation, in “compensation” to enslavers under the abolition legislation. Nothing was paid to the people who had been enslaved and trafficked.

The Black Lives Matter protests of 2020 prompted several high street banks and financial institutions to acknowledge their historical involvement in slavery. Dr Nicholas Draper, who led the LBS research, was also a lead investigator for the register and he discovered many more historic slave traders who were founders of private banks and other financial organisations.

Research by Bennett after the BLM protests found that the Bank of England had owned 599 enslaved people on two plantations.

An exhibition at the Bank in 2022 included the names of the enslaved people. Most of the men, women and children listed had European names such as Pierre, Catherine and Alexandre, with no information about the country from which they were taken.

The Bank also acknowledged and apologised for past governors and directors having been involved in the slave trade.

Humphry Morice, a longtime director and governor from 1727-29, was also an MP and defrauded the Bank to fund his trafficking operations.

Morice was described by Prof Matthew David Mitchell, in an article published on the Bank’s website, as “the biggest London-based trafficker of enslaved human beings from Africa to the British colonies in America.” Morice was responsible for equipping about 110 ship voyages between 1704 and 1732, transporting more than 30,000 enslaved men women and children to Jamaica, Barbados, Virginia and elsewhere in America, Mitchell wrote. “This was his principal commercial activity, and it is for this that he must chiefly be remembered.”

While the Bank has acknowledged this history and apologised, the Treasury has not publicly done so. This is in line with the government’s position of resisting the discussion of reparations and not acknowledging culpability for the centuries of trafficking and enslaving.

Bennett’s further findings will increase the pressure on the government to do so, which is building from Caribbean and African countries.

A Bank of England spokesperson said it had explored its connections to enslavement in depth in its 2022 exhibition, adding: “We are grateful for Dr Bennett’s collaboration on that work.”

In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing that the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a 10-year restorative justice initiative.

Fresh evidence of C of E’s role in enslavement uncovered as church wrestles with reparations debate

The Guardian Wed, 16 Sep 2026 05:00:11 GMT

Register of British Slave Traders shows clergymen financed company that trafficked enslaved Africans on hundreds of voyages

Nearly 250 years after the abolitionist Ottobah Cugoano made the Christian case for reparative justice, the archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, visited the Ghanaian shore where he was enslaved as a boy.

After witnessing the dungeons beneath the chapel at Cape Coast Castle, once run by the Royal African Company (RAC), Mullally recommitted the Church of England to its “journey of repentance” for its role in slavery.

Back in Britain, historians working on the newly digitised Register of British Slave Traders were uncovering evidence that C of E clergy financed the RAC, which trafficked more African men, women and children than any other single organisation in the history of the slave trade.

The register, which documents investors in Britain’s nearly 250-year transatlantic slave trade, includes 45 C of E clergymen, whose investments helped fund hundreds of slaving voyages and a 1720 relaunch of the RAC. Among them was Henry Brydges, later a canon at St Paul’s Cathedral, who bought half of his £10,000 shareholding on the day he became the Archdeacon of Rochester.

Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register showed a “truly national picture”. Profits from enslavement filtered down to communities “from Cumbria to the Cotswolds” through bequests to parishes – evidence of a history of the C of E “giving slavery its blessing” and raising fresh questions about whether the church is doing enough to atone.

In 2023, church commissioners – the C of E’s asset managers – launched Project Spire, a £100m impact investment fund for communities affected by slavery’s legacies, which has caused division within the church. It is not a reparations fund, but is central to the church’s determination to be a force for justice and healing in the world. It was launched nearly 20 years after Rowan Williams, the former archbishop of Canterbury, rejected the idea that today’s church bears no responsibility for the past.

However, Spire mainly responds to historic investments in the South Sea Company, which trafficked close to 45,000 enslaved Africans. That represents a “sliver of church complicity”, said Prof Alan Lester, a historical geographer at the University of Sussex.

That complicity helped shape modern Britain, Lester said. Plantation profits helped fuel the Industrial Revolution, railways, public health, welfare, universities, schools, church building and the public finances. “Look at Anglican parishes in Jamaica, their ability to withstand climate change, and compare that with the wealth generated in Britain by the plantation complex,” he said.

For the Rev Natasha Beckles, the dean of racial justice for Willesden, reckoning with this past goes to the heart of Christian faith.

“What was the purpose of the cross if we’re not able to talk about this?” she said. “Slavery made the image of God transactional. There has to be an understanding of the impact on the world.”

Dr Leona Vaughn of the University of Liverpool, a co-organiser of a 2025 Anglican “truth-telling” event, said: “The public and people within the church don’t even know the extent of the church’s involvement.

“We’ve not even started to come to terms with the ‘Slave Bible’,” she said, a C of E-sanctioned, heavily edited Bible, stripped of liberation narratives, that planters used as a tool of social control from 1807.

The history of the United Society Partners in the Gospel (USPG), the C of E’s 325-year-old missionary partner, shows how powerful Anglicans practised and perpetuated transatlantic chattel slavery – a uniquely racialised, violent system of human commodification and forced mass migration. Today, members of USPG – of which Mullally is president – have committed to “the gospel’s call to break every chain of injustice”.

USPG’s forerunner, the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts (SPG), supplied chaplains to the RAC at Cape Coast Castle. For more than 120 years, with the involvement of C of E leaders, SPG enslaved people on the Codrington estate in Barbados, which generated the equivalent of £5m a year in today’s money.

At Codrington, enslaved Africans were branded with the word “Society”, tortured with the lash, straitjacket and iron collar, and worked to death. In seven months in 1746, 19 enslaved people died – including Daniel, who was “shot by accident” – with three deaths in a single day.

Pettigrew said the “clear signal” sent by the C of E’s relationship with Codrington was “if the church is doing it, why shouldn’t I?”

After abolition, SPG and at least 96 clergy who enslaved people received millions in compensation for “loss of property”. In 2023, USPG launched its own £7m reparative justice programme.

Christian collusion can be traced back to a 1452 papal bull authorising the enslavement of non-Christians, the author Malik Al Nasir said. He wants the C of E to digitise its records in the UK and the Caribbean.

Sign up to Cotton Capital

Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world

after newsletter promotion

In the 17th century, John Cotton, a former Lincolnshire vicar, co-drafted a charter legalising slavery in New England. By the 1750s, high churchmen were codifying pro-slavery ideology: Thomas Newton, later the dean of St Paul’s Cathedral, argued Africans were destined to be “servants of servants”, while Thomas Francklin, later the chaplain to George III, said: “We use [African] bodies for our support and happiness.”

Some Anglican voices did oppose slavery. Condemning it in 1685, the preacher Morgan Godwyn said: “We have … conspired with Satan.”

Project Spire’s critics have instead focused on the legacy of Anglican abolitionist MPs, such as William Wilberforce. Wilberforce’s 1823 anti-slavery petition was followed by his colleague Sir Thomas Fowell Buxton acknowledging that “we owe a large and liberal atonement”.

In his 1787 book, Cugoano – who won his freedom in England – wrote that the injustice done to Africans “cries aloud for universal reformation and national repentance”. He drew on biblical scriptures such as Numbers, Leviticus, Exodus and Deuteronomy that included reparative principles.

Class shaped church complicity, Beckles said. “The oldest child got the land, the second child they put in the church, the third was sent to the Caribbean.” That meant, Al Nasir said, that “one sibling could profit from slavery while another absolved it – the right hand washing the left”.

Enslaved African Christian leaders helped force the issue of abolition – including Samuel Sharpe, the deacon executed for leading Jamaica’s 1831-32 Baptist war.

The posthumously published Demerara diaries of the English Methodist the Rev John Smith also educated the British public about the relentless beatings, toil and meagre diet – raw yellow plantains – endured by enslaved Africans. Smith’s preaching was blamed by Anglican planters for Guyana’s 1823 Demerara rebellion. He died awaiting execution.

The moral conviction of English non-conformists – such as Smith and Quaker abolitionists – contrasts with the 45 C of E clergymen in the register.

The C of E already has an impact investment fund, so insiders have expressed surprise at the backlash against Spire, which is facing a legal challenge. In the House of Commons in September, the MP Marsha de Cordova, the second church estates commissioner, rebutted claims from rightwing critics that Spire diverts money from English churches.

She said the church regarded historic links to slavery with profound regret, that Spire is funded from the commissioners’ own income rather than parish collections, and that the English ministry would receive £1.6bn over three years.

A 2023 report estimated Britain’s slavery debt at £18.6tn. For Beckles, no sum could be enough. “What do you say to a mother who has had her child taken from her? To talk about a figure is grotesque,” she said. “For that level of human suffering, you’d be writing a blank cheque.”

In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing that the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a 10-year restorative justice initiative.

The royal crown branded on enslaved Africans: Britain’s monarchy and the slave trade

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 05:00:25 GMT

From Elizabeth I’s backing of early voyages to royal investment in trafficking companies, generations of monarchs were central to Britain’s slave trade

Enslaved African people were seared with hot metal brands bearing the royal crown, according to research by historians who have documented the monarchy’s centuries-long involvement in Britain’s slave trade.

The Register of British Slave Traders identifies thousands of people who invested in Britain’s trafficking of enslaved Africans, including kings and queens.

In response to the Guardian’s reporting of the new research relating to the monarchy, a spokesperson for King Charles said he was “grateful to all those undertaking academic work in this area and thus contributing to the debate about how such issues might best be addressed”.

Dr Nicholas Radburn, a historian at Lancaster University, discovered evidence of the branding in the archives of the South Sea Company, a British crown-backed enterprise that trafficked thousands of enslaved African people to plantations in the 1700s.

Radburn found a letter sent by the company’s board to its agents in Buenos Aires, instructing them to brand enslaved people with hot metal. The brand bore a crown, a symbol of the British monarchy’s role in the trade. A doctor had warned against the branding, but the board, whose members included figures from England’s establishment elite including MPs and Bank of England directors, instructed the agents to proceed.

“It now comes out, that you never mark the Negroes,” the letter said, “giving for reason that the French never did it, and that Dr Dover said your mark being so large, might endanger the Negroes.”

Insisting the agents disregard the doctor’s advice, they wrote that it was “the most effectual … way to distinguish our Negroes from others”. The directors sent a crown brand with their letter and instructions for how to scar the enslaved African people with it.

“Herewith you will receive a small silver mark,” they wrote. “As to the manner of using it, the method of our other factorys, is to mark the Negroes on the left shoulder heating the mark red hot.”

The letter was signed: “Your affectionate friends, the court of directors.”

Radburn said the letter illustrated how detailed the company’s dehumanising cruelty was – and its awareness of it.

“These people were members of the London elite, in a boardroom, thinking in fine grain terms about the violence that needs to be done to enslaved people across the ocean,” he said. “And that will have happened as a result of that letter. People will have had their flesh seared with that brand.”

The Register of British Slave Traders, the new historical record for which Radburn was a lead investigator, documents how Britain’s enslaving and trafficking of more than 3 million African people for nearly 250 years was perpetrated as an official national enterprise, led by its monarchs.

The publication of the register, the most comprehensive research project into the investors in Britain’s trafficking of enslaved African people, will further inform calls for King Charles to finally acknowledge the monarchy’s deep involvement in the trade.

The kings and queens who powered the trafficking most ferociously were those after the monarchy was restored in 1660. James, Duke of York, who became King James II, was the governor and a substantial shareholder in the Royal African Company (RAC), founded in 1672, which trafficked more African men, women and children than any other single organisation in the history of the slave trade.

The RAC and its predecessor, the Company of Royal Adventurers, were established by James’s brother, King Charles II, and backed by royalist courtiers, politicians and financiers. These royal insiders, whose biographies are in the register, bore florid titles of the time: Edward Proger, “groom of the bedchamber”, the Earl of Falmouth, “groom of the stool”. The RAC meetings, where decisions about the trafficking of enslaved people were made, were held in James’s personal apartment in Whitehall Palace, the royal family’s London home before Buckingham Palace was built.

Prof William Pettigrew, the register’s lead historian and investigator, said these royal enslaving companies were crucial to the kings of the Stuart dynasty striving to solidify the restored monarchy as an institution.

“I view James II as the most important English slave trader of the 17th century,” Pettigrew said. “The African companies were central to the monarchy’s rehabilitation plan within the British constitution.”

James ran the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people with his cousin, Prince Rupert of the Rhine, described in the register as “the visionary for England’s fully fledged, state-backed slave trade”. Other royals, including Charles II’s Portuguese wife, Queen Catherine of Braganza, were also investors in these companies.

In her book The Crown’s Silence, Prof Brooke Newman has chronicled in detail the centuries-long involvement of the British monarchy in the enslavement of African people, from the first trafficking voyages backed by Queen Elizabeth I in the 1560s to King William IV, who relished drinking and debauchery on Caribbean plantations and opposed abolition for decades.

Newman wrote that the RAC also branded the African people it enslaved at its coastal forts and factories, with DY for the Duke of York, and RACE for the Royal African Company of England. An agent in Sherbro, an island off Sierra Leone, was told by company directors: “You are to mark them … on the right breast RACE and the children of them at three years of age.”

As part of a 1713 peace treaty, Queen Anne agreed with Spain’s King Philip V that Britain would be awarded the asiento – an agreement to deliver a stipulated 4,800 enslaved African men to Spain’s American colonies every year.

Anne announced it triumphantly in the House of Lords: “I have insisted and obtained, that the asiento or contract for furnishing the Spanish West Indies with Negroes, shall be made with us for the term of 30 years.”

Queen Anne was a significant investor in the South Sea Company, which was established in 1711, and had rights to almost a quarter share of its overall profits. Anne gave the asiento to the SSC, which contracted the RAC to fulfil it.

Anne’s successors, George I and George II, were also personal investors in and supporters of the SSC.

According to the Slave Voyages database, the SSC trafficked 43,220 African captives from west Africa and Madagascar to the Caribbean and Spanish Americas between 1714 and 1740. From there, Radburn said, they were trafficked again, shipped and forced to march for hundreds of miles overland to the Pacific coast of South America. The company also moved more than 50,000 enslaved people within the Americas.

The trafficking vessels, including ships named Crown, King William and William and Mary, all set off from London. Almost 7,000 people died in the ships’ notoriously appalling conditions.

“It was a merciless, monarchy supported company,” Radburn said, “and the trafficking of enslaved people was the heart of it.”

Pressure on Charles from African and Caribbean countries to acknowledge this history and go further than previous expressions of sorrow is expected to build before the next Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda in November.

But successive governments have not formally apologised for Britain’s role in slavery and have rejected any discussion of reparations. Even if Charles wanted to, as king he is constitutionally bound by the government’s stated position.

An official delegation from Jamaica delivered a petition to Charles last week, seeking a legal ruling from the privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries. It asks whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful, whether it constituted a crime against humanity, and whether Britain is obliged to provide restitution to Jamaica for slavery and its enduring consequences.

Charles has publicly expressed sorrow over enslavement, describing it as an “appalling atrocity” and referring to “the most painful aspects of our past”, but has not formally acknowledged and apologised for the role of Britain or the monarchy in perpetrating it. In 2023 he signalled for the first time his support for research into the British monarchy’s historical links to transatlantic slavery.

A spokesperson for the king said: “His majesty has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today.

“In that context, he is grateful to all those undertaking academic work in this area and thus contributing to the debate about how such issues might best be addressed.”

David Comissiong, the Barbados ambassador to the Caribbean Community, said he recognised that Charles’s constitutional role meant he must not contravene government policy.

“But just as other British establishment families have acknowledged their involvement in the slavery enterprise and indicated a willingness to make reparation, anybody conscious of the British monarchy’s history would have to conclude that the British royal family should act similarly,” he added.

Monarchs, MPs and merchants: the register laying bare Britain’s slave-trading past

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 05:00:24 GMT

Exclusive: New research identifies thousands who profited from trafficking enslaved Africans and traces some financial links to institutions still operating today

The enormous scale of Britain’s centuries-long trafficking of enslaved African people, supported by parliament and the monarchy, has been laid bare by new research.

The Register of British Slave Traders, the product of a three-year project by a team of specialist historians, documents the investors in Britain’s near 250-year transatlantic slave trade from the first traffickers in the 1560s to abolition in 1807.

The register provides biographical detail for as many of 10,500 investors as possible from historical records, building the most comprehensive single picture so far of those who perpetrated the enslavement of African people.

Britain’s trafficking operations, including royal companies led by kings and, later, a rush of entrepreneurs in Bristol, Liverpool and other port cities, violently transported more than 3 million enslaved African men, women and children to colonial plantations in the Americas and Caribbean.

The Guardian is reporting on significant findings of the project, led by Prof William Pettigrew of King’s College London, and the vast human damage it documents: the relentless involvement of the British monarchy, parliament and financial and business elites; the role of the church in legitimising it; and how the investors’ wealth was woven deep into the country’s fabric and used to fund hospitals, schools, welfare organisations, the arts, science and culture.

Key elements include:

A series of British kings and queens were leaders and investors in the trafficking of enslaved African people;

More than 100 MPs were investors in slave-trading companies, including scores in the Tory and Whig parties – the forerunners of today’s Conservatives and Liberal Democrats;

Dozens of directors and original financiers of the Bank of England were investors in the slave trade;

More than 1,000 women invested in slave-trading companies;

Forty-five Church of England clergymen were investors in the slave-trading Royal African Company.

The BBC is showing a two-part documentary about the register, presented by the historian David Olusoga.

The publication of the register will provide further evidence for the growing global movement calling on European governments to acknowledge their perpetration of enslavement, issue a full, formal apology and engage positively with discussions for reparatory justice.

Successive British governments have refused to do so, arguing there is no duty to make reparations because enslavement and the slave trade were not against the law at the time.

An official delegation from Jamaica delivered a petition to King Charles last week to seek a legal ruling from the privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries, on whether that government position is lawful.

It is a legacy of the dehumanisation inflicted on so many African men, women and children that much less was documented about them than about their enslavers. The register draws on copious permanent records for the traffickers: company documents; birth, death and marriage certificates; wills and biographical information, much of it official because many were MPs and members of the elite. Memorials and statues venerate many to this day. The enslaved people were treated as chattel, property, by British law, and there is no lasting documentation even identifying millions of them.

There are ongoing projects dedicated to addressing this deficit and to documenting the lives of the enslaved people as much as possible from the few records that were made.

Of the thousands of British slave traders identified in the register, some are household names: King James II, the last Catholic monarch to rule England, Scotland and Ireland whose statue celebrating him as a “defender of the faith” stands in Trafalgar Square, London; the composer George Frideric Handel; and the philosopher John Locke, both shareholders in the Royal African Company (RAC).

The historians’ broader research found that Sir Christopher Wren, the architect of St Paul’s Cathedral and many other churches in London, chaired a meeting in 1682 of the Royal Society, the institution dedicated to furthering science, when it voted to invest in the RAC.

It is an illustration of modern Britain’s scant discussion of its enslaving history that the legendary status of these men rarely encompasses recognition that they participated in the slave trade.

It is now better known that Queen Elizabeth I and her inner circle supported the enslaving voyages of the Plymouth-based privateer John Hawkins in the 1560s, lending him Royal Navy ships in return for a share of the profits.

For decades, piratical shipowners enslaved and trafficked people from the west African coast – mostly from present-day Ghana and Nigeria – to the Caribbean and North America. In the 1600s merchants followed, establishing plantations, including sugar in Barbados.

Perhaps the single British person now principally known as a slave trader, among the 10,500 in the register for whom the historians found records, is Edward Colston. He was an RAC investor and assistant, or director, Tory MP for Bristol and benefactor of schools and charities. That is the result of concerted campaigning and public education, culminating during the Black Lives Matter protests in 2020 in the toppling of Colston’s statue.

British plantation owners enslaved African men and women and children – who were born enslaved for life – to extract their unpaid labour, enforcing enslavement through extreme violence. It is a further twist of cruelty that this oppression was enforced to deliver treats to people in a modernising Europe: tobacco and sugar.

After the monarchy was restored in 1660, the crown took a leading role in the trafficking and established two royally chartered companies before the RAC was founded in 1672.

Led by James II and his cousin Prince Rupert of the Rhine, the RAC held a monopoly on the trafficking, enforced with the Royal Navy, the military and the state’s legal power. The RAC became the largest single trafficker of enslaved African people in the history of European enslavement, taking at least 150,000 captive men, women and children across the Atlantic.

Those who eagerly joined the king in this royal enslaving company were the elites of a nation developing into a modern state. The register gives character to the names of RAC shareholders, assistants and governors: royal courtiers; Tory and Whig members of parliament; financiers, bankers, merchants; and City of London aldermen, or councillors.

Arguments about Britain’s involvement in enslavement did develop in parliament. But moral condemnation came much later. The dispute that dominated for 25 years was led by independent, or “separate”, traders lobbying for the royal monopoly to be removed so that they too could become traffickers.

Full deregulation was approved by parliament in 1712, and the new British ideology of “free trade” enabled a dramatic increase in the number of African people denied their liberty, enslaved and trafficked.

A significant figure in the register during this pivotal period was Robert Heysham, an RAC assistant elected Tory MP for Lancaster in 1698. Heysham argued forcefully in parliament against the royal monopoly, then became instrumental in growing the slave trade.

“Heysham took the opportunity to outfit his own ships, making human trafficking his core concern,” according to the register.

Heysham later moved to vote with the Whigs, the advocates of free trade, and became one of the largest independent traffickers of enslaved African people during Queen Anne’s early 18th-century reign. On ships with names including Little London, New Adventure, and Liverpool, Heysham and his brother William, who lived in Barbados, trafficked about 9,000 enslaved African people, of whom about 1,350 died in the notoriously appalling conditions of the ships.

“Heysham lobbied persistently to expand the traffic,” the register says, “and worked more than anyone else to ensure that it became a national commercial concern.”

For these records, the historians drew on the landmark Slave Voyages database, which contains records of enslaving ships. The register also builds on the Legacies of British Slavery archive, compiled by historians at University College London, which documents the British “owners” of enslaved people.

Its starting point was the people paid £20m – the equivalent of £2.7bn today, according to the lowest method of calculation – in “compensation” for losing their human “property” when parliament abolished enslavement in 1833. That payment of public money to the enslavers, with no compensation ever paid to enslaved people, is still deeply felt today as an enduring injustice by those calling for reparations.

As Britain’s 18th-century transatlantic slave trade expanded, its participants spread from London elites to opportunists in other ports.

Bristol became particularly dominant and the register sets out many of the men who made fortunes there: Richard Farr, a ropemaker who became “one of Bristol’s most prolific and important slave traders”, outfitting at least 38 enslaving ships that trafficked more than 10,000 people to plantations; William Tyndall, who was “deeply engaged in slave trading in Jamaica”; and James Laroche, who over 42 years until his death in 1770 outfitted “at least 105 slave ships that carried more than 30,000 people into captivity”.

The details add to research carried out in Bristol documenting the extent to which the city’s political power bases, architecture and financing, as well as cultural institutions including the Bristol Old Vic theatre, were built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans.

Merchants in other port cities, including Lancaster, also became seriously involved and Liverpool became dominant from about 1750, driving another vast expansion of the trafficking.

That year, parliament passed legislation winding up the RAC and institutionalising free trade in the transatlantic trafficking. The act incorporated official wording that plainly set out the enslavement and trafficking of African people as state policy – and the racism at its core.

“The trade to and from Africa is very advantageous to Great Britain, and necessary for supplying the plantations and colonies … with a sufficient number of negroes, at reasonable rates,” the act stated.

For that purpose, “the said trade ought to be free and open to all his majesty’s subjects”.

The only stipulation was that slave traders should pay 40 shillings to join a company that would maintain the RAC’s old enslaving forts and settlements in Africa.

Many of the Liverpool men who seized this opportunity were working-class tradesmen who became the city’s establishment. Liverpool’s local politicians solidly supported the slave trade, tripling the size of the docks to facilitate it.

Prof Edmond Smith of the University of Manchester, one of the register’s lead historians, has found that 51 Liverpool mayors were traffickers and the city corporation repeatedly lobbied parliament against abolition of the slave trade.

Liverpool traffickers in the register include Arthur Heywood, who “participated in 80 slave-trading voyages between 1744 and 1780, transporting an estimated 21,648 captive African people” to Grenada, Jamaica, St Kitts, Virginia, Maine and other ports in America”.

Heywood established the Liverpool bank Arthur Heywood and Sons, which became linked to Barclays through a series of takeovers.

Bryan Blundell, who had worked as a mariner on ships from the age of 12, built a Liverpool slave-trafficking family business, became mayor of the city and founded the Blue Coat school.

William Earle, a mariner and merchant, participated in 117 slave-trading voyages that trafficked an estimated 36,565 captive African people. His family’s involvement made them “one of the most prominent slave-trading dynasties ever in Britain”.

The register’s historians have documented that British manufacturing in the Industrial Revolution was linked to the trafficking. “Triangular” trading routes began with goods, including guns from Birmingham, exported from England to be traded for enslaved people in west Africa.

The trafficking of enslaved Africans perpetrated by British men – and the surprising number of women identified in the register, more than 1,000 – was far from the guilty national secret it has since become. The register shows it was a very public, prestigious, royally supported and legislated-for imperial enterprise.

In March 2026, a large majority of countries voted for a UN declaration, led by the president of Ghana, John Dramani Mahama, describing the historical trafficking and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as “the gravest crime against humanity”.

Britain abstained, issuing an official explanation that it objected to the wording because it created “a hierarchy of historical atrocities”. The government also argued there was no duty to make reparations because slavery and the slave trade “were not, at the time those acts were committed, violations of international law”.

The explanation said the government recognised “the abhorrent nature of slavery and the transatlantic slave trade” but declined to state that Britain perpetrated it. Instead it referred to enslavement as a “most painful” element in “history that we share with other nations”.

The Register of British Slave Traders, documenting thousands of people from monarchs to mariners who took part in the atrocity, provides the latest clear record of Britain’s share in that most painful history.

Why Israel Wants More One-Ton Bombs From the U. S. and Why the Sale Is Controversial

The New York Times September 16, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The Trump administration plans to deliver 60,000 of the powerful munitions at a time when opposition is growing in Washington to arms sales to Israel.

By David M. Halbfinger and John Ismay

David M. Halbfinger reported from Jerusalem, and John Ismay from Washington.

The Trump administration’s decision to send 60,000 powerful one-ton bombs to Israel as part of a $2.8 billion deal — one of the largest arms agreements ever — will allow Israel to replenish its supply of a munition it considers vital.

The weapons became the focus of great tension between the Biden administration and Israel after one-ton bombs were widely used in densely populated areas of Gaza where Israel had steered civilians for their safety.

With opposition to military assistance to Israel growing in Washington, such a huge sale of heavy bombs, paid for by the U. S. government, could be an effort by the administration to stock up the Israeli arsenal before political shifts in the United States make such shipments impossible, analysts said. It is certain to set off an outcry in Congress.

The Israeli military pivoted toward the use of the one-ton bombs after the Hamas-led attack against southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, drastically changing its shopping list, U. S. government data show. In 2025, Israel bought nearly eight times as many one-ton bombs from the United States as it did from 2012 to 2015.

Israel’s emphasis on buying and using some of the largest bombs currently made runs counter to that of most other modern militaries, which have been making their aerial munitions smaller and even more accurate in the hopes of limiting civilian casualties during combat.

Israel has used a vast amount of the one-ton bombs in large part to target the tunnel network Hamas developed in Gaza for its fighters, weapons and command centers. Israeli officials have said that Hamas fighters intentionally embed themselves among civilians, forcing the Israeli military to risk killing civilians.

A New York Times investigation in December 2023 found that the Israeli military routinely used one-ton bombs in the weeks immediately after the 2023 attack and identified more than 200 instances of Israel dropping the powerful munitions, including in densely populated areas.

Here is a closer look at the transaction and its significance.

According to a U. S. official, Israel will receive 20,000 Mk-84 bombs and another 20,000 BLU-117 bombs. The two types of one-ton bombs are nearly identical.

The bombs are highly versatile, experts say. They can be set to detonate above ground, sending shrapnel 1,000 feet in any direction, or, with delayed fuses, set to explode underground. They can be fitted with kits that allow them to hit targets with precision and from a long range. The craters from one-ton bombs can be up to 50 feet deep.

In addition to the 40,000 Mk-84 and BLU-117 bombs, Israel will also receive 20,000 I-2000 Penetrator warheads, which explode on delay after busting through a surface like soil, rock or concrete, the U. S. official said. They also weigh a ton each, but because their casings are thicker and far heavier, they carry far less explosive power than the Mk-84 and BLU-117 bombs.

According to the U. S. Army office that oversees bomb procurement, “ideal targets” for one-ton bombs “are buildings, rail yards and lines of communication.” The 250- and 500-pound bombs more typically used by the U. S. military are designed for “soft, fragment sensitive targets” like troops, fuel storage tanks and radars, the office said.

The $2.8 billion purchase is being funded from the Pentagon’s budget for foreign military sales. That means the money effectively flows from U. S. taxpayers to Israel’s military and then to U. S. munitions manufacturers.

While congressional leaders can tell the administration they oppose the transaction, Secretary of State Marco Rubio can exercise emergency powers to proceed with it.

Mr. Rubio has repeatedly done just that, including in March, when he bypassed Congress to send $4 billion in weaponry to Israel, including more than 35,000 of the same kinds of one-ton bombs.

Opposition is likely to be heated. Some Democrats in Congress have called for ending U. S. military aid, or even all aid, to Israel in response to the huge civilian toll of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the Oct. 7 attacks on Israel.

Anger toward Israel is also growing on the right. The former Fox News host Tucker Carlson, an outspoken critic of Israel, wrote in a social media post on Tuesday that there was no justification for supplying Israel with so many of the bombs it had used in killing Palestinians in Gaza. He said it would only embolden Israel elsewhere.

“The 40,000 new bombs the Trump administration is sending will be used to do the same in Lebanon, and likely in other countries in the region,” he wrote. “If you wanted to extend the Iran war into the indefinite future, this is exactly what you’d do.”

Experts describe one-ton bombs as a workhorse of the Israeli Air Force, which has operated in seven theaters of conflict over the past few years: Gaza, the occupied West Bank, Lebanon, Iran, Syria, Yemen and Iraq.

Those campaigns have severely depleted the air force’s munitions. One former air force commander, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive information, said that Israel had learned it was necessary to amass a multiyear supply, in case of delays in replenishing stocks, and that 40,000 one-ton bombs were considered a full supply.

“The traditional concept of Israel’s defense doctrine was short wars,” said a retired major general, Amos Yadlin, a former deputy air force commander and former head of Israeli military intelligence. “What we saw in the last three years was Israel was dragged — and maybe even with some contributions of Israeli decisions — to a long war. And if you’re in a strategy of long wars, you need more ammunition.”

The New York Times reported in December 2023 that in the first six weeks of the war in Gaza, Israel routinely used one-ton bombs in parts of the enclave that it had designated as safe for civilians, including densely populated areas. The Times identified 208 craters of at least 40 feet across in an area of southern Gaza where Israel had ordered civilians to move to for their own safety.

Munitions experts say that bombs of that size are almost never dropped by U. S. forces in densely populated areas, and U. S. military officers have said such bombs are unsuitable for urban combat. Since the Vietnam War, U. S. forces have used one-ton bombs sparingly.

Israel reaches for them far more often. It says that the heavy bombs are necessary to strike enemy forces hiding in large buildings or in underground tunnels, and that its military always seeks to avoid or minimize civilian casualties.

The one-ton bombs became a source of friction between President Joseph R. Biden Jr. and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel in May 2024, when Mr. Biden held up a shipment of 1,800 bombs in an effort to deter Israel from attacking the city of Rafah, where many displaced Palestinians were sheltering.

Israel attacked and destroyed much of Rafah anyway. The Trump White House released the shipment of bombs days after Donald J. Trump took office in 2025.

At a time when the relationship between Mr. Trump and Mr. Netanyahu has been on a roller-coaster ride, the political dimensions of proceeding with such a large deal for heavy bombs cannot be ignored.

Chuck Freilich, a former Israeli deputy national security adviser, said the deal should not be seen as an attempt to aid Mr. Netanyahu’s campaign for a new term in next month’s election, in which he is behind in the polls. “If it was a new deal for F-35s, it would be worth a headline,” he said.

Still, General Yadlin said, the arms deal sends an important signal to Israel’s enemies that the United States still has its back. “This is a way to show that, even if there are some differences, on the basic security of Israel, the U. S. is still a very strong ally,” he said.

But Israel’s defenders are also mindful that the political winds have shifted and that it is not likely to become any easier to obtain such munitions from the United States in the foreseeable future, especially ahead of the 2028 election.

Jesse Weinberg, a researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, said that officials in Israel and many of Israel’s supporters in Washington were looking to “front-load” military aid to Israel “because we don’t know what the construction of the next Congress is going to be — and then there’s the eye to 2028.”

“The view at the Kirya,” he said of Israel’s military headquarters, “in the prime minister’s office and also among Israel’s supporters on the Hill is that if you want to move things, now is the time.”

David M. Halbfinger is The Times’s Jerusalem bureau chief, leading coverage of Israel, Gaza and the West Bank. He also held that post from 2017 to 2021. He was the politics editor from 2021 to 2025.

John Ismay is a reporter covering the Pentagon for The Times. He served as an explosive ordnance disposal officer in the U. S. Navy.
