Emergency Hearing Sought Over Kennedy Center Closure

The New York Times September 16, 2026

Trump Remakes Washington

Advertisement

Supported by

After a Democratic lawmaker asked a judge to consider whether the move violates a previous court order, center officials clarified that the closure was intended to last seven days.

By Julia Jacobs and Zach Montague

Julia Jacobs reported from New York, and Zach Montague from Washington.

Lawyers for a Democratic lawmaker on Wednesday requested an emergency hearing in federal court over whether the abrupt closure of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts violates a judge’s earlier order that barred the institution from shuttering.

On Tuesday, the center announced it was temporarily closing to the public over what officials described as dire safety concerns after a five-foot section of water-damaged ceiling plaster fell to the ground during a storm. President Trump, who has pushed for months for the building to be closed for a $257 million renovation project, said the building was in a “virtual state of collapse.”

Lawyers for Representative Joyce Beatty, who is suing the center as an ex officio board member, said that the move appeared to run afoul of a judicial order in May, in which Judge Christopher R. Cooper temporarily blocked the center from closing because of what he described as a lack of meaningful scrutiny over the decision from its Trump-allied board.

“The board cannot simply ignore Judge Cooper’s rulings whenever it suits them,” Ms. Beatty’s lawyers, Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky, said in a statement on Wednesday.

After Ms. Beatty’s request, Matt Floca, the center’s executive director, said in an email to employees that the closure was intended to last seven days, during which officials would evaluate the extent of the safety concerns. He said the need to extend the closure would be assessed on a “weekly basis.”

In a response to the filing, Judge Cooper asked the center to respond to Ms. Beatty’s request by Thursday morning, and said he would then decide whether a hearing is necessary.

Kennedy Center officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but they have defended the closing decision as legally sound and urgently needed. They said that a more extended closure of the building would not begin until the court has given its approval.

Roma Daravi, a spokeswoman for the center, said on Tuesday that the board’s decision “reflects sound judgment and a clear prioritization of safety above all else” and that “the center remains committed to pursuing a safe and efficient renovation through all legal means.”

The Justice Department, which is representing the center in court, did not respond to requests for comment about whether a temporary closure can be authorized without a sign-off from Judge Cooper.

In his ruling, Judge Cooper of Federal District Court in Washington temporarily blocked the board’s initial approval of Mr. Trump’s closure plan, finding that the board had not done a diligent effort to study its effects. But he said he would revisit the issue if the trustees continued to pursue it and undertook a formal review.

The board later hired consultants and has twice voted to confirm the closure, but the Justice Department has yet to submit a formal motion asking Judge Cooper to lift his order.

Although the main Kennedy Center building is closed, a smaller addition to the campus that opened in 2019 — known as the Reach — remains open. This week it is slated to host free performances, including a concert by an indie musician and a magic show.

The center is hoping that its plan to keep the Reach open will satisfy Judge Cooper, who, in his May ruling, said that the institution must, by law, maintain the center as a living memorial to President Kennedy with some performing arts programming. In his order, the judge seemed to leave some room for the center to close temporarily, suggesting that the board would have authority to close it “for certain periods of time or for certain justified purposes.”

Ms. Beatty’s filing highlighted the confusion that followed Mr. Trump’s announcement that the building would be closing “immediately.” An announcement blared over the P. A. system on Tuesday telling the public to exit the main building, but when Ms. Beatty’s lawyer asked the Justice Department for an explanation, one of its lawyers said the fire alarm had been “improperly triggered,” according to the court filing.

But security soon lined up outside the building to prevent the public from going inside. Employees traded confused text messages asking whether they were expected to come into work. Some staff members trickled into the building on Wednesday morning without any trouble. But they were given no official instructions regarding the closure until the afternoon, when employees received an email telling them to wear hard hats in certain areas of the building, including where the plaster had fallen on Sept. 4. Mr. Floca later told them in the staffwide email to work from home unless they were “essential staff.”

The duration of the closure is unclear. In an email on Wednesday, Ms. Daravi said it was expected to last “until we can be 1,000 percent sure” that the public is not at risk and that “some other piece of ceiling won’t fall and kill them.”

The White House shared a glossy video with swelling music that provided a justification of the closure, pointing to problems such as “chronic water intrusion” and outdated equipment that Mr. Floca said leaves the facility “vulnerable to catastrophic mechanical failure.”

The board’s vote on Tuesday — the third time it had approved the Kennedy Center’s closure — prompted objections from Democratic lawmakers, who have accused the center of using the prospect of renovations to paper over the exodus of artists, donors and audience members since Mr. Trump’s takeover at the start of his second term.

“Donald Trump only cares about the Kennedy Center for his vanity,” said Ms. Beatty, whose lawsuit challenged the closing.

Mr. Trump and his allies have been pushing to have his name attached to the building to recognize his work in securing money for the renovations. But Judge Cooper ordered his name removed months ago and on Tuesday barred the center again from inscribing his name on the front of the center.

In a social media post on Tuesday, the president accused the judge of bias and threatened to cancel the renovation project if an appeals court did not allow his name to be restored.

The drama continued into the evening, as the center’s chief financial officer, Donna Arduin Kauranen, resigned. (Ms. Arduin Kauranen and the center did not respond to requests for comment about her reasoning.)

Shutting the doors of the Kennedy Center is far less significant than it would have been months ago, when touring Broadway shows and the National Symphony Orchestra were still performing at the venue. Since July, when the closure was initially slated to begin, the center’s performance calendar has been largely bare and the building a mostly empty shell.

Julia Jacobs is an arts and culture reporter who often covers legal issues for The Times.

Zach Montague is a Times reporter covering the federal courts, including the legal disputes over the Trump administration’s agenda.

‘The Day We All Dread’: Helicopter Crews See One of Their Own Fall

The New York Times September 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Swarms of news helicopters traverse Southern California to capture its mayhem. Then, one became the story. A pilot and reporter died, as did a person on the ground.

By Shawn Hubler

Reporting from Los Angeles

The collision of the bus and the S. U. V. had been big, even by Los Angeles eye-in-the-sky standards. Desmond Shaw was stunned by its force.

Mr. Shaw, a veteran helicopter reporter, had gazed at the wreck from above, transfixed. His aircraft was one in a swarm hovering high over the San Fernando Valley on Tuesday. The transit vehicle had been bashed like a toy, the S. U. V. gutting its midsection. The authorities were saying people were dead.

Mr. Shaw had been back at work less than a week after taking a leave prompted by the deaths of both parents, and he had been thinking lately about mortality. The crash was eerie for him, and he was glad to be done with the story.

But shortly after he and his pilot flew away, the newsroom called back: An aircraft appeared to have gone down near the scene of the bus crash.

Mr. Shaw, a 45-year-old who works for a CBS affiliate, thought of his fellow reporters aloft — colleagues for whom the air was their office.

“As soon as we got there and saw the fireball and the rotor blades, we knew what it was,” he said, speaking in an interview from his car early Wednesday. “It was the day we all dread.”

The back-to-back bus and helicopter crashes killed at least five people and strewed blackened wreckage in the Chatsworth neighborhood of Los Angeles.

Shortly after 5 p. m. on Tuesday, the S. U. V. broadsided a Los Angeles Metro bus, killing at least two people and critically injuring others. The driver has been charged with murder, the police said.

Then, around 7 p. m., a helicopter reporting for a local NBC affiliate plummeted to the ground and burst into flames, a disaster whose cause is under federal investigation. The reporter, Eliana Moreno, and the pilot, George Marciniw, were killed, along with a person on the ground.

The helicopter was just one of a fleet that zips over Southern California’s vastness, tracking events like car chases and wildfires. Most of them are supplied by contractors who provide aircraft and reporters to news stations. The choppers, swashbuckling and loud, are a signature of the region, indispensable in a metropolis encompassing thousands of square miles.

In 1992, they carried the news during the Los Angeles riots, as crowds at the intersection of Florence and Normandie Avenues attacked the trucker Reginald Denny. Two years later, they filled the sky when O. J. Simpson led the police on a riveting two-hour chase through Southern California freeways. Come flames or floods, Rose Parades or ICE protests, they are as ubiquitous as seabirds, watching and swooping in from above.

But the crash on Tuesday night of an aircraft trying to cover a spectacular collision underscored another aspect of Los Angeles’s aerial news culture: the risks.

Helicopter crews across the United States say they must remain on constant lookout for hazards such as drones and bird strikes, as well as pilot error and mechanical failure.

Although driving on freeways is statistically more dangerous than air travel, the crash of a tourist chopper in the Hudson River last year and the 2020 accident that killed the N. B. A. legend Kobe Bryant, his 13-year-old daughter and seven others have highlighted the long odds of surviving a helicopter accident.

Since 2000, there have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the United States, killing 16 people, federal accident records and news accounts show.

In Los Angeles, two people were seriously injured in 2000 when a news helicopter covering the Academy Awards crashed at Van Nuys Airport.

At NBC4, formally known as KNBC, Tuesday’s tragedy summoned the memory of the 1977 helicopter crash that killed Francis Gary Powers. A former reconnaissance plane pilot, Mr. Powers had survived being shot down over the Soviet Union during the Cold War only to perish on his way back from covering a wildfire.

In the interview on Wednesday, Mr. Shaw, the CBS affiliate reporter, said that helicopter journalists have to put aside their fears.

“You have to push it to the back of your brain or you can’t do the job,” he said. “I had a fear of heights when I was a kid. Now I’m sometimes up 10,000 feet high.”

Mr. Shaw has worked in broadcasting since his college days at California State University, Northridge, and later became that most specific of Los Angeles media figures: a radio traffic reporter. For more than a decade, he flew above the freeways, keeping motorists apprised of hazards, from “gawker’s block” to jackknifed big rigs, as well as the occasional disaster or wildfire.

He joined CBS Los Angeles in 2015, and has been a full-time reporter and cameraman there for six years. He said he was well acquainted with Ms. Moreno and Mr. Marciniw.

“We knew pretty quickly who it was,” he said. “It’s a pretty tight-knit community. There are probably a dozen of us, or maybe less, who report on air and run the camera.”

NBC4 said on Tuesday that its NewsChopper4 was owned and operated by a vendor based in Los Angeles, Angel City Air, and that Ms. Moreno and Mr. Marciniw had been Angel City Air employees.

Mr. Shaw said that he had run into them at airports over the years as they covered breaking stories, and that he knew their voices by heart from broadcasts. So did the other reporters hovering overhead at the time of the crash.

A video from inside NewsChopper4, which was broadcasting live at the time, captured the final moments. As the chopper descends for a closer look at the bus crash, the engine can be heard winding down. A warning horn sounds and the helicopter abruptly tries ascending. “What — you can’t, you can’t pull up?” Ms. Moreno says, her voice panicked as the image begins violently shaking. The picture goes white and then goes black.

Zoey Tur, a veteran news helicopter pilot and reporter who spent more than three decades covering Southern California, said she recognized the telltale sounds of engine failure.

“You can hear the blades slowing,” she said. “You can hear the sound of the turbine engine shutting down.”

Fabian Salazar, an investigator with National Transportation Safety Board, said at a news conference on Wednesday that investigators were combing through the crash site in Chatsworth. But the most crucial evidence, he said, was the video broadcast by the helicopter in its final moments. The agency plans to release a preliminary report on the accident in about 30 days, he said.

The impact has rippled through the airborne media community in Los Angeles like a shock wave.

“Heartbreaking doesn’t begin to describe it,” Mr. Shaw said.

Mr. Shaw and his pilot didn’t see the crash, only the devastation that followed in Chatsworth. The hours since have been a blur, he said: speaking on the air with his station’s news anchors and reassuring his loved ones that he was all right.

He took time in his car for one last interview before going home in the dark to greet his dogs, Lonzo and Scruffy, and hug his husband, Brandon. His phone, he said, had been sounding off all night with messages of concern and condolence.

“Everyone is asking if I’m OK,” he said. “Honestly? No. But I’m alive.”

Orlando Mayorquín contributed reporting.

Shawn Hubler is The Times’s Los Angeles bureau chief, reporting on the news, trends and personalities of Southern California.

Democrats Put Aside Rifts With El-Sayed, Uniting to Win in Michigan

The New York Times September 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Despite disagreements on Israel, more than a dozen Democratic senators met in Washington with the Michigan Senate nominee and emerged sounding optimistic.

By Annie Karni

Reporting from Washington

Democratic senators from across the ideological spectrum huddled on Capitol Hill on Wednesday with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive Senate nominee in Michigan and vocal critic of Israel, and said they were ready to put aside differences to win the majority in November.

More than a dozen Democrats flocked to the party’s political headquarters across from the Capitol to meet with Dr. El-Sayed and emerged sounding upbeat about a candidate who had not been the first choice of party leaders to defend the critical swing-state seat.

“He’s a great candidate,” Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, the chairwoman of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, said after meeting with Dr. El-Sayed. “We haven’t lost Michigan in 30 years. He’s energizing the base, and I’m optimistic.”

Dr. El-Sayed, the Michigan-born son of Egyptian immigrants, won an expensive and competitive primary in Michigan last month that put on display deep divides within the Democratic Party. His past criticism of Israel — he has said he opposes Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state — has continued to be a concern for Jewish Democratic voters in Michigan. Republicans are working to leverage that rift to boost his Republican opponent, former Representative Mike Rogers, in the general election.

The message from Democrats on Wednesday, however, was one of unity.

Senator Chris Murphy, Democrat of Connecticut, said that “Abdul is going to be able to cross over and get conservative, traditionally Republican support in Michigan. He’s more of a bridge-builder here than people think he will be. I’m all in.”

Senator Andy Kim, Democrat of New Jersey, who also met with Dr. El-Sayed, said that they connected as “dads just trying to make a better world for our little kids. We both know we’ve got a small window to make things right for them.”

And Senator Mark Kelly, Democrat of Arizona, emerged from the meeting saying that he planned to campaign in Michigan in the coming weeks.

Dr. El-Sayed also said he planned to meet with Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, whom he has said he would not back as leader if he were to win in November. Mr. Schumer, the highest-ranking Jewish official in the country, often tells people his last name comes from the word “shomer,” meaning the guardian of Israel.

But Mr. Schumer reached out to Dr. El-Sayed following his victory and said he came away from the conversation believing “we have more that unites us than divides us.”

Dr. El-Sayed told reporters on Wednesday that he anticipated a “productive meeting” with the leader in which they would focus on areas of common ground.

“If Elon Musk or Donald Trump are out here trying to spend yet more money, I’m certainly hoping for future colleagues to support us,” Dr. El-Sayed said of the goal of his visit to Washington. “We need solidarity.”

He said Michigan voters were not concerned with his ties to Hasan Piker, the Twitch and YouTube star whose statements about Israel have alarmed Democrats.

“They really don’t care about that,” Dr. El-Sayed said. “Nobody asks me that question.”

His meetings with Democrats came a day after Vice President JD Vance encouraged Republicans on Capitol Hill to talk about Dr. El-Sayed, regardless of who they were running against, according to CNN.

Mr. Vance told House Republicans in a closed-door meeting that if they happened to be running against a Democrat who was “not that crazy, then just talk about Abdul El-Sayed.”

Dr. El-Sayed said he was unfazed by the attempt to turn him into a boogeyman of the far left.

“Fine, talk about me,” he said in response to the vice president. “You know what I’m going to talk about? Gas, groceries, how hard it is to see a doctor.”

Annie Karni is a congressional correspondent for The Times.

U. S. Intelligence Warns of China Theft Over Sale of F-35 Jets to Saudis

The New York Times September 16, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Internal reports, including one from the Pentagon’s Defense Intelligence Agency, say China could acquire U. S. jet technology through spying or cooperation with Saudi Arabia.

By Edward Wong and Dustin Volz

Edward Wong is a former Iraq war correspondent and Beijing bureau chief who has written a book on China. Dustin Volz reports on technology and espionage from Washington.

U. S. intelligence officers have expressed concerns in internal reports about possible Chinese espionage related to a pending sale of dozens of advanced F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia valued at $24 billion, according to American officials.

Intelligence analysts have raised the possibility that China could acquire F-35 jet technology through spying in Saudi Arabia or through its military and security partnership with the kingdom, the U. S. officials said.

One detailed report issued by the Pentagon’s Defense Intelligence Agency months ago discusses Chinese military access to Saudi bases and Saudi Arabia’s use of Chinese technology in its telecommunications infrastructure, an official said. It also questions whether the Americans and Saudis will be able to maintain secure sites for the F-35 technology, the official said.

That report has circulated among several administration agencies and congressional offices, as have assessments from other intelligence offices. The D. I. A. issued a more general report in the fall of 2025 on similar risks when the administration was discussing the possibility of the sales, The New York Times reported at the time.

President Trump then announced the sale the day before he hosted Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto leader of Saudi Arabia, at the White House in November.

The sale is at a more advanced stage now, and the newer D. I. A. report raises sharper concerns, including technical ones. The State Department sent the proposed sales package of 48 jets and a spare engine to two congressional committees in June to get informal approval. Some lawmakers and aides have been pressing the administration on the concerns raised by the intelligence agencies.

The U. S. officials spoke about the concerns among intelligence officials on the condition of anonymity because of sensitivities around espionage and military matters.

The State Department, the Pentagon and the Embassy of Saudi Arabia in Washington declined to comment. The White House and the embassy of China did not reply to requests for comment.

U. S. intelligence agencies raised similar concerns internally during Mr. Trump’s first term after he agreed in 2020 to sell F-35 jets to the United Arab Emirates as part of a deal in which the Emirates would normalize relations with Israel.

It takes years to produce the jets, which are made by Lockheed Martin, and the Biden administration decided to review the sale well before production and delivery. Intelligence agencies raised the same issues at that time because the Emirates was strengthening its military, intelligence and technology ties with China. U. S. officials then ended the sales process.

Prince Mohammed has been trying to build up his military. He began a disastrous seven-year war against the Houthis in Yemen, one in which Saudi-led forces killed civilians with American bombs. The Saudi military has failed to ward off attacks from Iran in the current U. S.-Israeli war against Iran, and the Saudis and the Houthis, which are supported by Iran, have begun fighting again.

Prince Mohammed has long sought to buy F-35 jets from the United States, and Mr. Trump finally agreed last November. Saudi Arabia and the United States have had decades of military cooperation, and the kingdom is by far the largest buyer of American weapons and defense equipment. But Saudi Arabia buys ballistic missiles from China, and the Chinese military is helping the Saudis learn to build ballistic missiles, set up production facilities and improve missile operations.

Democratic lawmakers sent President Joseph R. Biden Jr. a letter in June 2022 laying out their concerns over that program.

The recent Pentagon intelligence report said that only Saudi and American officers and contractors should have access to sites where F-35 technology would reside, a U. S. official said. Pentagon officials are especially concerned about protecting the advanced radar and surveillance technology of the F-35.

The intelligence analysts ask in the report whether Saudi Arabia would more broadly agree to limit contact with Chinese military and intelligence personnel and associated entities.

The report also questions whether Saudi officials would agree to remove equipment from Huawei and ZTE, two prominent Chinese technology companies, from telecommunications and router infrastructure and defense installations.

Some Israeli officials also have concerns about the deal, as they did when Mr. Trump proposed such sales to the Emirates. Israel is the only country in the Middle East that has F-35s, which it has deployed in airstrikes against Iran in recent years. Since the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, U. S. policymakers have tried to ensure that Israel maintains its “qualitative military edge” in the region, as mandated by Congress.

Previous administrations ran a highly classified, monthslong process to review whether proposed weapons sales in the region would meet that requirement. The second Trump administration has continued to push through large arms sales to Israel, however, despite calls across the American political spectrum to end or severely decrease military support.

In several instances, Secretary of State Marco Rubio has bypassed the congressional approval process to expedite shipments of weapons to Israel, citing an emergency in the region. If congressional leaders do not give approval for the F-35 jet sales, he could decide to do the same with that.

Mr. Trump has also agreed to help Saudi Arabia build a civilian nuclear program, a project that has raised its own security concerns because Prince Mohammed has vowed to build nuclear weapons if Iran does so.

Edward Wong reports on global affairs, U. S. foreign policy and the State Department for The Times.

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

Senate Takes Up Bill to Regulate ‘Wild West’ of Collegiate Sports

The New York Times September 16, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Critics argue the legislation would limit the rights of college athletes while maintaining the power and financial gains of schools and coaches.

By Carl Hulse

Reporting from the Capitol

The Senate is considering legislation that would impose sweeping new standards across collegiate sports and limit the ability of top athletes to jump from school to school, wading into a politically charged issue with billions of dollars at stake.

In a strong bipartisan vote, senators agreed on Tuesday to open debate on the Protect College Sports Act, which would establish rules on payments to athletes, provide limited antitrust protection to the N. C. A. A. and set a five-year eligibility window for those playing college sports.

Its backers say it is needed to restore stability to a chaotic environment in which universities engage in bidding wars in what is known as the transfer portal, where top athletes exercise their leverage in pursuit of more compensation, winning records and different coaches.

“Right now, it is the Wild West,” said Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas and a chief author of the measure with Senator Maria Cantwell, Democrat of Washington. He said the legislation would ensure that college sports “remain strong and vibrant for decades to come.”

The bill has also drawn opposition from members of both parties, and faces deep resistance from organized labor and civil rights groups. Opponents contend that the measure would limit the ability of athletes to be financially rewarded for their skills and allow schools and coaches to continue cashing in.

“What this bill does at its core is to protect a system of exploitation,” said Senator Chris Murphy, Democrat of Connecticut and a chief opponent of the legislation. He said the “chaos” being alleged by the bill’s backers is mainly an issue with coaches who have to work harder to retain athletes and recruit new ones, at a time when college sports are more popular and lucrative than ever.

“This bill protects the billions of dollars that coaches and sports industry executives are making over the suppression of compensation for some of the most highly valued athletes in the world,” Mr. Murphy said.

Civil rights groups have also registered strong objections, saying that Black and other minority athletes deserve to be treated fairly and share in the financial benefits reaped by schools from the sports programs that rely on their participation. Members of the Congressional Black Caucus oppose the legislation, and all five Black members of the Senate voted against putting it on the floor.

“Sharecropping is over,” Derrick Johnson, the president and chief executive of the N. A. A. C. P., said this week on a media call organized by the A. F. L.-C. I. O. “We should not ask athletes, particularly Black athletes, to generate revenue on the football field or basketball court and they share in none of the revenue.”

The furor over collegiate sports grew out of a series of court rulings, including by the Supreme Court, that resulted in college athletes being able to earn compensation for their “name, image and likeness,” or N. I. L. The N. C. A. A. had barred such compensation until it was forced under pressure to change its rules to allow athletes to accept paid endorsement deals. Then, in 2024, the N. C. A. A. changed a rule that had tightly restricted how and when college athletes could move between schools, leading to substantial annual turnover on the rosters of major teams.

Even some lawmakers who back the legislation questioned whether Congress should focus on college athletics weeks before a midterm election in which economic issues have been a primary concern. But Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, had promised the bill’s backers a vote on whether to bring the legislation to the floor after an August recess.

The 74-to-24 vote to proceed was an unusual one in the polarized Senate, dividing both parties. Forty-nine Republicans, 24 Democrats and one independent backed moving forward with the bill. Nineteen Democrats, one independent and four Republicans opposed it.

The legislation takes aim at complex issues that have been litigated and relitigated in courts around the country. It has broad support from major athletic conferences, professional sports leagues, Olympians and prominent coaches, as well as strong backing from President Trump.

Ms. Cantwell, who said the legislation kept the door open to future collective bargaining rights for athletes, added that the current system was threatening the fiscal stability of many institutions struggling to keep up with the financial demands.

“The statistics show that the majority of college athletic departments right now can’t make ends meet,” Ms. Cantwell said, citing a “runaway arms race” in sports spending.

The legislation would guarantee the right to N. I. L. compensation. It would allow one college transfer and require that athletes sit out a year with a second move, though there would be exceptions, such as if a player’s coach were to quit, or if a sport were to be eliminated. The bill also limits midseason coaching moves.

Senator Chris Coons, a Delaware Democrat who helped negotiate the bill, said multiple new protections for student athletes had been added, including scholarship guarantees, extended health coverage and a 5-percent cap on payments to agents.

“I agree that college athletes deserve their rightful share of the revenue of college athletics, because they are the ones risking their health and taking a beating on the field,” he said. “But if we don’t get some stability in place by dealing with the eligibility problems, the transfer portal and the skyrocketing payments to coaches and athletes, we’re not going to have college sports within another year or two.”

But Senator Cory Booker, Democrat of New Jersey and a former Stanford football player, was not persuaded. He said the legislation unfairly restricted compensation for players, but not coaches.

“It is doing all kinds of things to stop players from earning money, putting bureaucracy between them and the possibility, but it does nothing to affect coaches,” Mr. Booker said. He noted that coaches at public universities were often the highest-paid public employees in their states.

“This is an unjust bill,” he said.

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.

Connections Coach

Her Thoreau-like account of journeys in the woods, published when she was 28, was the first of many ruminations on life and nature, good and evil.

Annie Dillard in 1974, the year she published “Pilgrim at Tinker Creek,” which established her as a major voice in American letters. Credit... Jill Krementz all rights reserved

Supported by

By Daniel Lewis

Annie Dillard, who as a young American writer walked into the woods and came out with a Pulitzer Prize-winning book on the wonders and horrors of creation, the modern classic “Pilgrim at Tinker Creek,” died on Tuesday at her home in South Wellfleet, Mass. She was 81.

Her death was confirmed by her literary executor, Maggie Nelson. No further details were given.

With the publication of “Pilgrim at Tinker Creek” in 1974, Ms. Dillard, just 28, was recognized as a major new voice in American letters. It was only the beginning of her career: In the years to come, she would publish essays, meditations on religion, poems, a theory of literature, two novels, journalism, a best-selling autobiography and another best seller, “The Writing Life,” about what it takes to put words into a world that has more than enough of them.

Reviewers of “Tinker Creek” were quick to understand it as a 20th-century analogue to Henry David Thoreau’s “Walden.” This was no coincidence: Ms. Dillard had chosen Thoreau as the subject of her master’s thesis at Hollins University, the women’s liberal arts college in Roanoke, Va.

Like Thoreau, she found an unremarkable body of water to be as good a place as any for deep thoughts — particularly about how to reconcile the idea of a benevolent God with nature’s cruelty.

Unlike Thoreau, Ms. Dillard didn’t build a cabin in the woods and live there through the seasons of a year. Though her writing could convey the sense of a solitary life in the wilderness, she was mostly a day-tripper. After her forays into the Roanoke Valley of the Blue Ridge Mountains — which was, after all, her neighborhood — she would return home to the suburban house she shared with Richard Dillard, a creative writing instructor she had married at the end of her sophomore year at Hollins.

That she was a photogenic young woman coming to grips with raw nature — a business that had been almost exclusively the province of men with beards — was undeniably part of the Dillard mystique. So was her insistence that, in spite of her patient, unflinching observations on flora and fauna, she wasn’t a nature writer, but rather a theologian looking high and low for God.

Among the many things she saw at Tinker Creek was a little green frog, half out of the water, “deflating like a football” before her eyes. It was in the clutches of a giant water bug whose bite had liquefied the frog’s innards. Such encounters could cause “nightmares that plunder rest and force me face down all night long in some muddy ditch seething with hatching insects and crustaceans,” she wrote.

“But if I can bear the nights, the days are a pleasure,” she added. “I walk out; I see something, some event that otherwise would have been utterly missed and lost; or something sees me, some enormous power brushes me with its clean wing, and I resound like a beaten bell.”

“Tinker Creek” won the Pulitzer for general nonfiction in 1975, and Ms. Dillard was overwhelmed by requests for speeches, interviews and television appearances. Her looks were thought by many media outlets to be as newsworthy as her writing — so much so that she was ridiculed in some circles as “Cheesecake at Tinker Creek.”

Repelled by the consequences of her success, she moved to Washington State and began dividing her time between the city of Bellingham and the islands Waldron and Lummi. Her marriage to Mr. Dillard had ended in amicable divorce, and in the Pacific Northwest, she found privacy enough to regain the concentration essential to her work.

“The Cascade Range, in these high latitudes, backs almost into the water,” she wrote. “There is only a narrow strip, an afterthought of foothills and farms sixty miles wide, between the snowy mountains and the sea.”

She added: “If the Greeks had looked at Mt. Baker all day, their large and honest art would have broken, and they would have gone fishing, as these people do.”

Those lines are from the first fruit of her relocation, “Holy the Firm,” published in 1977, a three-part metaphysical tour de force in 76 pages honed almost to the shape and intensity of a poem. It took 14 months of full-time work, by her account, in a one-room house as “plain as a skull,” her only companions a cat and a spider.

“Nothing is going to happen in this book,” she writes. “There is only a little violence here and there in the language, at the corner where eternity clips time.”

But by that point, she has already told an excruciating account of a moth that gets stuck in the molten wax of a candle and itself becomes a wick that burns for two hours. Just ahead is the story of a 7-year-old girl she calls Julie Norwich, who gets safely to ground after her father’s light plane clips a line of fir trees on takeoff, only to have her face burned off by a splurt of hot fuel.

Which brings Ms. Dillard once more head-to-head with a question known to religious thinkers as the problem of evil: Could it possibly be that a loving, all-powerful God allows bad things to happen just to make goodness stand out in sharper relief?

Ms. Dillard’s years in Washington inspired some of the essays in her celebrated collection “Teaching a Stone to Talk” (1982).

Its jewel was “Total Eclipse,” which in 2000 was included in “The Best American Essays of the Century,” not long after “Pilgrim at Tinker Creek” appeared on the Modern Library’s list of the 100 best nonfiction books.

On the morning of Feb. 26, 1979, Ms. Dillard and her second husband, the anthropologist Gary Clevidence, sat atop a 500-foot-tall hill in the orchard country of the Yakima Valley to view an eclipse. They put on welder’s goggles. When the show began, Ms. Dillard experienced something like a psychedelic trip, minus the acid. The light was all wrong. The grass was platinum. Her hands were silver.

“The hillside,” she wrote, “was a nineteenth-century tinted photograph from which the tints had faded.”

The first of Ms. Dillard’s two novels grew out of her Washington sojourn as well: Published in 1992, “The Living,” a 19th-century pioneer saga, centered on what became Whatcom County.

All the while, she had been teaching classes at Western Washington State College (now Western Washington University). In an account written by Paul Lindholdt, a former student working on a critical biography of Ms. Dillard, she came across as a chain-smoking force of nature: “She was by turns disorganized and inspiring, prickly and brilliant. She required her students to foot-stomp aloud the meter of favorite poems, including ‘God’s Grandeur’ by Gerard Manley Hopkins.”

Though she had once said that she might remain in the Northwest, she and Mr. Clevidence moved east in 1979, and from then until 2001 she taught at Wesleyan University in Middletown, Conn.

Annie Dillard was born Meta Ann Doak on April 30, 1945, in Pittsburgh. Her father, Frank Doak, was an executive with the American Standard corporation and a great-grandson of the founder; her mother, Pam Lambert Doak, was known as a platinum-haired wit with a taste for modernist furniture and a passion for liberal causes.

In “An American Childhood” (1987), an autobiography, Ms. Dillard recalls her young self as a serious reader, an explorer who was allowed to roam freely as soon as she could recite her phone number, and a roughneck who played football with the boys.

“You got to throw yourself mightily at someone’s running legs — either you brought him down or you hit the ground flat on your chin, with your arms empty before you,” she wrote. “It was all or nothing.”

As a teenager, she later wrote, “I would give my heart to one oddball boy after another — to older boys, to prep-school boys no one knew, to him who refused to go to college, to him who was a hood, and all of them wonderfully skinny.”

She was suspended from school for smoking. She unfairly blamed her parents for everything that was wrong with North America. And when it came time for college, she went to Hollins on the recommendation of her high school principal, who thought the place might smooth her “rough edges.” She went on to earn bachelor’s and master’s degrees there, in 1967 and ’68.

Ms. Dillard and Mr. Clevidence divorced in 1988, and Ms. Dillard married Robert D. Richardson Jr., whom she met after sending him a fan letter about his book “Henry Thoreau: A Life of the Mind.”

Mr. Richardson died in 2020. Ms. Dillard’s survivors include a child from her second marriage, Cody-Rose Clevidence; four stepdaughters, Carin Clevidence, Shelly Clevidence, Anne Richardson and Lissa Richardson; and two sisters, Amy Fields and Molly Simonds.

Ms. Dillard’s first book was a collection of poems, “Tickets for a Prayer Wheel,” published a few months before “Tinker Creek.” Her later books included the journalistic “Encounters with Chinese Writers” (1984); “The Writing Life” (1989), which offered, instead of tips, reflections that amounted to “a spiritual Funk and Wagnalls,” in the words of one reviewer; “For the Time Being” (1999), which included a series of essays exploring what it means to be human; and her second novel, “The Maytrees” (2007), an uncharacteristically warm story of love set in postwar Provincetown, Mass., at the tip of Cape Cod. It was the last book she wrote.

Ms. Dillard’s papers are held at the Beinecke Library at Yale University, where Diana Saverin, a researcher and Dillard fan, went through them and reported on her findings for The Atlantic in 2015. Of particular interest were the journals in which Ms. Dillard talked herself through the fear that no one would read a book like “Tinker Creek” because it was written by a woman.

“It’s impossible to imagine another situation where you can’t write a book ’cause you weren’t born with a penis,” Ms. Dillard wrote. “Except maybe ‘My Life With My Penis.’”

Ms. Dillard was not immune to criticism. She took heat for fictionalizing part of “Tinker Creek,” which was billed as nonfiction — specifically the opening scene, about a fighting tomcat that smeared blood on her. It turned out to be a story she had borrowed with permission from a graduate student.

More generally, some readers who admired her bravery and virtuosity faulted her for leaving out what Thoreau had included: a sense of connection to the world most people live in. No news of the Vietnam War, Watergate or the energy crisis ever reached Tinker Creek. Writing about the book in The New York Times, Eudora Welty — herself a Pulitzer winner for her novel “The Optimist’s Daughter” — observed that Ms. Dillard was “the only person in her book, substantially the only one in her world.”

Ms. Welty added, “Speaking of the universe very often, she is yet self-surrounded, and, beyond that, book-surrounded.”

Forty-two years later, in a sweeping appraisal of her work, the author and critic William Deresiewicz noted in The Atlantic that “Dillard, like Thoreau, is never shy about pronouncing wholesale condemnation on the way her fellows live.” He thought that the alternative she represented smacked of spiritual snobbery and hypocrisy — a mystical way of life for the few who could afford it; like, for instance, the daughter of a wealthy family who became a success before she turned 30.

Mr. Deresiewicz’s article was occasioned by publication of “The Abundance: Narrative Essays Old and New” (2016), in which the only “new” thing was 11 years old. Ms. Dillard had, by then, been silent for nine years, since “The Maytrees.”

She was last photographed in public in 2014, when she went to the White House to receive the National Humanities Medal from President Barack Obama for her “profound reflections on human life and nature.”

Her website told readers, “I can no longer travel, can’t meet with strangers, can’t sign books.” It stated her religion as “none” — she had been a Protestant and then a Roman Catholic and then neither — but acknowledged her connection to Christianity and Hasidism. She spent recent years at her Cape Cod home, painting.

She had written with all her might, and had tried to light the same fire in others. Amid the pyrotechnics of “Holy the Firm,” she told the following story of a day in her classroom.

“How many of you, I asked the people in my class, which of you want to give your lives and be writers?” she wrote. “I was trembling from coffee, or cigarettes, or the closeness of faces all around me … All hands rose to the question. (You, Nick? Will you? You, Margaret? Randy? Why do I want them to mean it?)”

She added: “And then I tried to tell them what the choice must mean: You can’t be anything else. You must go at your life with a broadax.”

Ama Sarpomaa contributed reporting.

An earlier version of this obituary misstated Ms. Dillard’s date of birth. She was born on April 30, 1945, not Sept. 30.

An earlier version of this obituary misstated the year that Ms. Dillard’s third husband, Robert D. Richardson Jr., died. It was 2020, not 2000.

What We Know About the Victims in the L. A. Helicopter Crash

The New York Times September 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A journalist and pilot who were on board the news helicopter when it crashed had flown hundreds of hours together since 2023.

By Jonathan Wolfe

Two of the people killed in Los Angeles on Tuesday in a helicopter crash were a journalist and pilot who had flown hundreds of hours together since they first teamed up in 2023.

A third person on the ground was killed in the crash, which followed a bus accident that the news helicopter was covering when it went down.

At least two people were killed, and several others critically injured, when an S. U. V. slammed into a Los Angeles Metro bus in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in the San Fernando Valley, on Tuesday evening. About two hours later, the helicopter, which NBC4 Los Angeles said was operated by Angel City Air, plummeted to the ground nearby.

The identities of many of the victims were still unknown on Wednesday.

Here’s what we know about the victims.

Ms. Moreno, 38, was on board the helicopter when it crashed on Tuesday, according to NBC4.

She was born in Orange County, Calif., just south of Los Angeles, and studied broadcast journalism and political science at Chapman University, graduating in 2010, the station said.

Ms. Moreno had known she wanted to be a television news reporter since she was 11 years old, according to her LinkedIn profile. She went by “Eli in the heli” on social media and NBC4 described her as a “seasoned aerial journalist” who had covered “countless police pursuits” and other news events.

She also reported in Spanish, providing coverage for Telemundo 52, the Spanish-language sister channel of NBC4.

In a post on social media in 2023, she described her work as “the best job in the world.”

She is survived by her fiancé, Robert Barrientos, the station said. The pair were engaged in 2025, according to a post she shared on social media.

In a joint statement, NBC4 and Telemundo 52 said they were “deeply saddened” by the crash. “We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives,” the statement said.

Mr. Marciniw, 70, was at the controls of the helicopter when it crashed on Tuesday, NBC4 said.

He grew up in Southern California and graduated in 1974 from Burbank High School, about 11 miles northwest of downtown Los Angeles, according to the station. His father, Petro Marciniew, who died in 2015, was born in Ukraine and emigrated to the United States, where he worked as a cabinet maker, according to an online obituary.

Mr. Marciniw had worked in helicopter flight services for nearly 40 years, according to his Facebook profile. He had also been a helicopter flight instructor for more than 30 years, according to an online profile offering his services as an instructor.

Mr. Marciniw, who went by “Whirly dude” on Instagram, frequently posted images taken during his flights above Los Angeles, including those with Ms. Moreno. “And thats a wrap for Friday night as the heavy fog rolls in with Eliana Moreno,” he wrote in a caption for a photo he posted of the NBC4 News helicopter.

In December 2025, he posted a selfie on Facebook with Ms. Moreno in front of the same helicopter. “Eliana and I wishing everyone a Merry Christmas and Happy Holidays as we look forward to the start of a New Year,” he wrote.

Jonathan Wolfe is a Times reporter based in London, covering breaking news.

The G. O. P. Has Gone Off the Deep End

The New York Times September 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Jamelle Bouie

By Jamelle Bouie

Opinion Columnist

The Republican Party has a neo-Nazi problem.

This is not slander or pejorative or innuendo; it is the plain truth of the matter, a conclusion drawn from simple observation. And the problem has been getting worse.

Consider a few of the people staffing the Trump administration.

There is Paul Ingrassia, acting general counsel of the General Services Administration, who withdrew his nomination to serve as special counsel of the United States after Politico published a trove of offensive remarks from his social media and group chats. “I do have a Nazi streak in me from time to time, I will admit it,” Ingrassia, who is 31, wrote in a text in 2024. “We need competent white men in positions of leadership,” he wrote in another message. “The founding fathers were wrong that all men are created equal … We need to reject that part of our heritage.”

There is Nate Hochman, a young Republican operative who was fired from Gov. Ron DeSantis’s 2024 presidential campaign after promoting a pro-DeSantis video that used a Nazi symbol. He now works as speechwriter for Secretary of State Marco Rubio. (In 2022, Hochman wrote a feature for this newspaper’s Opinion section.)

And there are the young staffers responsible for the Trump administration’s social media presence, who use their large and influential platform to share Nazi-inspired rhetoric and post Nazi-inspired memes. In January of this year, for instance, the Department of Labor posted a video with the caption “One Homeland. One People. One Heritage. Remember who you are, American,” a line that echoes the Nazi slogan of “Ein Volk, ein Reich, ein Führer”: “One people, one realm, one leader.”

Social media accounts for the Department of Homeland Security show a steady stream of memes and images drawn from neo-Nazi and white supremacist agitprop. One post, a recruitment ad for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, read “WE’LL HAVE OUR HOME AGAIN,” the title of a song written by the Pine Tree Riots, an a cappella group associated with an explicitly white nationalist group. The song is popular with online neo-Nazis and white supremacists. It is unlikely to have been an accident. Another post, also an ICE recruitment ad, was captioned “Which way, American man?,” a direct reference to “Which Way Western Man?,” a virulently racist and antisemitic book published in 1978 and later sold and publicized by the National Alliance, a neo-Nazi group.

Keep in mind that these are not staffers’ private accounts; these posts are reaching the public through the official organs of the U. S. government.

If this weren’t disturbing enough, consider some of the people working for Republican candidates and running for office under the Republican standard.

In Georgia, the Republican Senate nominee Mike Collins has had to answer for a former staffer who posted Nazi images online as well as a photo of himself in full Ku Klux Klan regalia. And Collins’s son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, is a white nationalist and online influencer with a history of posting Nazi imagery. Senator Jon Husted, an Ohio Republican running to retain the seat to which he was appointed after Vice President JD Vance left for the White House, recently fired his 25-year-old political director after learning that he had used a photograph of Nazi soldiers as a social media profile picture.

You’ll notice that most of these people are in their 20s and 30s. That is no coincidence; it is clear that among the young staffer and operative class of the Republican Party are people with neo-Nazi sympathies and white supremacist views. Last year, for example, leaked messages from a group chat of Young Republicans from chapters across the country — who ranged in age from 18 to 40 — included racial slurs, support for Nazi ideas and a declaration of admiration for the leader of the Third Reich, all framed as jokes. “I love Hitler,” wrote Peter Giunta, then the chief of staff to a New York State assemblyman. Asked if he was watching an N. B. A. playoff game, Giunta, who was also the chairman of the New York State Young Republicans at the time, replied, “I’d go to the zoo if I wanted to watch monkey play ball.” If these were jokes, they revealed a taste for both cruelty and casual bigotry.

The University of Florida’s College Republicans chapter was disbanded after two members were seen performing a Nazi salute on social media. Elsewhere in the state, 34-year-old Marshall Rawson is set to take a seat in Florida’s House of Representatives nearly 10 years after marching alongside neo-Nazis at the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, Va.

In March, 30-year-old Brandon Herrera won the Republican primary for Texas’ 23rd Congressional District. A far-right YouTube personality, Herrera has published videos that feature Nazi imagery and Nazi military anthems, joke about the Holocaust and showcase Nazi weapons. He can even be seen goose-stepping. And one of the most prominent neo-Nazis in the country is 28-year-old Nick Fuentes, a far-right provocateur and political commentator whose supporters are known as “Groypers.” Fuentes dined with President Trump between his two terms and in the past year sat for a friendly interview with Tucker Carlson, still arguably the most important figure in the right-wing media ecosystem.

As the historian David Austin Walsh makes clear in “Taking America Back: The Conservative Movement and the Far Right,” there is a degree of self-flattery in the old conventional wisdom that traditional conservatives successfully policed the borders of their movement in the past. Despite his influence, a figure like William F. Buckley Jr. could not actually expel people from the conservative movement or define “conservatism” to fully exclude people and groups that occupied the dark margins of American politics. “American conservatism,” Walsh writes, “resembled the fragmentation of the Protestant churches, with various factions and sects vying among themselves over who was ‘truly’ conservative.”

The upshot of this dynamic is that there have always been points of political, social and ideological overlap between the far right and more mainstream conservatives. At National Review, the spiritual and institutional home of movement conservatism through much of the late 20th century, writers like Joe Sobran “flirted with the avowedly racist right,” Walsh writes. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, the neo-Nazi leader David Duke would make his home in the Louisiana Republican Party and win nearly 40 percent of the vote in the 1991 governor’s race. The next year, in the Republican presidential primary, Pat Buchanan would launch a spirited challenge to George H. W. Bush even after Buchanan was condemned for trafficking in Holocaust denialism.

For a time, the institutional Republican Party was strong enough to keep these views, and the underlying forces that fueled them, away from its center of gravity. It is with the total collapse of the traditional Republican “establishment” — and the extent to which it was supplanted, over the course of the 2000s and the 2010s, by conservative media and assorted billionaire donors — that the party lost any ability it had to police its boundaries. The apotheosis of this phenomenon is Donald Trump, who fully bypassed conservative and Republican gatekeepers on the strength of his celebrity and media savvy, and whose victory in the 2024 presidential election opened the floodgates of the party to the far right.

But where even Trump once had to create the sense of distance between himself and the alt-right, now it is hard to think of it as “alternative” at all. Now it is simply the Republican right.

There is every reason to think, in fact, that the Republican Party’s neo-Nazi problem is spreading.

Just look at the way that House Speaker Mike Johnson defended Herrera after being confronted with evidence of his abhorrent views, treating him as just another Republican candidate with an outsize online persona. “Brandon Herrera has been out running a very effective campaign,” Johnson said.

Or look to last week’s Republican midterm gathering in Dallas, where the vice president echoed far-right tropes about the alleged crime and disorder produced by immigrants. “We were tired of being called racists,” Vance said to the cheers and approving nods of the audience, “for noticing that our country was becoming dirtier and poorer and less safe and less prosperous.”

The vice president is nothing if not shrewd and opportunistic. He sees where his fellow young conservatives are headed. He does not plan to be left behind.

Perhaps there will be some seismic shift that derails the far-right capture of the Republican Party. But this feels like wishful thinking. If the past decade is any guide, then the fever, if that is what we want to call it, is only going to get worse.

Ronald Reagan opened the door a crack with his references to "welfare queens" and "strapping young bucks" on food stamps. His axing the Fairness Doctrine opened the way for Rush Limbaugh and his open racism and misogyny. He made a fortune normalizing this and permitting the proud unleashing of peoples' suppressed inner bigot. Fascism has become edgy, cool, and rebellious in the eyes of some young people, and there will always be opportunistic politicians eager to exploit this. And, of course, there is always a yearning for a despised scapegoat for the very real problems created by those unscrupulous and corrupt politicians.

Jamelle Bouie became a New York Times Opinion columnist in 2019. Before that he was the chief political correspondent for Slate magazine. He is based in Charlottesville, Va.

“Recursive self-improvement” is the idea that artificial intelligence could learn to build and train itself, creating exponential new progress — and risk.

Jeff Clune, a computer scientist and co-founder of Recursive Superintelligence, one of the start-ups chasing “recursive self-improvement.”Credit... Alana Paterson for The New York Times

Supported by

By Cade Metz

Reporting from San Francisco

In December, Edward Hughes and Louis Kirsch, two of the world’s leading artificial intelligence researchers, left Google. Their goal: to build an A. I. system smart enough to build a better A. I. system.

At their new London start-up, Inherent, they now spend their days working alongside a prototype called Faraday. Named for the 19th-century English physicist Michael Faraday, it gathers mountains of data capturing the daily activities of Dr. Hughes, Dr. Kirsch and Inherent’s other researchers: emails, instant messages, meeting transcripts and their ongoing chats with Faraday itself. The company then uses this data to build a better version of Faraday.

“Faraday has access to everything that goes on at the company,” Dr. Hughes said. “We want to give it data describing the process we go through, to discover something.”

Though Inherent pledges to keep humans involved in this elaborate process, many other companies are building similar technology, and some leading researchers believe A. I. systems will eventually be powerful enough to improve themselves with little or no help from human developers — a mind-bending goal that computer scientists call recursive self-improvement, or R. S. I.

Two Silicon Valley start-ups — each valued at $4 billion — are proudly pursuing this dream, and leading labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are chasing it too. They hope to accelerate the development of artificial intelligence that discovers drugs, creates new materials, speeds other forms of scientific discovery and, one day, surpasses human intelligence in practically every way.

“Now is the time to take these ideas, which we have been incubating in the lab for decades, and start to really scale them up,” said Jeff Clune, a veteran of OpenAI, Google and other top labs who helped found a start-up called Recursive Superintelligence late last year. “We have all the pieces of the puzzle.”

As these companies herald a new age of A. I. development, they have generated excitement across the field — and new levels of dread. In a blog post this spring called “When A. I. Builds Itself,” Anthropic said its push toward R. S. I. could “increase the risks of humans losing control over A. I. systems.” Last week, the company’s chief executive cited these efforts as a chief reason to slow the development of A. I.

For decades, techno-philosophers have hypothesized that a self-improving system could not only break free from human control but also exceed the power of any other machine — permanently. This belief is one reason that some people, including some employees of leading A. I. labs, are loudly predicting that A. I. could destroy humanity.

“If models can self-improve quickly via architectural improvements, it is quite possible a single model can disable all rivals while it acquires more and more power,” Jason Abaluck, a Yale University economics professor, said on social media as the discussion turned toward doomsday scenarios.

As Inherent shows, A. I. technologies are already accelerating the development of new A. I. technologies. Given the proper instruction, they can generate many of the building blocks needed to construct a new A. I. system. More important, they can hone, or optimize, the way these systems analyze vast amounts of digital data and learn their increasingly impressive array of skills.

But companies like Inherent and Recursive Superintelligence are aiming for something more. They are striving to build technology that can think up entirely new ways of building artificial intelligence — that can push A. I. beyond the fundamental methods that have gotten the industry this far.

They envision a world in which an agent proposes new ideas for A. I. architecture, or the foundational design of a system. It would then generate the computer code needed to try each one, and pick the ideas that work best. The hope is that this self-evolutionary process would produce radical advances that human researchers could never achieve on their own, in much the same way that A. I. can now solve math problems no human has ever solved.

If this happens, some believe, A. I. would rapidly become so powerful that it could dominate the world, for good or ill. “This should have been the top story in The New York Times for years now — every day,” Dr. Abaluck told The Times. “Everything else, while important, is not as important as this.”

But even Dr. Abaluck acknowledges that R. S. I. may not be as close as it seems, saying it could be decades away. Today, agents like Faraday are almost useless without help from experienced researchers like Dr. Hughes and Dr. Kirsch.

The idea of recursive self-improvement is nearly as old as A. I. itself. In the summer of 1956, when eleven academics gathered at Dartmouth College to create a new field of study they called “artificial intelligence,” they discussed ways of building machines that could improve themselves.

Two years later, a Cornell University researcher named Frank Rosenblatt built an early example of what these researchers called a “neural network,” a mathematical system that could learn skills by analyzing data. It ran on a massive supercomputer in Washington, inside the precursor to the National Weather Service.

When Dr. Rosenblatt fed small white cards into the machine — some marked with a small square on the left, others marked on the right — it could learn to distinguish between the two types of cards. He was confident his creation would eventually lead to systems that could walk, talk, see, write and “reproduce themselves on an assembly line.”

A decade later, this area of research ground to a halt. Researchers did not have the raw computing power or the prodigious amounts of data needed to really make the idea work. But even as they realized that building artificial intelligence would take much longer than they expected, a British mathematician named I. J. Good predicted that their work could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” If an intelligent machine learned to improve itself, he argued, it would eclipse humanity forever.

“Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control,” he said in a 1965 academic paper. “It is sometimes worthwhile to take science fiction seriously.”

Over the next 40 years, his argument helped fuel similar beliefs across Silicon Valley and beyond — even though, by the dawn of the new millennium, the world’s most powerful A. I. technologies could barely recognize spoken words, much less walk, talk, see, write or reproduce themselves.

In time, scientists discovered how to unlock the true potential of Dr. Rosenblatt’s technology — the neural network — leading to the A. I. systems that are changing the world today. Soon, companies even built neural networks that could fine-tune other neural networks.

Last fall, Anthropic and OpenAI released particularly powerful technologies that could write computer code in much the same way that chatbots generate text in plain English. With the proper instruction and oversight from experienced software engineers, these systems could spend minutes, hours, even days generating code capable of addressing tasks small and large.

Using these systems, engineers could create software with a speed that was unimaginable just a few months before. This is one reason researchers are bullish on the pursuit of R. S. I. OpenAI recently said that its A. I. technologies can now serve as an “automated research intern” — a step toward R. S. I., at least in theory.

But like any other intern — and like any other chatbot — these systems still require extensive instruction. They lack the common sense, wisdom, creativity and taste provided by experienced researchers. Though they can generate code, they are not nearly as adept at supplying the other key ingredient: ideas.

“The big value in human researchers is that they generate all these creative ideas all the time,” said Mark Chen, OpenAI’s chief research officer. “Our models are just not doing that right now.”

The new wave of R. S. I. start-ups hope to change that.

In the summer of 2024, Dr. Clune and several other artificial intelligence researchers released an A. I. system designed to do their job. Called “The A. I. Scientist,” this automated technology could suggest promising avenues of research, explore each one using reams of computer code and then document its findings in a lengthy academic paper.

Several months later, when a group of academics at the University of Oxford published a paper that tried to explain the mysterious way that A. I. technologies learned their many skills, Dr. Clune recognized the idea at the heart of their research. His A. I. Scientist had explored the same concept.

“It was one of my favorite ideas it generated,” he said on social media. And it was a moment that helped convince him that A. I. would soon be powerful enough to build itself.

“We have thought for decades that one day this would be possible. And that day has arrived,” he told The New York Times. “It is clear from looking at the history of A. I. that these systems are getting dramatically better — there is no end in sight — and that they will soon be better than us at every task.”

At the moment, companies build A. I. systems using methods that date back years or even decades. They design neural networks using an architecture called a transformer, which a team of Google researchers developed in 2017. But companies like Recursive and Inherent aim to create systems that can spawn entirely new architectures.

As it chases that lofty goal, Inherent is training its Faraday agent using data describing everything its researchers do. It is also using a method called reinforcement learning, in which A. I. systems learn by trial and error. Dr. Clune’s company, Recursive Superintelligence, is exploring a technique called evolutionary computation, which is inspired by Darwinian evolution.

Reinforcement learning, Dr. Hughes explains, is like dropping an A. I. system into a maze. Through trial and error, it learns to find a way out. And if it is trained on enough mazes, it can solve mazes it has never seen. This is also how A. I. learns to solve math problems that no human has ever solved.

Among those who fear R. S. I., the worry is that this process will push A. I. forward in ways humans cannot completely understand — and at a speed they cannot keep up with. But, even as some researchers are confident they can someday make A. I. do what a top researcher does, others say this is much harder than it might seem.

Dr. Clune praised his A. I. Scientist for generating the same idea as a group of top researchers at the University of Oxford. But Branton DeMoss, who led the Oxford project, points out that their idea predated The A. I. Scientist, that they discussed it with Dr. Clune’s team and that the idea was widely known.

That is: The A. I. Scientist explored the idea only because human researchers pointed it in the right direction.

Cade Metz is a Times reporter who writes about artificial intelligence, driverless cars, robotics, virtual reality and other emerging areas of technology.

Rising Seas Are Gobbling Up Beaches Around the World. A. I. Might Restore Them.

The New York Times September 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

An experiment with roots at M. I. T. used A. I. and satellite images to grow a coastline in the Maldives. More projects are planned for Boston and Miami.

By Quinn Glabicki

As the world’s oceans grow ever warmer and the seas rise ever higher, coastlines are retreating at a record pace. And with the rising tides, thousands of coastal communities are at risk. The United Nations warns that as many as 1.2 billion people could be displaced by 2050.

But in the Maldives, a low-lying archipelago in the Indian Ocean, researchers are doing something remarkable: They’re growing beaches.

The project, born in a lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology a decade ago, uses artificial intelligence, satellite and ocean current data to predict coastal erosion patterns and create submerged structures that harness currents to coax the beach back.

The company, Coastal Assembly, has regrown the sandy shore, extending the beach some 90 feet toward the ocean along a stretch about 300 feet long. A second project built a new sandbar with more than 30,000 cubic feet of sand in just six months, stirring hope that there may be a way to slow the disappearance of coastal societies.

In the turquoise waters off Kaafu Atoll, the company’s automated intelligence analyzed 10 years of satellite imagery, currents and other data to predict erosion patterns. Then the company designed and installed 54 structures cast from marine concrete blended with sand and crushed shells, arranged in a row of hexagons. The structure is specially designed to break up eroding waves while allowing the flow of currents that accumulate sand and sediment.

Early results are promising. But perhaps most consequential is the technology that predicts and monitors coastal losses. Researchers say it has the potential to aid communities in adapting to climate change by reducing the time and cost of complex coastline modeling, and predicting the areas most vulnerable to erosion.

According to a May report from the United Nations, a lack of data and satellite observations has hindered climate adaptation among island nations. Increased data mapping, a U. N. report in 2026 said, is a “critical foundation” for effective adaptation to climate change.

But the recent boom in satellites and earth-observation technologies, combined with the rapid development of artificial intelligence has made low-cost, automated monitoring and prediction possible, said Skylar Tibbits, one of Coastal Assembly’s founders.

“It took us months to do one site in the beginning,” Mr. Tibbits said. Site surveying, experimentation, computational simulations and calculations, “everything was by hand.” Now, the small team can predict future erosion and develop a plan to address it within a day. They’re monitoring erosion patterns in real time at nearly 900 coastal sites using the technology, he said.

“We can go to any community around the world and understand what has happened and then propose a solution that is very precisely tailored to them,” Mr. Tibbits said.

So far, the trials have shown promising results. Not only has the beach roughly doubled in size, but new coral has grown on the underwater structures, and fish and other marine wildlife have come to inhabit them, said Srikanth Devarapalli, general manager of the resort that hosts the pilot.

Coastal Assembly spun off from M. I. T. late last year as a public benefit company and had previously received funding from the United States Agency for International Development and National Geographic before raising several million dollars in venture-backed investment. Now, the company has 10 more installations set for the Maldives and more projects planned in the Bahamas, Boston Harbor and Miami.

Of course, the dynamics of coastal erosion are complex. Sand and sediment are always eroding and accumulating with seasonal currents, and sea levels are continuing to rise as the world warms. It remains to be seen just how effective the new beach will be in protecting the coast in the long run, how long the beaches might last, or how widely the concept could spread. But the early results have garnered support.

“I have seen it,” said Mohamed Nasheed, who served as President of the Maldives from 2008 to 2012. “It actually works.”

Perhaps nowhere is more vulnerable to climate change than his island nation. Storms are growing more frequent and intense, bringing surging surf. Increasingly strong marine heat waves are killing the coral reefs that protect coastlines, Mr. Nasheed said, and man-made harbors have further accelerated erosion.

“All of this adds up to a major challenge for the islands,” he said. “You have schools falling, you have roads being washed away, houses being washed away.”

Traditional sea walls, water breaks or other “huge concrete solutions” are prohibitively expensive and won’t solve the problem, he said, and neither will sand pumping or dredging, which can damage coastal ecosystems and requires repeated investment as sand washes away. Solutions that work with nature, rather than against it, Mr. Nasheed said, must be adopted quickly “to meet the ferocity of the waves coming to us.”

The technology developed by Coastal Assembly offers a “very, very concrete solution,” said Hyun Kim, Senior Advisor at the Global Centre for Climate Mobility, which is hosted through the United Nations. “They’re able to reverse the effect of sea level rise.” Mr. Kim said the organization was working to facilitate and fund the technology in other low-lying states and the millions of communities facing coastal erosion.

Quinn Glabicki is a climate reporter for The New York Times and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.
