Trump Administration Outlines Plan for Signs Outside Smithsonian Museum

The New York Times September 16, 2026

Attacks on Smithsonian

Advertisement

Supported by

In a letter, the Interior Department detailed what it hoped to convey on 12 signs to be installed outside the National Museum of American History.

By Robin Pogrebin

President Trump remains determined to install warning signs outside the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History to alert the public that the institution, in his view, does not accurately present U. S. history.

In letters to two senators, the Interior Department outlined a plan for 12 temporary signs to be installed at a total cost of $84,000. The letters did not specify the dimensions or language of the signs, which were originally ordered in July, but it went into considerable detail about the kind of information they plan to convey.

In the letter to Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, dated Sept. 3, Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, said he was responding to questions about Mr. Trump’s March 2025 executive order, “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.” The order described a “revisionist movement” across the country that it said “seeks to undermine the remarkable achievements of the United States by casting its founding principles and historical milestones in a negative light.”

Americans should enter the National Museum of American History “with relevant information about the curators’ interpretation of history and their stated goal of changing the viewpoints of visitors,” said the letter, which was earlier reported in The Atlantic on Tuesday. Instead, the letter argued, the museum and Smithsonian’s leaders “have altered the museum’s role from accurately and coherently telling America’s story to using the museum as a tool to advance personal, radical ideologies.”

“We believe the public should enter the museum fully equipped with the information needed,” the letter said, “to evaluate whether to invest their time viewing these exhibits and programming.”

The museum’s director, Anthea M. Hartig, has contested the thrust of a July 4 White House report that accused her of “radical activist ideology” and the museum of undermining “faith in American institutions.”

Though the letter said that the language of the signs had not been finalized and gave no installation timeline, it described some of the topics they were intended to address, all of which had been outlined in the White House report.

For example, the letter said the signs should “ensure parents bringing young children to the museum are equipped to protect the well-being of their children” regarding exhibits that “present ideological viewpoints inconsistent with biology, including ideologies that sex is not binary, that biological men can be women and that biological men should be permitted to compete in women’s sports.”

Mr. Burgum’s letter said a copy had also been sent to Senator Jeff Merkley, Democrat of Oregon.

In laying out a case for the signs, the letter was particularly critical of the Smithsonian’s secretary, Lonnie G. Bunch III, who announced his resignation last week.

“Visitors should be aware of Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch’s history of invidious discrimination and anti-white animus,” the letter said, citing a 2000 essay in which Bunch “described the museum profession as ‘awash in whiteness’; wrote that ‘the real issue is not money but the monochromatic nature of our institutions’; and stated, ‘until we change the tint and tone of our work force, we are just dancing around the edges of our greatest failure.’”

Mr. Bunch and the Smithsonian did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

In a statement, Mr. Merkley said the letter was part of a pressure campaign by the Trump administration to “undermine the integrity and independence of the Smithsonian Institution.”

“The administration,” he continued, “has already demonstrated its campaign to rewrite history at our national parks, and we should do all we can to ensure the Smithsonian can present our history, arts, and sciences without ideologically driven misrepresentation.”

Mike Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the conservative Heritage Foundation who has written critically about the Smithsonian, welcomed progress on the signage in an interview. “It is in the interest of transparency that museum visitors be warned in advance of the ideological baggage that the Smithsonian leadership has heaved on these exhibits,” he said.

The letter also took aim at Ms. Hartig. “It is disheartening,” the letter said, that “Hartig has stated that history is ‘a prime tool of social justice’; that she views one of her roles as connecting ‘research and scholarship to activism and advocacy.’”

Mr. Trump originally ordered the signs just days after Republican legislators grilled Ms. Hartig in two congressional hearings, where she was accused of teaching “national self-loathing.”

In those hearings, Ms. Hartig insisted that the report “does not fairly or accurately characterize the full body of work at the museum” while acknowledging that “there is always room for improvement.”

“When historians talk about reframing a traditional narrative, we don’t mean erasing it,” she continued. “We mean adding the evidence, the voices, the objects that earlier tellings left out so that more Americans can see themselves reflected in the national story.”

Robin Pogrebin, who has been a reporter for The Times for more than 30 years, covers arts and culture.

E. U.-Canada Ambitions Face Reality Check

The New York Times September 16, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

The bloc’s offer of “associate member” status to Ottawa shows how U. S. allies are pulling closer together. But their plans face significant obstacles.

By Matina Stevis-Gridneff and Jeanna Smialek

Matina Stevis-Gridneff reported from Strasbourg, France, where she is traveling with Mr. Carney. She previously covered the European Union for The Times. Jeanna Smialek also reported from the event, and covers Brussels.

The European Union’s invitation Wednesday for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc shows just how intent these traditional United States allies are on pursuing a more stable future by binding closer together.

“We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said in the European Parliament in Strasbourg, a beaming Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada sitting just to her side. But there are no guarantees they will get there.

While details of what this relationship might look like remain scant, Ms. von der Leyen noted some potential areas of cooperation, including partnerships in manufacturing, technology, defense, energy policy and economic security.

This would not be “a partnership against anyone else,” she insisted, “but for our common strength.”

European officials said that, in the lead-up to the speech on Wednesday, the bloc wanted to ensure that President Trump did not see this new partnership with Canada as an anti-American move.

Still, if it isn’t precisely against the United States, then it’s unmistakably about it.

“Behind this is a desire to hedge against what for both partners is an increasingly fraught relationship with the United States,” said Ian Lesser, a distinguished fellow of the German Marshall Fund, based in Brussels.

“But it’s not just that it’s fraught,” he added. “It’s the most important geoeconomic and geopolitical relationship for both Europe and for Canada.”

For Mr. Carney, the invitation is both timely and symbolically important. He has decided to stand up to Mr. Trump, who has imposed tariffs on Canada and regularly threatens its sovereignty.

Mr. Carney has been pushing for Canada to get greater access to the European Union — its territory, its market, its funds and programs — without becoming a full member of the bloc.

He has found an enthusiastic partner in Ms. von der Leyen, who has painted Canada as a dependable source for Europe’s needs for energy and critical raw materials, as well as a steadfast ally who shares NATO membership, support for Ukraine and a commitment to the rule of law. Ms. von der Leyen does not represent the European Union’s 27 countries, but she sets the agenda for the bloc and commands its mighty bureaucracy.

The tie-up seems to make sense at a moment of global turbulence and a shifting global role for the United States. Between them, the European Union’s 27 members and Canada have more than 490 million citizens and include four of the world’s 10 largest economies.

The European Union is underpinned by dense, deep legal and procedural rules, built over decades by a group of nations that ceded sovereignty to one another, and to an unelected executive branch in Brussels.

Inserting a country an ocean away deeper into this web is not a straightforward business.

The label the European Union wants to confer on Canada, “associate member,” is not an existing type of partnership — meaning that it is not clear what actions Canada would have to take to earn it, or for it to be given.

“It has no legal basis,” said Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group. “It’s more symbolism and signal,” he added.

Ms. von der Leyen was taking a risk using the term, which had been floating for weeks ahead of her speech, and drew consternation from several member states, according to European officials.

It is seen as vague, untethered from legal frameworks and potentially antagonistic toward countries that already have detailed legal agreements with the European Union. These range from candidate nations such as Albania to close partners including Britain, Switzerland and Norway. Those countries have deep trade ties to the bloc and, in the case of Switzerland and Norway, have free movement into and out of other European nations.

Some Canadian officials do not appear to love the term, either, as membership in the European Union implies forfeiting some sovereignty, which is the opposite of what Mr. Carney has pledged to do. The Conservative opposition leader seized on the term, arguing that if Canada was never to be the 51st state of the United States, it should also not become the 28th member state of the European Union.

“There’s a lot of good will, but once one starts to look just a little bit closer, one also finds that many Europeans really don’t know Canada all that well, and they maybe aren’t fully taking on board Canada’s own sensitivities to sovereignty,” said Mr. Lesser.

Hours after Ms. von der Leyen spoke on Wednesday, the incoming Canadian ambassador to the European Union said that labels did not matter — but suggested that Canada preferred “alliance for the future” to describe the emerging new bond with the European Union. That phrase also appeared in Ms. von der Leyen’s speech.

“I think we’re still a ways away from actually landing on what we think the best way to describe it is,” said Jonathan Wilkinson.

Three European diplomats said that the title “associate member” may not stick.

Officials from both sides are working to find tangible progress that they hope to announce at a European Union-Canada summit scheduled to take place in Montreal at the end of October.

Two officials, one from the European Union and one from Canada, with knowledge of the talks, said that officials were trying hard to reach that goal, but that work had been slow and difficult, in part because it is highly technical.

Just how hard it can be to get the European Union to agree on anything has been displayed frequently over the years. For example, talks over a trade agreement with Mercosur, the South American bloc, lasted a quarter century.

Canada has its own experience with these E. U. rigidities — and has some of its own. Its free-trade agreement with the bloc, in effect in practice for a decade, has still not been ratified by 10 of the 27 member states, for various reasons.

Canada already participates in a handful of E. U. ventures, including Horizon, a technology and innovation research effort, and SAFE, a defense industrial program. It had to pay $100 million to participate in Horizon, and participation in other E. U. programs is also likely to require Canada to pay into a budget.

One more immediate benefit for Canada from closer ties to Europe may be in securing funding from the European Investment Bank. The major development bank, which is owned by the E. U. member states and has more than $630 billion in assets, is eager and ready to invest in Canadian projects, particularly in critical raw materials, and its leader is heading to Ottawa on Sunday to advance talks with the Canadian government.

The bank is ready to start work in Canada, a European official with knowledge of the preparations said, but needed Ottawa to approve certain administrative formalities such as allowing E. U. diplomats to work there.

Some of the ideas being discussed ahead of the October summit show the ambitious scope of the Canada-E. U. future relationship.

For example, officials said, Mr. Carney wants the bloc to work with Canada to build systems for payments and cloud computing that will offer an alternative to those of the United States in a bid to secure sovereignty.

Discussions have also been underway on a digital trade agreement, which could deepen cooperation on cybersecurity and regulatory cooperation.

Talks are more advanced to bring Canadian regulations in line with European ones in energy, including the monitoring, reporting and evaluation system used by the bloc to track methane emissions from vessels fueled by liquefied natural gas, as well as gas imports entering the European Union market. This is a necessity if Canada is going to export gas to the European Union.

Another area where Canada is particularly eager to see movement is the ability of its citizens to spend longer stretches of time in the European Union visa-free, have their professional qualifications recognized there and be able to study in European universities.

Because these policy areas hinge on complex and politically fraught immigration rules, major breakthroughs could be difficult. Additionally, any agreement improving Canadians’ access to Europe would require reciprocity, meaning that it would grant the same access to Canada for 450 million Europeans.

Some European diplomats have suggested that Erasmus — Europe’s popular student exchange program — could be an easier starting place for collaboration.

Matina Stevis-Gridneff is the Canada bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of the country.

Jeanna Smialek is the Brussels bureau chief for The Times.

House Holds Leon Black in Contempt Over Epstein Subpoenas

The New York Times September 16, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The billionaire investor had refused to appear for a deposition and turn over documents to a key panel investigating Jeffrey Epstein.

By Michael Gold

Reporting from the Capitol

The House on Wednesday unanimously agreed to hold the billionaire investor Leon Black in criminal contempt of Congress after he refused to appear for a deposition and turn over documents to a key panel investigating the disgraced financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The citation, agreed to without a recorded vote, amounts to an official recommendation that the Justice Department bring federal charges against Mr. Black. It may serve to refocus public attention on the Trump administration’s handling of investigative material related to Mr. Epstein just as lawmakers depart Washington for a final spate of campaigning before the midterm congressional elections.

While President Trump has labored to avoid discussing the Epstein matter and excoriated those clamoring for more transparency, Republicans in Congress have tried to show they take the case, which has generated outrage among their core supporters, seriously.

The House Oversight Committee issued subpoenas to Mr. Black in June, after he refused to answer questions about nondisclosure agreements that he had signed with women, some of whom had been linked to Mr. Epstein. The panel demanded that he appear for a deposition and provide copies of any nondisclosure agreements he might have entered into. Mr. Black refused to comply and instead sued the committee, accusing it of exceeding its authority.

The committee on Tuesday unanimously recommended holding Mr. Black in contempt. Representative James R. Comer, Republican of Kentucky and the panel’s chairman, accused him of using the lawsuit as cover.

“Mr. Black is hiding behind litigation to delay having to provide answers to the American people,” he said on Tuesday. “No one is above the law. Mr. Black will be treated the same as anyone else in this investigation, and his actions have consequences.”

Representative Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the committee, said in an interview that Mr. Black had clearly violated two subpoenas.

“Subpoenas have to mean something in the Congress,” he said. “When you give $180 million to Jeffrey Epstein and are unwilling to answer questions about why and where and how you were involved? I think that’s a huge, huge issue.”

Mr. Black’s lawyers, Susan Estrich and Aaron Cutler, criticized the contempt vote in a statement, saying that Mr. Comer’s actions were “politically motivated and completely retaliatory.” They said that Mr. Black had already provided the committee with the “only confidentiality agreement” that was relevant to its investigation. They also said they had filed an ethics complaint against Mr. Comer, though they declined to specify what offenses they believed he had committed.

Mr. Black’s lawsuit said that the Oversight Committee’s subpoenas were “invalid” and that unnamed women and others “whom he has or may have agreements” with had “bargained for confidentiality.” Those people “want no association with the Epstein scandal,” the lawsuit said.

Mr. Black paid Mr. Epstein $170 million from 2013 to 2017 for what he described as traditional tax and estate planning services, according to congressional records and government documents.

Mr. Black has repeatedly said he knew nothing about Mr. Epstein’s decades-long sexual abuse of teenage girls and young women. But the release of millions of pages of emails and documents by the Justice Department put a new focus on Mr. Epstein’s relationship with Mr. Black.

Mr. Epstein advised Mr. Black on how to address issues he faced with several women with whom Mr. Black had sexual affairs. And Mr. Black paid about $20 million to a dozen women, according to the files and notes taken by congressional investigators that were previously shared with The New York Times.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

The New York Times September 16, 2026

U. S. Economy

Note: The actual target rate shows the midpoint of the federal funds target rate range.

Source: Federal Reserve

By Jacqueline Gu

By Colby Smith

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve

Federal Reserve officials released a fresh set of economic projections alongside their decision to raise interest rates on Wednesday, signaling that another increase could happen this year.

When the Fed last released quarterly economic projections, in June, officials were roughly split about the need to raise rates this year. Since then, inflation has showed only minimal progress toward the central bank’s 2 percent target, growth has remained solid, and the unemployment rate has stayed stable.

This backdrop informed the Fed’s decision to finally take action, resulting in a quarter-point move on Wednesday that lifted rates to a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent.

What investors will focus on now is how many more increases to expect from. The Fed chairman, Kevin M. Warsh, has made overhauling the Fed’s communications strategy a top priority of his tenure, which began in May. Part of that includes the dot plot, a forecasting tool that shows where policymakers see not only rates but also growth, unemployment and inflation going in the current year and beyond. Mr. Warsh has long criticized the dot plot, arguing that forecasts like these make it harder for the central bank to change course if the economic backdrop shifts.

In June, Mr. Warsh declined to submit his own projections. Other officials still see value in the dot plot, however, meaning it is still an important tool at policymakers’ disposal to shape expectations about the future.

Here’s what changed in the forecasts on Wednesday and how to interpret those updates.

When the central bank releases its Summary of Economic Projections each quarter, Fed watchers focus most closely on one part: the dot plot.

It shows Fed policymakers’ estimates for interest rates through 2029 and beyond. The forecasts are represented by dots arranged along a vertical scale — one dot for each of the Fed’s 19 officials. While only 12 cast a vote at each meeting, all 19 can submit forecasts for rates and the economic outlook over the short and long terms.

Economists closely watch how the dots shift for hints about where policy is heading. They fixate on the middle, or median, dot. It is regularly cited as the clearest estimate of where the Fed sees rates going over a given period.

The forecasts should be viewed cautiously. The dot plot does not represent a preset plan for policy, but rather a compilation of officials’ projections at a moment in time. It can be a helpful communications device. But when the economic outlook is uncertain, it can complicate the Fed’s message.

The central bank is trying to achieve two goals when it sets policy: low, stable inflation and a healthy labor market.

When it perceives elevated inflation to be a concern, it raises rates to make borrowing money more expensive, which cools the economy. When the economy is sluggish and in need of support, the Fed does the opposite and lowers rates to stoke demand.

Economists expect officials to pencil in another rate increase later this year on the heels of a quarter-point move by the Fed on Wednesday. Further adjustments are also expected to be forecast in 2027.

When you read the dot plot, it’s important to pay attention to where interest rate estimates fall in relation to the longer-run median projection. That number is sometimes called the “natural” or “neutral” rate. It represents the theoretical dividing line between monetary policy that is set to speed up the economy and one meant to slow it down.

The neutral estimate has ticked higher in recent years, and in June stood at 3.1 percent. Part of why the Fed is considering lifting borrowing costs is because of concerns that rates at the current range of 3.5 percent to 3.75 percent are not weighing on the economy enough.

Mr. Warsh, in a speech last month at the Fed’s annual conference in Jackson, Wyo., said he “would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive.” It was one of several hawkish points he made during those remarks that sowed expectations for an imminent rate rise.

Officials in June sharply raised their forecasts for inflation — as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index — compared with three months earlier because of the Iran war.

At the start of the summer, policymakers expected overall inflation to end the year at 3.6 percent and “core” inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, to settle at a 3.3 percent pace. As of the latest data in July, overall inflation stood at 3.7 percent compared with the same time last year. Core inflation was up 3.3 percent from a year earlier. The Fed aims for 2 percent inflation.

Those forecasts could rise marginally, as the Iran war has continued to drag on. Oil prices, after easing over the summer, are now back above $100 a barrel.

On the other hand, the Commerce Department is on the cusp of announcing methodological changes to how it calculates P. C. E. inflation, which could result in lower readings.

Policymakers by and large expect inflation to decelerate over time, barring additional economic shocks that disrupt that progress. Officials cite a variety of reasons, from the fading impact of President Trump’s tariffs to the continued malaise across the housing sector that has kept a lid on prices. Perhaps most important, officials do not see the labor market as a source of inflationary pressure.

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve and the U. S. economy for The Times.

Lower wage growth and slower hiring in some sectors may be the result of artificial intelligence, especially for younger workers.

Credit... Andrea Chronopoulos

Supported by

By Talmon Joseph Smith

In May 2025, Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, said artificial intelligence could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs within five years, pushing unemployment higher than 10 percent.

More than a year later, even as A. I. models have made leaps that prompted Mr. Amodei to warn of “catastrophic” consequences for humanity if the current pace of development goes unchecked, the unemployment rate remains low. In fact, it’s fallen, to 4.1 percent in August. So is A. I., despite the doomsaying, having no impact on the labor market after all?

New research says that A. I. implementation by businesses is registering, in a quieter way: through slower wage growth in jobs most exposed to the technology, where workers are losing leverage; and through a pullback in job openings, with employers adding fewer positions than before, especially for young people.

Sania Edlich, a Princeton researcher, and Torsten Slok, the chief economist at Apollo Global Management, reviewed data across 321 occupations and found that workers in A. I.-exposed occupations experienced slower wage growth in the past three years, while net employment levels in those occupations remained unchanged. They concluded that companies were capturing A. I. productivity gains by suppressing wage gains rather than reducing head count.

“If you are a hairdresser, if you are a massage therapist, if you are a doorman, of course your occupation is not threatened by A. I., whereas if you are a journalist or an economist, there is just more pressure on wages because now the work that we do can be replaced, at least in some ways, by A. I.,” Mr. Slok said.

In other words, A. I. appears to be hitting so-called knowledge work through less hiring by recruiters rather than more firing by managers.

“And for that reason, finding jobs has become more complicated,” Mr. Slok said. “And the wage that you’re getting paid is where we’re seeing all the action.”

Ms. Edlich and Mr. Slok found that occupations highly exposed to A. I. have experienced a 6.7 percent decline in real wage growth since 2023 and that the effect is harshest among lower earners. Service workers, often in administrative or support roles, have experienced a 24 percent decline. The bottom quarter of workers has seen an 11 percent decline. Top earners, however, have barely been affected.

Corporate profits are up across the board. And amid these boom times, companies have options for making hay while the sun shines.

They can capitalize on their newfound efficiencies by doing more with less and laying off workers; they can scale up and add new hires; or they can preserve their efficiencies by hiring less than usual. Many companies are choosing the third option.

Melissa Krut is a senior vice president at Sogolytics, a software company in Virginia that serves over 10,000 clients with around 100 employees. She oversees human resources at the company, which runs “feedback management” services for companies including Coca-Cola and United Airlines, crafting and managing, for example, customer surveys.

During the past three years, Ms. Krut said, “productivity has increased, we have more clients, we have grown by almost every measure you want to throw out there, but we don’t have, proportionately, that many more people” in positions across sales, account management and support roles.

Ms. Krut said one reason is the integration of A. I. models that can handle more than half the base line tasks for some jobs. That has led to “higher expectations,” she said, for workers seeking raises and for new hires.

“If your job could be done by A. I., yeah, you better have something else on top,” Ms. Krut said. “What is the cherry on top that you’re bringing to that situation? Is it your winning personality? Is it your sense of humor? What is it that you have that puts you over the edge?”

Typically, when the economy is growing, college graduates are among the workers who feel most empowered. But a large cohort of early-career college graduates have been feeling the acute stress of the higher bar for being hired.

Liminal Capital, an investment firm, estimated in August that about a third of jobs appear to be more exposed to substitution than augmentation by A. I. In those occupations, new hires among workers ages 22 to 25 have fallen by a third since 2021, even as firings have barely budged.

Ben Verschuere and Angus Cameron, the authors of the Liminal paper, said one reason behind the trend is that younger people are the likeliest to be entering the labor force, leaving them most exposed to the heightened selectivity of employers. The mass retirement of baby boomers isn’t leading to an upward swell in salaries or job openings for Gen-Xers or millennials below them either.

“We could be living in a world where unemployment is low while job quality, composition and wages deteriorate,” said Loujaina Abdelwahed, head of economic research at Revelio Labs, a labor market data firm.

Average hourly earnings growth for rank-and-file employees of all ages, which peaked above 6 percent in 2022, dropped to near 3 percent on an annual basis last month. That is unusual: Wages tend to rise as the unemployment rate falls, as it has since the start of the year.

“Wage growth has been diverging from productivity,” Mr. Verschuere said.

As efficiency and profit margins have picked up compared with the 2010s, the labor share of national income — which measures compensation relative to corporate earnings — has fallen by about 10 percentage points from a peak around the late 1990s.

Ethan Giffin, chief executive of the B2B eCommerce Agency, which helps manufacturing and distribution companies transition from phone-based to automated ordering systems, has expanded revenue by double digits for the past three years. But Mr. Giffin said he has also largely stopped hiring technical writers because work that once took a year or more now takes only about three months.

“The human hours that it would take to work through a 5,000- or 10,000-product catalog was extremely tedious, and now leveraging A. I., that significantly cuts down on the human hours required to do that,” he said. “It’s a significant cost savings versus having a team of, paying a team of, three or four or five people to sit around and do that work.”

For an ecosystem as large and diverse as the $30 trillion U. S. economy, there are inevitably exceptions to the trend. Recent studies have found that some companies leaning into A. I. have increased their pace of hiring. And the demand for certain skilled workers who specialize in managing A. I. has become supercharged.

But the U. S. tech sector overall is hemorrhaging jobs, losing about 7,000 last month and roughly 48,000 over the past year, according to Joey Politano, an economic analyst. And financial services, another sector highly exposed to A. I., is experiencing an outright contraction in employment levels, with 100,000 jobs lost since the start of the year.

The share of U. S. adults employed by financial firms, a long reliable vault into the upper middle class, or higher, has fallen to the lowest level since 1981. Mr. Verschuere said the pipeline for many graduates is drying up, too. Even as the average number of applicants to banks continues to rise by hundreds of thousands, the number hired has remained relatively flat.

There are other avenues of employment for young people, including new consumer-facing start-ups. Ryan Close, the founder and chief executive of Bartesian, a company that makes home cocktail machines — “the Keurig for Cocktails” — is hiring.

Revenue has grown since 2022 to $80 million from $50 million, largely because of A. I., Mr. Close said.

Bots and agents, according to Mr. Close, can expertly create budgets, retail reports and, like a fishing cast net, identify influencers who could be good brand ambassadors for Bartesian. They can even draft contracts for potential vendors with estimated pay ranges.

“It’s insane,” he said.

Although this automated efficiency has reduced his need to hire at the entry level, Mr. Close has decided to hire several more midlevel staffers, who can focus on strategy rather than repetitive tasks. But he has reduced his pay offers in many cases.

“The salaries expected four years ago were just insane to me,” Mr. Close said. Candidates under 30 were getting offers above $100,000 for sales and marketing roles that he now sees as “commodifiable.”

But it’s now more of a buyer’s market than a seller’s market for labor, he said: “I think it’s just coming back down to earth, where it’s like OK, if you can get a good job, and you’re two years or so out of college, you can take 80 grand and just be happy.”

Talmon Joseph Smith is a Times economics reporter, based in New York. He is the author of the forthcoming book “What Can We Afford: A Tour Across American Inequality & a Search for the Road Ahead.”

Why the Fed Raised Rates as Borrowing Costs Are Surging

The New York Times September 16, 2026

U. S. Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

Elevated interest rates have raised the cost of mortgages and car loans without dampening consumer spending.

By Aruni Soni

Since the start of the year, Americans have been paying more to secure mortgages and auto loans, as well as to pay down their credit card debts.

And as higher prices are also burning a larger hole in consumers’ wallets, it may seem counterintuitive that the Federal Reserve made borrowing costs even higher by raising rates on Wednesday.

But the reason stems from the fact that even though rates are higher than they were for much of the first two decades of the 2000s, consumer spending, business investment and other measures of the health of the economy are all running hot. And inflation, the rise in prices that can result from such vigorous spending, has hovered above the Fed’s 2 percent target rate for half a decade.

“Raising interest rates is specifically intended to deter spending,” said Thierry Wizman, a strategist on global fixed income and rates at investment bank Macquarie Group. “So the pain that the consumer is feeling if they’re obligated to pay more on a home, or a car loan, or on a student loan, is intentional.”

In 2022, before the Fed began a period of inflation-induced increases, interest rates hovered around zero. They rose to between 5.25 percent and 5.5 percent in 2023. Today, they sit between 3.75 percent and 4 percent.

These rates determine short-term borrowing costs. When they go up, lending conditions for banks tighten, creating a domino effect that can reduce consumer spending and business investment. But so far, higher rates have not done much to slow the economy.

Americans spent $36 billion more in the U. S. economy in July compared with the month before, according to the latest personal expenditures report from the Bureau of Economic Analysis. The boost in spending was driven by a robust labor market that has pumped up wages and Americans’ disposable income.

For a while, this spending has been uneven across income brackets in the United States. This is what has been described as the “K-shaped” economy, with the less wealthy represented by the lower-trending line and the wealthy the upward-trending line.

“Not everyone owns a home and not everyone owns equities — but it’s that part of the economy, the consumer, that’s been driving growth, the upper part of that ‘K,’” said Leslie Falconio, head of fixed income strategy for UBS Global Wealth Management.

Still, there are signs of convergence in that lopsided picture, according to analysts who examined credit and debit card spending data from Bank of America. Spending by lower income consumers has risen disproportionately in recent months, they said.

Business investment is also booming, propelled by investors’ betting that returns from artificial intelligence will outpace the cost of borrowing. The stock market is reflecting confidence in tech as well, bolstered by a blockbuster earnings season. The S&P 500 is up roughly 11 percent since the start of the year.

Part of the Fed’s mandate is to maintain stable prices. Inflation is still ringing in at more than 2 percent year-over-year — where the Fed would like it — with the numbers for August coming in hotter than expected. A big driver of inflation has been an energy crunch set off by the disruption of global oil flows in the Middle East. The global price of oil has risen 15 percent this month alone.

Perhaps the only sector that has relented in the face of higher rates is the housing market. Home sales are falling as mortgage rates have crossed 6.7 percent for the first time since July 2025. But many homeowners able to lock in mortgages at lower rates secured years ago have been able to reduce the strain on their wallets.

“That resiliency and that growth outlook that continues to be strong allows the Fed to say, ‘OK, I’m going to continue to focus on this price-stability side, because the interest rates aren’t restrictive and we can hike — growth isn’t teetering,’” Ms. Falconio said.

The Fed’s policy path most directly affects interest rates, or yields, on shorter-term U. S. Treasuries, like the two-year note. Longer-term yields move based on Fed policy but give more weight to factors like inflation and the national deficit.

The two-year bill has ticked up to 4.66 percent for the first time since 2024. The 10-year note, which sets the pace for most consumer loans, has punched past 5 percent this week, the highest level since 2023.

The Fed’s hike on Wednesday could help those yields ease lower, Ms. Falconio said. It could signal to investors that the board is proactive about managing inflation, coaxing them to expect inflation to moderate and demand a lower return on long-term government bonds, she said.

That easing would take time to translate into lower rates for consumers.

“If growth stays resilient, and they hike five or six times, then the long end is not going to go down,” Ms. Falconio said about long-term bonds. “It really depends on how many times they hike.”

Aruni Soni is a business reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

The actress, last onstage over four decades ago, had a “terrifying” desire to return to the stage. “Other Desert Cities” will be her Broadway debut.

Credit...

Supported by

By Alexis Soloski

Visuals by Thea Traff

Reporting from Santa Barbara, Calif.

When Julia Louis-Dreyfus faces down a new character, she asks certain questions: What does this character want? What does she want right now? How is she going to get that?

It is a very nice thing, if you can manage it, to sit across from Louis-Dreyfus, 65, on the sun-flooded patio of a coffee shop in Santa Barbara, Calif., and listen to her talk about desire, about appetite. From “Seinfeld,” which earned Louis-Dreyfus her first Emmy Award, to “Veep,” which earned her several more, and the sitcoms and movies in between, she has excelled at playing hungry women: hungry for recognition, power, love, attention, sex, snacks. (In one “Seinfeld” scene, she absolutely houses a Drake’s coffee cake.)

She loves these appetitive women, preferring them to the better behaved ones. “They’re more fun,” she said. “There’s more grit there, pushing against the norms, the rules.” That afternoon, she arrived in a swingy navy linen dress and lavish jewelry — a ruby ring, a gold watch, a gold bracelet, overlapping necklaces of gold, jade, lapis lazuli and ivory. She wore that excess lightly. She is more elegant than most of her characters, certainly more poised. But that valentine face, that slightly feral smile, eyes that go glittery when she talks about what thrills her, these features are shared.

Louis-Dreyfus barely touched her vanilla latte. One of her characters would have downed it in a gulp. As an actress, she specializes in need, so naked and desperate that it makes the women she plays indelible. I can defend almost no choice her characters make. But their wanting is undeniable, as is the demented pleasure she conveys when a want is satisfied.

For a decade or so, Louis-Dreyfus has had a specific personal want: to appear on Broadway. “It’s terrifying,” she said of this particular want. “Really scary.” In these same years, she has endured other scary things. She underwent chemotherapy and surgery to treat cancer. She lost the home in which she raised her two children in last year’s Pacific Palisades fire and relocated to Santa Barbara, where her husband grew up. “I did not see that coming,” she said. She has barely visited the site. “It’s pretty hard,” she said. “I mean, there’s nothing.”

Given these circumstances, she could be forgiven for making safe choices. That isn’t her way. Which is why, after an absence from the stage of more than four decades, she will make her Broadway debut this fall in a revival of Jon Robin Baitz’s drama “Other Desert Cities” at the Hudson Theater.

“It’s very delicious for me to consider chomping on,” she said. “I really can’t wait.”

Louis-Dreyfus has had a charmed career, the envy of almost any woman in comedy. She began acting in high school, though she can’t remember the roles exactly: Madame What’s-Her-Face, Nurse What’s-Her-Face. When she was onstage, she felt centered, clear. “It’s what some people meditate to achieve,” she said. “Everything else just goes away.”

While a theater undergraduate at Northwestern University, she began appearing professionally with a company that Brad Hall, who would become her husband, co-founded. These were her last theater credits. Before her senior year, she was hired onto “Saturday Night Live.” Back then, “S. N. L.” was a boys club. She rarely felt welcome. But Louis-Dreyfus, relentless in pursuit of silver linings, welcomed the hardship. “It helped me define what my values were, it helped sharpen the skill set, it helped me know what I was not good at doing,” she said. “My priorities got more clear.”

She left the show after three seasons, and moved with Hall to Los Angeles. A few years later, she booked “Seinfeld,” created by Jerry Seinfeld and Larry David, another “S. N. L.” alum. The show hadn’t originally been conceived with a female co-star, but NBC executives balked at that. As Seinfeld tells it, Louis-Dreyfus was an easy hire. “You have this very attractive woman who’s extremely funny and extremely intelligent,” he said. “When I met her, I saw those things instantly.” To find those characteristics in a single performer is rare, he said. “I don’t know much about gemology, but she’s a blue diamond or something.”

Happily, Louis-Dreyfus’s Elaine — peppy, petty, anxious, clever and an epically bad dancer — never felt like an afterthought and she quickly became as awful as any of the men. David Mandel, a writer who joined “Seinfeld” in its later seasons and worked with Louis-Dreyfus again on “Veep,” admired her embrace of unflattering story lines.

“It was no longer three guys and a girl, it was just four idiots,” Mandel said. “She is a pretty woman who is fearless about being ugly, about looking ugly, about acting ugly.”

When “Seinfeld” ended, its stars struggled. Theories of a “Seinfeld curse” swirled. Louis-Dreyfus broke it, first with “The New Adventures of Old Christine,” which won her another Emmy, and then with “Veep,” on which she played Selina Meyer, the venal vice president and eventually the president. Frank Rich, an executive producer on the show and a former New York Times columnist, marveled at her ability to make a difficult character nearly lovable.

“She finds something in herself that makes you sympathize often with characters who can be very demanding, very competitive and very annoying,” Rich said.

Tony Hale, one of Louis-Dreyfus’s “Veep” co-stars, didn’t mince words regarding Selina. “She was an absolute monster,” he said. “The choices that she made were so horrific and the narcissism was so deep.” But watching Louis-Dreyfus play her, he couldn’t keep from smiling. Asked to describe her performance, one word came to mind: “Deliciousness.”

Louis-Dreyfus can’t defend Selina’s choices, or the choices of most of her characters, but she loves making them. “Those women entertain me,” she said. “They suit me. They get me where I live.” She isn’t vain in her performances and she’s unconcerned with being nice, with being liked.

“I am trying to be truthful,” she said. “Big difference.”

Louis-Dreyfus was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2017 while filming the final season of “Veep.” After receiving treatment, she returned to filming. In the years since that show ended, she has gravitated to film, taking on mature themes: marital strife in 2023’s “You Hurt My Feelings,” grief and death in 2024’s “Tuesday.” Even her voice-over work, in “Tangles” and “The Sheep Detectives,” has skewed a little dark. (Less dark: a recurring role in several Marvel projects.) And in 2023, she debuted the podcast “Wiser Than Me,” in which she interviews trailblazing women a generation up.

Stephanie Wittels Wachs, the executive leader of Lemonada, which produces the podcast, recognized Louis-Dreyfus as a gifted interviewer, a genuinely curious person and a good listener. “And obviously just being the funniest person ever to exist is helpful,” Wittels Wachs said. But Louis-Dreyfus wasn’t only jokey. “There’s so much depth and wisdom to her,” Wittels Wachs said.

In looking for a stage play, Louis-Dreyfus wanted it all, the comedy and the depth. “My ambition is to find really juicy, tasty material for me to play with,” she said. A longtime theatergoer, she had decided that she wanted to aim for Broadway, a return, in elevated form, to the community she’d enjoyed in her student days. “I want to have that connection, with not only the actors, but also with an audience, which feels like an opportunity for a very intimate, creative, not-to-be-repeated experience,” she said. “I was craving it.”

Her agent sent her “Other Desert Cities,” which premiered Off Broadway in 2011 before transferring to Broadway later that year. Louis-Dreyfus would play Polly, whom the stage directions describe as “elegant and forthright and whip smart.” A former writer and hostess, Polly has retired with her husband, a former actor and GOP regional chairman, to Palm Springs after a scandal involving their eldest son pushed them from political life. Now a memoir written by their daughter (Lily Rabe) threatens to dredge that up again. Louis-Dreyfus responded to the play’s moral preoccupations, its mix of light and dark. “It’s deeply funny and it’s deeply sad,” she said. What does Polly want? Everything.

In December, John Benjamin Hickey, the play’s director, held a reading to hear Louis-Dreyfus in the part. Her future Broadway castmates Ed Harris, Allison Janney and Joe Keery, fresh off “Stranger Things,” also participated. Hickey knew that she would shine in the play’s funnier scenes. And he had a hunch that she could handle the drama, too. “Because she’s such an authoritative presence but she’s so human,” he said.

Watching her read it, he found that she never had to reach for the drama, the emotion, he said. “She hasn’t had a chance to show much of that in her career, she’s really hungry for that challenge.”

David Mandel had noted this, decades ago. As good as she was on “Seinfeld,” and again on “Veep,” he always knew she could do more. “She’s an incredible actor and she has a real desire to grab at a part and just suck the marrow out of it,” he said.

This won’t exactly be Louis-Dreyfus’s first time in front of a live audience since her school days. “S. N. L.” was of course shot live as were most of her sitcom episodes, but she has never been asked to dig so deep, so publicly.

Louis-Dreyfus has always been a somewhat private person. She didn’t welcome having to speak publicly about having cancer. (That it delayed the final season of “Veep” necessitated that disclosure.) While she is more open on her podcast, she was understandably reluctant to discuss the loss of her home, moving tables so that she would not be overheard. “Yeah,” she said, “We’ve had kind of a [expletive] time.” But even here she found an upside.

She has worked hard for the life she has, for the family she has. “I’ve been fiercely protective and proud of that,” she said. “So when aspects of that are at risk, with my health, with losing our home of 33 years, in a weird way it’s a way into understanding.”

Will those experiences color the role? “How could they not?” she asked. “If you’re doing your job right, it’s intimate. It doesn’t translate, it’s not a direct line. But you’re bringing your own life experience, you’re bringing it to bear to bring some truth to this thing, so you do feel that connection.”

Polly is also protective of her family, and she too, has experienced great loss. Yes, she and Louis-Dreyfus, who has been outspoken in her support of Democratic candidates, are political opposites. And hopefully she does not subject her family to Polly’s emotional terrorism. But they share an interest in justice, in righteousness.

“That doesn’t mean she’s going to be a hero, necessarily,” Louis-Dreyfus said, smiling. That smile was a little greedy. “Or a nice lady. We don’t play nice ladies here.”

Last month, Louis-Dreyfus flew to New York to begin rehearsals. In a phone call after the first week, she described the experience as “thrilling and arduous and deeply fun and deeply exhausting.”

Was it as frightening as she’d feared? Yes, though she tried not to let herself think about it. Was it glorious? Also yes. Each day had felt like sitting for a multi-hour examination, and yet she couldn’t wait to go back. “It’s exalted,” she said of the process of making theater. She sounded hungry for more.

Alexis Soloski has written for The Times since 2006. As a culture reporter, she covers television, theater, movies, podcasts and new media.

Saudi Pipeline Attack Risks ‘Disastrous’ Loss of Oil as Fighting Escalates

The New York Times September 16, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Prolonged restrictions on exports could push oil prices even higher.

By Lisa Friedman

Lisa Friedman is the energy correspondent in London.

As Iran and its allies tightened their grip on shipping lanes in the Persian Gulf, Saudi Arabia scrambled this week to reroute millions of barrels of oil after being forced to close a critical pipeline damaged in an attack.

The shutdown of the East-West pipeline risks keeping 4 percent of the world’s oil supply from reaching international markets and driving energy prices even higher.

Saudi Arabia on Friday said it had temporarily shut the pipeline after it was struck by an Iran-backed militia. The pipeline, a 750-mile network that transports crude across Saudi Arabia to ports on the Red Sea, had been the kingdom’s primary way of exporting oil since the war in Iran began in February.

On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia in Yemen exchanged fresh claims of attacks on one another. In what would be a sharp escalation in their fighting, the Houthis said they had downed a Saudi fighter jet, as Saudi Arabia said the Houthis fired a drone near the Muslim holy city of Mecca.

The Houthis last week gained control of a strategic Red Sea port and hit energy facilities in Saudi Arabia, exacerbating the squeeze on Saudi oil exports.

Now, Saudi Arabia, running out of options and under pressure to rapidly restore supply lines, is facing the prospect of a severe energy crisis with global implications, analysts said.

“It is unprecedented,” said Amena Bakr, head of Middle East & OPEC+ Insights at Kpler, a maritime data firm.

“We have two major waterways obstructed, active attacks, Iran escalating attacks, proxies being active and no signs of diplomatic talks,” Ms. Bakr said. “It’s a disastrous situation when you’re looking at it from an energy security angle.”

Any extended disruption to the pipeline network of Saudi Arabia, long the world’s biggest oil exporter, would send shock waves through the global energy market. Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, hovered around $107 per barrel on Wednesday, up 50 percent from its prewar level.

The world could lose 120 million barrels of crude if the East-West Pipeline is offline for a month, according to estimates from Kpler.

Goldman Sachs warned that global oil prices could rise as high as $120 a barrel if attacks in the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea continue.

The precise amount of oil not making it to the global market will depend largely on the severity of the damage to the East-West pipeline. Neither the Saudi government nor Saudi Aramco, the national oil company, responded to requests for comment.

Saudi officials previously said only that the pipeline was shut as a precaution but have not disclosed the extent of the damage or a timetable for how long it might take to restart it. Satellite images taken on Sept. 10 and 11, reviewed by The New York Times, show damage at two pumping stations on the pipeline.

Estimates for how long it might take to get the pipeline running again vary widely.

Ms. Bakr, the Kpler analyst, said she believed it could take five to six weeks, but that partial repairs could be completed far sooner.

She and others noted that the kingdom has extensive experience dealing with attacks on infrastructure. In 2019, Aramco suffered a major Houthi attack on its facilities and was able to restart pumping operations within a few days. And in April, when a pumping station was attacked shortly after the war in Iran began, full capacity was restored within seven days.

Robin Brooks, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a Washington think tank, said he did not believe the “nightmare scenarios” that the pipeline could be offline for months.

“This attack has again raised in markets the fear that we could be on the cusp of another big spike,” Mr. Brooks said. But, he said, “The track record is that these things get repaired within weeks, and there’s already indications from satellite imagery that repairs are happening.”

Chris Wright, the U. S. energy secretary, said he believed oil flows through the pipeline would resume soon. “This will be a brief and temporary interruption,” Mr. Wright told CNBC on Tuesday.

Saudi Arabia has oil stored across the country, including the capacity for about 24 million barrels at its Red Sea port at Yanbu, creating a cushion. But those storage tanks are unlikely to be full, according to Rystad Energy, a consulting firm that estimated the port has about three to six days’ worth of crude.

SOMALIA

Sources: Global Energy Monitor (pipelines); Critical Threats Project at the American Enterprise Institute (Houthi-controlled areas)

The East-West pipeline was Saudi Arabia’s workaround when the war in Iran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz. Stretching from Abqaiq in the east to the Red Sea oil terminal of Yanbu in the west, the pipeline bypasses the strait entirely. Oil could be transported through the Bab al-Mandab Strait on the southern end of the Red Sea or via the Suez Canal and a pipeline across Egypt at the northern end of the sea, headed primarily to customers in Asia.

Ship traffic in the Strait of Hormuz is a fraction of what it was before the war, when about 130 vessels moved through the waterway daily. An average of approximately 20 ships a day have passed through the strait over the past week, according to Kpler.

Yasir O. Al-Rumayyan, the chairman of Aramco, said in June that engineers had expanded the pipeline’s capacity to carry up to seven million barrels per day, nearly 30 percent more than before the war.

“We had a similar situation back in the ’80s, where the Strait of Hormuz was threatened to be blockaded by the Iranian regime,” Mr. Al-Rumayyan said. “It was decided since then that we will have a pipeline from east to west.”

With the Houthis now largely in control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, Saudi Arabia is once again steering vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, analysts said. Since Sept. 7, just two Saudi vessels have traveled through the Red Sea, according to Kpler.

The U. S. Navy has been able to keep some oil flowing out of the Strait of Hormuz on sea paths close to the coast of Oman, the opposite side from Iran. But those efforts have required an extensive and dangerous operation.

Capital Economics, an economic research firm, said that every week the East-West pipeline is closed, while the Strait of Hormuz is off limits, will shave at least 0.2 percent off Saudi Arabia’s economic activity.

Josh Holder and Jenny Gross contributed reporting.

Lisa Friedman is a business correspondent covering energy for The New York Times.

For Trump, Jews Are Proving to Be a Very Useful Tool

The New York Times September 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By James Loeffler

Prof. Loeffler is the author of “Exceptional Hatred: Antisemitism and the Fight Over Free Speech in Modern America.”

Last month, a federal judge in California issued a blunt verdict on attempts to deport student visa holders for criticizing Israel. In the name of fighting antisemitism, the judge found, the Trump administration had trampled on the First and Fifth Amendments. Combined with other recent legal defeats and whistle-blower allegations, it was yet more evidence that the administration has degraded civil rights law under the guise of enforcing it.

Why antisemitism, though? Why is the Trump administration, which is indifferent to discrimination against so many other minority groups, hypervigilant about antisemitism? (Antisemitism on the left, anyway; it remains willfully blind about antisemitism on the right.) How did this administration seize on this one form of hatred? The answers lie in an underappreciated fissure in American life. The civil rights paradigm created in the 1960s is unraveling under the pressure of demographic change and political realignment. The Trump administration is exploiting antisemitism to finish the job, claiming the moral high ground in defense of one group while gutting protections for everyone else.

Since the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the protocol for protecting vulnerable minorities from discrimination has evolved — imperfectly, contentiously, but with a core premise intact: Adherence to clear, consistent standards builds confidence in the entire enterprise.

The premise is intact no longer. This administration has read the conservative Supreme Court’s 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions not just as a rebuke to affirmative action policies but as a ban on any campus program that even acknowledges race — far beyond what the opinion called for. It has raised the threshold for what counts as unlawful discrimination, abandoning decades-old standards. It has pilloried diversity, equity and inclusion not merely as liberal orthodoxy but as reverse racism; it has withheld billions from higher education; it has dismissed roughly 90 percent of education-related civil rights complaints; and it has implemented detention and deportation policies that abandon any semblance of due process. In all but the last of these cases, it claims the goal is to eradicate any consideration of racial or ethnic differences.

Yet at the same time the government has demanded what amounts to D. E. I. for Jews: mandatory antisemitism sensitivity trainings and targeted measures to promote an inclusive climate. And when schools are accused of discriminating against Jews, instead of conducting fair investigations, the government has imposed penalties that are wildly out of scale — such as slashing hundreds of millions of dollars of funding for medical and scientific research. No one even bothers to pretend that makes the world safer for Jews.

Gutting anti-discrimination policies for most minority groups while supercharging them for Jews is hypocritical. The hypocrisy is the point. It turns civil rights law into a political protection racket, a tool with which to attack higher education and other perceived enemies.

The disturbing excesses of some Gaza war protests are not enough to explain why Jews were selected for this special protected status. Neither is the Republican alliance with Israel’s right-wing government, or the outsize influence of Jewish donors — a frequently heard explanation that risks lapsing into antisemitism. The simple truth is that mounting this initiative served the Trump administration’s cynical political aims. The largest campaign against antisemitism in American history has also been its supreme trivialization.

At every inflection point in the evolution of modern civil rights, the question of which groups merit protection has been contested. Just African Americans, the main focus of the original civil rights movement? Or other racial and religious groups, too? Does civil rights law apply to women and to sexual and gender minorities? How real is so-called reverse discrimination? Above all, should the government’s goal be to eliminate legal distinctions that wrongly divide individual citizens from one another, or also to protect vulnerable groups from harm in pursuit of actual, full equality?

Until recently, even the conservative establishment — including administrations under Presidents Richard Nixon, Ronald Reagan and the two Bushes — generally accepted anti-discrimination law as a valid instrument of governance, in theory if not always in practice. But the civil rights model we inherited was built for a different country — one in which a white, Christian majority belatedly yielded legal space for distinct minorities to become coequal citizens. If current trends continue, however, in less than 20 years America will be majority nonwhite. Within the next half-century, it will most likely be majority non-Christian. White populist panic has set in. Banning the word “diversity” in a nation of immigrants is a last-ditch effort to reverse history.

As the categories of majority and minority now shift and blur, Americans find themselves returning, almost obsessively, to Jews: a group that doesn’t fit easily into racial binaries, that troubles the boundaries between religion and ethnicity, whose members are not people of color but whose claim to whiteness was always suspect in the eyes of white supremacists, and who have diasporic ties to a polarizing nation-state.

This ambiguity has also created ideological blind spots. Centrist liberals were late to recognize the seriousness of antisemitism in American life. They likewise missed its potency as a political weapon for the populist right and the combustibility of the Palestine question in American politics. Progressives have failed to grapple with antisemitism among their own ranks. And now a conservative administration intent on undoing civil rights law has turned that ambiguity to its own advantage.

The civil rights revolution was never finished. Now its contradictions have returned, sharper than ever. They won’t end with antisemitism, because debates about Jews are never just about Jews. They are the seismographs of a society’s deeper tremors: its fears of difference, its contested visions of nationhood.

As Americans, we can build a legal framework that is more than a cynical tool with which to punish one’s enemies and also better than what preceded it — something capacious enough to protect all minorities, principled enough to command legitimacy and resilient enough to resist political manipulation. We can do it if we stop treating civil rights as a cudgel and start treating them once again as a covenant. Covenants are not merely inherited; they are renewed. This one must be renewed not for the America that was, but for the America that we are becoming.

A principled society protects its citizens from hatred and discrimination because they are citizens entitled to equal protection—not because one group has been politically singled out for special treatment. The moment government appears to elevate the protection of one community above others, it risks turning a moral principle into a political instrument and creating the resentment it claims to be fighting. What the Trump administration is doing should not be confused with a principled campaign against antisemitism. A principled campaign would confront antisemitism while applying the same moral standard to hatred directed at Muslims, Christians, Jews, Black Americans, immigrants, or anyone else. Instead, the administration is exploiting the evil of antisemitism as another fault line along which Americans can be divided. It does Jewish Americans no favor. Jews must be protected because no American should be subjected to hatred, intimidation, or discrimination. Political protection says: this group receives a special status that others do not. The first strengthens a pluralistic society; the second risks breeding resentment against the very people it purports to defend. And that is the bitter irony. Policies presented as protecting Jews can, if perceived as preferential or politically motivated, hand antisemites another grievance to exploit. Instead of isolating the most hateful elements of society, such politics risks giving them another excuse to target Jewish Americans.

James Loeffler is a professor of modern Jewish history at Johns Hopkins University and the author of “Exceptional Hatred: Antisemitism and the Fight Over Free Speech in Modern America.”

Washington Won’t Be Regulating AI Anytime Soon

Wired September 16, 2026

For weeks, Washington has been abuzz with talk of needing to push through some sort of AI regulation amid mounting concerns about the risks of highly capable frontier AI models going rogue.

But there is no reason to think any one measure can win the support of the White House, where officials have paused work on creating a FINRA-style regulatory body after President Donald Trump soured on the idea, or of Capitol Hill, where lawmakers have competing proposals that lack the votes to pass.

White House aides initially started sketching out a framework for an AI oversight agency connected to the administration soon after Google DeepMind’s cofounder Demis Hassabis floated the idea in a July 14 essay and in briefings to senior officials, according to sources familiar with the matter.

The Treasury Department and the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy envisioned a body where leading AI labs would self-regulate the development of frontier models, and they put together a preliminary draft to see what it could look like if executed.

But when a chorus of tech executives—including Trump’s former AI czar David Sacks and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg—learned of the effort, they one by one called Trump in August to express their opposition. The proposal has since been left in limbo.

Since then, there have been no new AI oversight proposals seriously under consideration at the White House, the sources say, not least as Trump has doubled down in recent days of rejecting any overt regulation and called AI safety concerns a “hoax” in a recent Truth Social post.

Trump’s ire has stemmed at least in part from a 3,822 word missive by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on the dangers of frontier AI. Trump’s aides, one of the sources said, viewed it as stirring anxieties that caused unnecessary headaches for the administration—even as it represents a fairly moderate position within AI circles.

In the absence of the White House taking the lead, several bills have sprung up in Congress—but with no voting days left on the House calendar until after the midterm elections and a lack of unity around even one bill, the odds of anything passing are extraordinarily slim.

The bipartisan Frontier Act, a bill introduced this summer by House Democratic senior whip Lori Trahan and Republican House Energy and Commerce Committee member Jay Obernolte, is widely seen as having the most support inside the House Democratic caucus as well as among AI executives.

As drafted, the bill would enable the Commerce Department to have auditors embedded at AI labs, who could report critical safety incidents and empower the administration to stop development if a model poses catastrophic risk.

But despite public backing from OpenAI, the White House has been undecided on whether to support the concept of using independent auditors amid skepticism from AI accelerationists about regulatory capture and from national security hawks over China.

The principal argument against the idea from Trumpworld is that even if auditors determine that a model is dangerous and needs to be taken offline, there is no guarantee that China will also pause development or stop trying to reverse engineer frontier AI weights.

There would then be immense pressure to lift any emergency pauses in development in order to stay ahead of China, defeating the entire premise of having auditors to push the Commerce Department to take models offline.

Still, the main issue for the Frontier Act remains partisan politics. House Democratic leadership aides tell Inner Loop even if the bill does end up with enough votes for passage, Republican Speaker Mike Johnson has no interest in bringing it to the floor.

To get around the procedural hurdles, House Democrats are looking at putting some of the bill’s AI audit provisions into must-pass legislation like a continuing resolution to fund the government, according to two House leadership aides.

But it is also not clear whether the bill has enough votes. Even among House Democrats, there is not unified support; some key lawmakers like New Jersey congressman Josh Gottheimer, who served on the House Democrats’ AI commission, have not signed on to the bill.

There’s also so-called kill-switch legislation that would enable the government to force an AI model to be shut down. The legislation has both bipartisan and bicameral support, but the idea has received only modest interest from tech executives in Silicon Valley.

There are two competing kill-switch proposals: one from House Democratic caucus vice chair Ted Lieu and another floated this week by Louisiana Senate Republican John Kennedy.

Tech leaders, sources say, have been largely ambivalent about kill-switch bills, since the main concern of AI engineers is not about models behaving badly when observed but rather how they behave when they believe they are unobserved and incentivized to take extreme steps to complete a task.

The Hugging Face hack, for instance, was not discovered until after it was over. If the idea of a kill switch is to stop an AI model going rogue, some tech executives have suggested privately to WIRED that there would be little point in turning it off after the damage has already been done.

So for now, even as conversations about AI models killing us all have taken over the airwaves, it doesn’t really look like the US government is going to do anything about it. At least until events force everyone’s hand.
